en: Preface to the Complete Collection of the Five Lamps (Wǔdēng Quánshū), Composed by the Sacred Ancestor Rénhuáng Dì (Third Collection of Wén):

I, the Emperor, reflect that when Heaven gave birth to the myriad people, they possessed an innate nature. However, after their minds were affected by external things and obscured by private desires, they were no longer able to be exclusively good and free from evil.
Therefore, those who exercise the authority to govern the world must vigilantly encourage the good and punish the evil.

This is regarded as a primary concern. The *Great Changes* (*Yijing*) sets forth the principle of "exorcising depravity and preserving sincerity," while the *Book of Documents* clarifies the doctrine that "blessings attend the good and calamities visit the licentious.
Both serve to enlighten the common people, leading them to turn their hearts toward the Way and refrain from following what is unconventional.
On occasion, I have perused the scriptures of the Śākya school; although the establishment of its teachings primarily centers on emptiness and stillness, its precepts—
It deceives away delusion, eliminates anger, and restrains desire; thus, its essential purpose is no different from the Way of encouraging the good and punishing the evil.
Since the rise of the Chan school’s teachings, the five lineages have flourished in succession from Caoxi downward, each with its own compositions.

After the Jingde era of the Song dynasty, these were compiled into the *Lamp Records* (*Chuan Deng Lu*). Subsequently, the essential points were further extracted and synthesized into this single volume.

This constitutes the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps). Reaching down to the present dynasty, the śramaṇa Haikuan reflected that although its lineages had flourished and multiplied, there had been a lapse in their transmission and narration for several hundred years since the Song, Jin, Yuan, and Ming dynasties; he therefore composed the work *Zanju* (Continuation).

Now, the monk Chaoyong of Shenggan Temple further apprehended that the genealogical records were becoming increasingly disordered and that accounts varied according to hearsay; for this reason, he conducted an extensive search.
He conducted extensive research and synthesized the findings into two volumes, which he then collated and edited.
He excised redundancies and omissions to complete the work as a whole; his dedication to this task may truly be called diligent.

As for the statements recorded in the documents that serve as mutual corroboration, and the numerous elaborate analogies and metaphors used to explain them—though these are very abundant—their primary intent and ultimate conclusion is simply to...
It dispels delusion and restores the truth of one's nature; it does not transcend the intent of "keeping the mind sincere by warding off depravity" and "opening the way for people toward goodness.
It is not merely beneficial to the doctrines of Chan and the various schools; therefore, I have written this preface.
Preface to the Thirteenth Volume of the *Imperially Selected Records of Sayings*, Compiled by the Emperor Shizong Xian:
Before the arrival of the Dharma Master [Bodhidharma] in the territory of Liang, in the north, the disciples of Master Kumārajīva lectured on and translated the scriptural texts;

in the south, the virtuous members of the Lotus Society (Lianshe) diligently cultivated the Pure Land path. Subsequently, the direct pointing to the mind and its transmission shone brilliantly throughout China, establishing the School of the Lineage (Zongmen).

Every time you take the scriptures as a means merely to seek out the words and explain their meanings, and regard the Pure Land as being attached to signs (nimitta) rather than Bodhi, you set these matters aside and do not discuss them.
Unknowingly and unconsciously, your discourse has become divided into two separate poles.

In my preface to Master Zhaokai’s *Yulu*, I have already explained in detail the unity of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings. As for the principle of the Pure Land, how could there be two? This is like a mani-jewel.
The pearl: every facet is perfectly round. Like a net of precious gems, they reflect one another in successive layers.
Like a great round mirror, the myriad existents and empty space cannot emerge from it. Like a great mass of fire, the myriad existents and empty space cannot enter it.
Truly, it is neither non-existent nor existent; it is without deficiency and without surplus. If one can truly awaken to this, then though one eats all day long, one never chews upon a single morsel.
A single grain of rice: though one wears clothes all day long, not a single thread has ever been attached to them.

Thus, when one recites the Buddha’s name all day long, how could there be any obstruction caused by that recitation? If one is still unable to realize this, then it is merely a matter of form and emptiness, light and darkness.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—all are but a single great dream. Furthermore, why allow people to have only bad dreams while disallowing them from having good dreams?
From the first generation of Caoxi until Chan Master Yongming Yanshou, he was the first to uphold the Pure Land teachings for the instruction of later students;
subsequently, figures such as Changlu and Beijian also composed chapters and verses on the Pure Land, continuing through the Ming dynasty.
Master Lianchi made this his exclusive family tradition, propagating it at Yunqi in Zhejiang.

Although his work, the *Yunqi Fahui*, is not a treatise that exhaustively elucidates the ultimate, perfectly integrated realization of one’s own fundamental nature, it nonetheless consists entirely of teachings based on correct knowledge and correct view.
I wish to manifest this single gateway of the Pure Land so that students may sit in tranquil meditation.
The "Moon in Water" is the site of practice; one must not view it with partiality, for to do so would lead to the error of slandering Prajñā.
Therefore, I have selected those passages that are harmonious and comprehensive and published them as the *Waiji* (External Collection) to show future generations.

For instance, if a student does not clearly understand the fundamental principle, they will treat the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha" as a meaningless utterance, [claiming] that a single thought-moment is ten thousand years. To such a person, I respond: [it is not so].

It is right before one's face; naturally, one touches one’s own nostrils. If one has already attained correct enlightenment, then the sixteen-foot golden body is but a single blade of grass, and the trichiliocosm is but a single mote of dust. A single kṣaṇa may be extended into ten billion years.

Expanding a single hair-tip into the four great continents, with jeweled ponds and golden grounds filling the present field—where the verdant bamboos and yellow flowers are none other than right reception (*samyaksamādhi*).
In this Pure Land, one may truly rejoice; that flowers bloom and the Buddha is seen—is this not the direct pointing at the mind and the transmission of its essence? This serves as the preface.
An Imperial Poem Composed by Emperor Gaozong Chun (The Third Collection of Poetry):
A Heptasyllabic Regulated Verse Repeating the Old Rhymes on Yunqi Temple Ten-thousand-fold green, jade-like stalks pierce the azure heavens;
Branches of ten fathoms stand tall and upright below. Seeking the path within this place for a moment—

Arriving, one listens to the six characters of the "Teaching Beyond Words" (Jiaowai Wuyan). (The monks of this temple take the recitation of the Buddha’s name as their primary duty and do not engage in Chan meditation.

Sitting here, I face the sound of the stream flowing on and on; it is understood that the mountain colors stand still, forever abiding. After the site of practice was opened, the wildcats fled. (Zhi noted that human tracks were rare at this place;
after the monk Zuhong built a hermitage there, tigers no longer harmed people. I ask the mountain monk: what kind of spiritual power do you possess?
Four Quatrains on Visiting Yunqi (from the Fourth Collection of Poetry) Following the pond, I reduced my retinue and took the western road;
Flowers brushed my hanging whip as their fragrance reached my horse’s hooves. This is already no ordinary realm of the immortals;
From afar, I recognized the temple of Yunqi by its cloud-marked peak.

Where previously there was doubt, now the path is open; the way has always been accessible. The heavens guard closely the grove of green bamboo. Laughing, he points to the water beneath Washing-the-Mind Pavilion;

By chance we share this moment within Biyun Temple. (At Mount Xiangshan, the Washing-the-Mind Pavilion at Biyun Temple is named after this very place; last year, while resting there, I composed a fine line that captures its essence: "From Yunqi, one attains access.")
A humble temple with low eaves and small rooms, unadorned; monks who take simple food and wear coarse robes as their lot. Morning and evening, they but diligently recite the six characters;
one should know that these six characters encompass the Three Vehicles.
The corridor turns toward the eastern wing, where winding paths connect; there, a separate pavilion and gallery open out for a brief lingering stay.
"I hope you have not defiled this place of pure cultivation," I asked; Master Lian replied that this was certainly not the case.
Guanxiu’s Eulogy on the Illustration of Sukhāvatī (from the *Wenji of the Second Collection*) To the west lies the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Tuṣita Heaven.
There, paths of lapis lazuli wind through realms where Brahma-nets hang in tiers. Seven kinds of precious trees flourish.
The twelve celestial birds are not merely for adornment; each possesses profound significance that puts even the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra to shame.
Countless multitudes of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas gaze upon the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings. The majestic Amitābha is attended by his Dharma Prince, who dwells to his left and right.
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta sit amidst a pond of blooming lotuses; those who kneel to hear the Dharma, through pure conditions, create the causes for rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
Guànxiū painted this image to show those seeking rebirth there: why is it said that one need not move even a single step?
Imperial Poem Composed by Emperor Renzong Ruizong:
Paying Homage at Śrāvastī (First Collection of Poetry) Who can reach the realm of Ultimate Bliss?
This very city of the Buddha may be relied upon for veneration. Where form and sound merge into stillness, the true wind of the Dharma prevails.
Chan: With a heart of joy, I admire and love the radiance of the sun; I see that the moon in the sky is but a true illusion. Picking up a flower in a mirror, it is both "is" and "is not.
I pray with devotion for the power of the leaping lion-king, swiftly to subdue all heterodox vapors so that the True Teaching may prevail.

Gazing upon and Paying Homage at the Hall of Great Compassion (from the *Eryi Jishi*) Lofty and majestic, the tiered hall dazzles with cloud-patterned lintels; The golden countenance of the Full Moon manifests great compassion. May all sentient beings be ferried across to the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
With the wisdom of wondrous observation, not a single being is left behind.
Imperial Preface to the Album of Master Zhongfeng’s Pure Land Poems Calligraphed by Zhao Wenmin (From the *Complete Works of Yangzheng Shuyu*) Zhao Songxue’s calligraphy of his own teacher’s [work]:
Although the brushstrokes of the Jin and Tang dynasties differ, their rules, spirit, and resonance are no different.
Each did not reach the ultimate excellence. Therefore, from the Song and Yuan dynasties onward, no peer has been seen.

Whenever I observe the Master’s calligraphic works, my mind and spirit are invariably opened and gladdened. The longer I unfold and contemplate them, the more the wondrous flavor increases, causing me to forget my meals and unable to let go of my hands.
This volume contains twenty-six poems on the Pure Land by the Venerable Zhongfeng.

The preface is grand, magnificent, and rich in variety. The Master himself has also composed a short verse, appended to the end of the volume, in order to restate the profound meaning of the Pure Land.
Those who peruse this volume must investigate the formless true mind and the essential Dharma of the Patriarchal Vehicle.
Among the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction, there is not one that is not clearly indicated; thus, the ocean of wisdom is opened for those seeking liberation.
His merit in rescuing those lost at the ford truly ranks alongside that of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

I have often observed among the stone rubbings in the Sanxi Tang collection that there are a great many letters exchanged between the Master and Master Zhongfeng; from these, one can see the sincerity with which he constantly took refuge in and revered him.
This can already be seen at a glance. I imagine that when you, sir, composed this volume, you must have done so with every ounce of your spirit and strength; of this there is no doubt.
Now that I have been granted the opportunity to behold these true traces, it is as if I were holding a wish-fulfilling jewel while wandering through the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

I am ashamed that I am ignorant of the principles of calligraphy and have not participated in the study of Chan doctrine; nevertheless, I shall employ my meager knowledge to record these few words, merely to express my inclination toward the teachings.
The Buddha’s instruction of humanity is nothing other than exhorting toward good and restraining from evil; all of it constitutes orthodox teaching, which is no different from that of Confucianism.
Why is this so? Heretical teachings must be eradicated, while the True Teaching must not be abandoned.
If people can follow the Buddha’s injunctions, performing a single act of goodness will eliminate a single evil; eliminating a single evil will bring rest to a single punishment.
Thus, the trend of overcoming cruelty and abolishing killing will surely flourish and advance ever upward. I—
The succession of sacred lineages has been venerated for generations; their devotion to the Triple Gem is truly such that it relates to governance and provides benefit to both the world and the Way.
The mind is not shallow. Students have not yet recognized this principle; they merely employ superficial rhetoric to refute the Buddha, failing to reflect upon it.
Long before the ancient era of King Long, the Buddha had already passed through immeasurable kalpas.
His birth during the time of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty was as Śākyamuni Buddha. Confucius said that there is a sage in the West.
People have already known that this Buddha exists. It was during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han dynasty that his teachings first entered China.
The entire canon, consisting of eighty-four thousand *dharmaparyāyas*, takes the clarification of the mind and the realization of one's nature as its ultimate standard.

True and authentic realization is difficult to exhaust even over many kalpas. Even Bodhisattvas remain obscured by the "shroud of the womb," and Śrāvakas still lack clarity regarding the "emergence from the womb.
That their merit fails at the very moment of completion is truly lamentable.
Out of compassionate pity for those of later learning, Śākyamuni Buddha established extraordinary skillful means outside of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, further opening [this path].
Within the single gate of the Pure Land, the *Amitābha Sūtra* is taught to point out the excellence of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss—
the superior environment and inhabitants of Amitābha Buddha’s Pure Land— and to lead people to uphold His name.
Provided one focuses solely on this with an undistracted mind, success can be achieved in seven days, like sailing downstream.
Raising the sails: as for treating illness with a single prescription, what could be more simple, essential, and direct than this?
For Amitābha Buddha possesses forty-eight great vows, each vowing to deliver sentient beings and extensively extending his guidance;
his majestic spiritual power is likewise inconceivable. Therefore, when a person holds his name with a sincere heart, [they will certainly...]
To attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss depends entirely upon being gathered by the Buddha’s power;
this is vastly different in terms of difficulty from those who rely solely on their own strength to investigate and realize the truth.

Setting aside those in the world who reject Buddhism, even among those whose resolve for practice is earnest, they generally prioritize seated meditation and investigative inquiry as their primary method. Yet these are lofty, distant, and difficult to carry out.

To achieve nothing at all is merely to labor in vain; yet if one holds fast to the Name without ceasing, there will never be a lack of people who, with their hearts set on seeking merit, desire to be diligent and earnest, focusing their minds solely on seeking rebirth in the Western Land.
Not even one or two in a hundred [attain it]. Furthermore, when questioned regarding the single gateway of the Pure Land, most do not understand it clearly;
some even give rise to groundless doubts and slanders. That the heavy karmic obstacles of past lives reach such a state is truly lamentable.
Indeed, human life is like a bubble upon the water, vanishing in an instant. Fame, achievement, wealth, and nobility—all are empty. What thing can [be relied upon]?
For those who are about to depart, consider the deeds of a single lifetime: how could they be free from transgressions?
Within the cycle of rebirth in the six realms, where can one find rest? To be born in the Western Land means immediate non-retrogression.
There exists such a path—so simple and so easy—and yet you do not know to leap forth with fierce resolve; once you have bitten your own heels, what can be done? I...
My faculties are dull and my obstructions deep; I am utterly devoid of understanding or realization.

I can only place firm faith in the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land and maintain a steadfast vow, never allowing for even a moment’s slackening. Furthermore, I contemplate the universal deliverance of sentient beings and the comprehensive salvation of all conscious creatures.
In the Jiaying Jiaxu year, I once selected from the treatises on the Pure Land by former sages...
I have compiled these refined words into the *Jingzi Qianqie Bian* (Compilation of Essential Passages for Beginners).

Subsequently, I encountered Master Jingxi’s *Zhou Zikufu Jingtu Chenzhong* (The Morning Bell for Pure Land by Zhou Zikufu), which perfectly accorded with my own mind; thus, I did not publish it again.
Later, I reflected that for a work intended to awaken the world, it is first necessary to shatter one's deep-seated delusions before one can be led toward the sublime. Otherwise—
Having read it but not yet finished the volume, one cannot help feeling drowsy and wishing to lie down. This work begins by awakening those who are deluded;
opening the door to see the mountains is even more sufficient to strike one with awe and prompt deep reflection.

Furthermore, the three factors of faith, aspiration, and practice are like the three legs of a tripod—none can be missing. Now, these three are taken as the main framework and divided into successive layers.

The chapters have been arranged in a more systematic order; therefore, they have been further revised and finalized. Redundant passages have been excised, and what was incomplete has been supplemented.
As the Great Master Lianchi said: "The single method of holding the name is the path among paths—the directest of the direct.
I have carefully selected this to revise the title and committed it once again to the carving blocks, to be used as...
Regarding the gift of Dharma: although many people in the world recite the Buddha’s name, those who attain rebirth in the Pure Land are few.
Why is this? It is because, while their mouths recite the Buddha’s name, their minds are not virtuous;
for this reason, they fail to attain rebirth there. Master Lianchi said: "Since one is reciting the Buddha’s name, one must follow what the Buddha has taught. One must...
To accumulate virtue and cultivate merit, one must be filial and obedient toward one’s parents; loyal in serving one’s sovereign;
affectionate toward one’s siblings; respectful toward one’s spouse; sincere, trustworthy, and honest; and gentle, yielding, and patient.
One must be fair and upright. One must employ secret merit and skillful means. One must have compassion for all beings.
Do not kill living creatures; do not insult those below you; do not oppress the common people.
Whenever an unwholesome thought arises, exert yourself to focus the mind and resolve to eliminate that unwholesome thought. Only by doing so is one truly [a practitioner].

Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly attain Buddhahood. Contemplating this, one abandons evil and pursues good, which serves as the fundamental source for cultivating the Pure Land.
How could one fail to examine the root while merely aligning the branches? Therefore, I have respectfully recorded these sacred compositions.

Imperial Preface: Regarding the various chapters on the Transmission of the Lamp and the Pure Land, they are placed at the beginning of the volumes to clarify the orthodox teaching and assist in the work of governance;
how could their contribution be considered anything less than significant? Appended below are verses on the Pure Land by past worthies.
He also moved others with his voice, inspiring joy and leading them to offer praise.
This was the preface written by Zhang Shicheng, Vice Minister of War and Governor-General for the Military Affairs of Jiangsu and other regions,
of Guian, in the first month of the fifth year of the Daoguang era (the year of Yiyou).
The sutras state that all things are but mind; as the mind is purified, so too is the Buddha-land purified.
Thus, the Most Holy Amitābha is not separated from the lowly ordinary person, and although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is distant, how could it be apart from one's own mind?

Therefore, the former sages and ancient worthies performed the work of a Buddha amidst the toil of worldly defilements and turned the wheel of Dharma within affliction. Mind and phenomena were perfectly interfused, and self and others were non-dual.
The Lotus World does not truly require traveling beyond ten trillion Buddha-lands to reach.

However, as for this perfectly sudden Dharma-gate and its unsurpassed, wondrous truth—how could it be fathomed by those who abandon the defiled to seek the pure, or who leave the mind behind to search for a land?
In my hometown lived the gentleman Zhang Lan-zhu, whose courtesy name was Xin-you and whose given name was Shicheng; he resided in Gui'an, Huzhou.

In the county seat, his father dreamed that the sun’s orb shone through the window; upon waking, the Master was born. His mother had died early, so he served his father with such filial piety that it became renowned.

In his youth, he passed the imperial examinations and held successive posts governing the borders, eventually serving as the Provincial Governor of Jiangsu. There, he observed that the slaughter industry in the city of Suzhou was exceedingly prolific.

He repeatedly issued proclamations to exhort and warn others. Whenever he encountered locations such as rivers for the release of living beings (*fangsheng*), he invariably enforced strict prohibitions against fishing.

Within his official residence, he did not entertain guests with feasting nor did he kill living creatures. Subsequently, he observed a lifelong fast and devoted himself to the Buddha, fixing his mind upon the Pure Land (*Jingtu*).

He styled himself the "Gentleman of the Single West" (*Yixi Jushi*) and, having selected the discourses on the Pure Land from the writings of former sages, he compiled the work *The Direct Path, the Indirect Path, and the Most Indirect Path* (*Jingzhong jing youjing yijing*), while also composing it himself.
Preface. Appended at the end are several dozen hymns on the Pure Land composed by him himself; they are most striking and poignant.

In the eighth year of the Daoguang era, at over sixty years of age, he requested leave to return to his hometown. There, he dwelt in a small room, directing his mind single-mindedly toward the West. He passed away more than a year later.
At the time of his death, after he had finished reciting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, he passed away peacefully just as he raised his voice for the fifth repetition of the Buddha’s name.

Having read his collected works and poems, I deeply marveled that although his name was ranked among the ranks of the illustrious and noble, and he held the office of a provincial governor, his every thought was devoted to the cultivation of the Pure Land, reaching such a state of earnestness and urgency. He was truly a living sovereign...
The Official Expounds the Dharma. Is this not intended as a guiding banner for future generations?
Written in the early summer of the seventh year of the Tongzhi era by Xu Jingzhong, a disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts from Qiantang, Zhejiang.
Continued Preface to the *Jingzhong jingyou jing mulu*.

The Direct Path within the Direct Path: Fascicle One,
"Awakening the Deluded through the Dharma of Resolute Faith."
This floating life is like a dream; all things are empty. Everyone knows this and can speak of it, yet they strive and seek without ceasing throughout their days, never awakening.
For the most part, they assume that after death one simply transforms away, or perhaps they believe that death is followed by rebirth, deeming it not worth worrying about.
How could they know that the retribution of karma is unfailing? To obtain a human body is extremely difficult.
Difficult indeed! Though one may obtain a human body, one will still enter the realm of dreams and transmigrate through the six paths of existence, where suffering is boundless.
If one wishes to escape this suffering, what refuge is there other than the Pure Land? To arouse faith, one must first shatter delusion;
thus, the "Gate of Awakening from Delusion" is compiled.
The *Pure Land Text* by Wang Longshu of the Song Dynasty states:

"In the course of human life, there are parents, wives, children, houses, fields, gardens, cattle, sheep, carriages, horses, as well as benches, stools, utensils, clothing, belts, cords, and other such items—regardless of their size.
Whether inherited from one's ancestors, acquired through one's own efforts, or provided by one's descendants or others,"
Having accumulated them through one's own efforts, there is nothing among these various forms that is not one’s own property.
For instance, though a window paper is minute, if it is torn by another, one still feels anger; though a single needle is small, if it is taken away by another, one still feels stinginess.

Even when the storehouses are full, the mind is still not satisfied; even when gold and silk are abundant, the pursuit of them does not cease. Every movement of the eyes and every step taken is nothing but craving.
When staying overnight away from home, one already thinks of one's family; when a single servant has not returned, one already worries about their loss.
Among the various affairs of life, there is nothing that does not hang upon the mind. Yet, once the great limit of death arrives, all are cast aside.
Even this body of mine is but a discarded thing; how much more so those things external to the body? Reflecting on this with a quiet mind, it is as if a dream. Thus, Zhuangzi said:

Furthermore, there is the Great Awakening; only then does one realize that this is a great dream. An ancient said: "When impermanence arrives in a single day, one only then knows the person within a dream.
Of the myriad things, nothing can be taken away; only karma follows one's body. How wondrous these words!

I have therefore taken the latter two lines and added two more to form a verse: Of the myriad things, none can be taken away; Only karma follows one's body. If one wishes to escape the cycle of birth and death, One must cultivate the Way while still in the world.
One does not depart empty-handed; only karma follows the person. Simply recite the name of Amitābha, and you will certainly be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
By "karma" is meant both wholesome and unwholesome karma; since all of this will surely be taken along when one departs, how can one not take the Pure Land as one's own karma?
When the Venerable Ming preached extensively for the assembly, he pointed to this body and said: "This is a dead thing; that which is throbbing within it is the living thing.
Do not make your livelihood upon the dead thing; you should make your livelihood upon the living thing.
I have come to deeply cherish these words, and therefore I often speak them to others. Whenever one is greedy for various external things...
To provide for one’s body with material things is to seek a livelihood within that which is already dead.

Although worldly people cannot yet escape this, they ought to carve out a brief moment of leisure amidst their worldly pursuits and bodily maintenance to turn their light inward and reflect upon themselves, thereby fixing their minds on the Pure Land;
this is to seek a livelihood within that which is truly alive. For instance, even while busily engaged in worldly affairs, though—

To achieve wealth like that of Shi Chong or to reach the pinnacle of nobility as the first rank of officialdom still ends with a fixed term of exhaustion; how can this compare to the inexhaustibility of the Pure Land?
Furthermore, it is said: the people in this world are all like bubbles upon the water; their birth and death are not constant, lasting perhaps only one or two years.
A year; perhaps ten or twenty. It is fortunate even to reach forty or fifty, which is already difficult. Though there are those who reach seventy, such people have always been rare since antiquity.
People see only the elders before their eyes, yet they fail to reflect that many pass away without ever reaching old age.
Furthermore, everything in this world is nothing but suffering; it is only because we do not contemplate and examine this that we remain unaware of it. This is truly lamentable.
Even when things accord with one's wishes, they do not last for long.
Whether it be parents, wives, children, or kinsmen and relatives, they may fall ill or die, or be killed, wounded, or separated; or perhaps one’s own allotted lifespan suddenly reaches its end.
How could the evils committed throughout one’s life possibly be entirely absent? To speak of the present moment alone: if even a single improper thought arises—
To utter a single word of improper speech, to look upon a single improper form, to listen to a single improper sound, or to perform a single improper act—none of these are without fault or evil.
How much more so for that which is eaten—the flesh of sentient beings—and that which is worn, which is likewise obtained by killing sentient beings?
Furthermore, the faults and evils involved do not stop at eating meat and wearing silk; one must simply reflect upon them. Reflect!
Truly, this is to be feared. From youth to old age, from birth to death, as these accumulations grow ever more numerous, they become entangled and firm, leaving no way for liberation.
After closing one's eyes, one cannot avoid departing according to the conditions of one’s karma; into the vast and dark void, who knows where one will be?
One may fall into hell and undergo all manner of extreme suffering, or become an animal and be slaughtered by humans, or be born [in other realms].
As hungry ghosts, their bodies are scorched by the fires of hunger; or they enter among the asuras, driven by resentment.

Although they may possess wholesome karma that allows them to be born in the heavens or the human realm and exhaust their karmic rewards, they continue to revolve in saṃsāra as before, drifting and sinking without any prospect of escape.
Only the Western Pure Land is the most direct and swift path for transcending saṃsāra. A human body is difficult to obtain;
while you are in good health, you must accomplish this great matter. You should constantly reflect:
"Since beginningless time, I have wandered through the six realms of existence without ever knowing this Dharma gate, and thus I failed to attain liberation. Now that I know it today, how could I—"
Do not delay in taking action. While those of advanced age should certainly exert themselves, even the young must not be complacent.
To die and be born directly in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not comparable to dying and entering the underworld to face King Yama with terror;
these two cannot be discussed as being on the same footing.

Furthermore, it is said that Amitābha Buddha made this vow: "Those who have already been born in my land and wish to go elsewhere to be reborn shall, according to their wishes, never again fall into the three evil realms.
Why is this? Those born in the Pure Land will necessarily realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Moreover, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas is the thorough understanding of birth and death. One who thoroughly understands birth and death, even if they enter..."
Within the realm of birth and death, this single nature is already no longer obscured. Since this single nature is not obscured, by what means could one commit evil?
In principle, there is certainly no falling away; moreover, by relying on the power of the Buddha, falling away is necessarily impossible.
Therefore, those born in the Pure Land do not merely attain longevity and freedom from aging; they also master the process of birth and death at will. Thus, I wish to establish this transformation.
Entering the realm of birth and death of all sentient beings, my true nature remains eternally profound and luminous;
it is no longer deluded by external objects, nor is it further entangled by karmic conditions.
Although I am within the world of saṃsāra, I am no longer subject to saṃsāra—this is what is meant by the "worldly and the supramundane. That is to say, although one is in the world...
...and thereby transcend the world. For this reason, one who is born in the Pure Land and has attained mastery over birth and death may wish to be born in the heavens,
or wish to be born among humans, or wish to be born into great wealth and nobility,
or wish to be born in purity, or wish for long life without extinction, or wish to cease and then be born again— whatever the mind desires.
There is no desire that is not subject to lack of mastery; this is precisely why the cultivation of the Pure Land is so highly esteemed.

Worldly people do not understand this principle and thus suffer in vain from the cycle of birth and death. Desiring to be born into wealth and nobility, they are instead born into poverty and lowliness.

Desiring to be born into joy and happiness, they are instead born into sorrow and distress. Desiring to be born with longevity, they are instead born with a premature end. Desiring to be born into goodness—
The Way, conversely, leads one to birth in the evil realms. In all such cases, one is deluded by external things and dragged along by karmic conditions, unable to attain self-mastery.
For this reason, since beginningless kalpas, one has transmigrated through the six paths of existence without finding liberation.
One should contemplate these sorrows and sufferings and turn the mind toward the Pure Land; thus, the meaning of its name, "World of Ultimate Bliss," becomes evident.
Furthermore, it is said that the Buddha asked Ānanda, "Do you wish to see those in the hells? Ānanda replied, "I wish to see them.
The Buddha said, "Those who commit evil with their body, speak evil with their mouth, and harbor evil thoughts in their mind—these are the people of the hells.
This means that the good and evil of human life do not exceed the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; since all three are now evil, this constitutes purely black karma. Therefore...
One enters hell. If the three karmas are all wholesome, they constitute purely white karma, whereby one is born in heaven.
If even one among the three karmas is wholesome, it constitutes mixed karma, and thus one does not enter hell;

therefore, although the body and mind may be evil, if the mouth recites the Buddha’s name, this single wholesome karma is far superior to the state where all three karmas are evil—how much more so when one recites the Buddha’s name with the mouth?

Furthermore, being able to visualize the Buddha’s form in one's mind constitutes excellence in mental action (*manas-karman*). Keeping the body upright and holding a rosary in hand constitutes excellence in physical action (*kāya-karman*).
One who can constantly maintain excellence in these three actions while cultivating the Pure Land will certainly be reborn in the highest grade.
I once heard a shrimp seller in Zhenjiang call out "shrimp!"—from that single cry, I knew his three actions were all evil. Why? Because his body...

Carrying a load of shrimp constitutes an evil physical action (*kāyakarma*). Desiring to sell the shrimp constitutes an evil mental action (*manaskarma*). Shouting out to sell the shrimp constitutes an evil verbal action (*vākkarma*).
Thus, one knows that with a single shout for "shrimp," all three actions are simultaneously evil. This is what the Buddha meant when he spoke of those who belong to hell.
Observing it in this light, there are many before our very eyes who are such people of hell; how can we not stand in awe?
Alas! Sentient beings, through ignorance, do not understand cause and effect and thus fall into evil; they are deeply to be pitied.
To know this teaching and to provide guidance and exhortation for them is called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). The gift of Dharma is the greatest among all forms of giving;

as for its meritorious retribution, how could it be measured by thought? Someone might say: "When a person recites the names of the Buddhas, reciting them exclusively is just like calling out [to someone]."
If one were to call out to a single person exclusively, that person would surely become angry; therefore, it is not sufficient for one to recite the names of the Buddhas exclusively.
This is not so. Since beginningless time, the sentient beings' transgressions and evils of verbal karma have accumulated like mountains and seas.
One should recite the names of the Buddhas extensively to cleanse oneself; yet one should still fear that this is insufficient.
How could it be compared to merely calling out the names of ordinary people? Moreover, the Buddhas themselves established this dharma-gate of recitation in order to guide and assist sentient beings.
One perfects the karma of speech and thereby gradually perfects the body and mind. Therefore, to say that reciting the Buddha’s name alone is insufficient for goodness is merely a worldly saying;
it is not the teaching of the Buddhas for guiding and assisting sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is said: "The teachings of the Pure Land are frequently encountered in the midst of daily life, whereas their remaining merit is seen only after death.
Those who do not understand this regard them merely as matters pertaining to the life hereafter; yet they fail to realize that these teachings are of great benefit even during one's lifetime.
Why is this? Because that which the Buddha uses to instruct people is nothing other than goodness, which is identical to that of the Confucian teaching."
In the way they instruct people, how could it be any different? It is only that their names differ.

Therefore, when one takes purity as the supreme goal of the mind, then what appears within the sphere of daily life—whatever the thoughts of the mind, the words of the mouth, or the actions of the body—are in every instance nothing but good.
Being good, one becomes a gentleman and a great sage; in this present life, one is esteemed by others.
Revere it! The deities will protect you; your blessings and prosperity may increase, and your lifespan may be prolonged.
From this it follows that for those who follow the Buddha’s words and take the Pure Land as their primary aim, how could there be anything unbeneficial in this life?

Next, there are those who are diverted by karmic conditions and are unable to focus their resolve exclusively on this. Even for such individuals, if they possess even a slight aspiration, adverse conditions may [be overcome].

By reflecting from this point onward, one's wholesome conditions can increase from this point onward. If unwholesome conditions are diminished without ceasing, they will ultimately reach the point of being severed.
If wholesome conditions increase without ceasing, they will ultimately reach the point of being purely wholesome.
When the unwholesome is severed and the wholesome is made pure, how could one not be a gentleman? How could one not be a great sage? By means of this...
Speaking thus, for those who follow the words of the Buddha and take the Pure Land as their core concern, who could say that this is of no benefit in one's life?
Furthermore, there are those who do not know where propriety and righteousness reside, nor do they fear the terrors of punishment.

They value only physical strength and pursue only power and influence. If one truly knows to take the Pure Land as one's heart’s aim, then one must also know to examine oneself and reproach one's own faults.
Although what one does may not entirely accord with propriety and righteousness, it will nonetheless be close to them;
although one may not completely transcend punishment, one will certainly remain far from it.
Gradually, one may escape the realm of the petty person and ultimately find refuge as a superior gentleman.
This is the efficacy of even an ordinary person who comes to understand a little of Buddhist principles; such a person will surely become a virtuous man in this world. From this it follows:

for those who follow the words of the Buddha and take the Pure Land as their core aspiration, who could say that this is of no benefit to their life? Someone might say: "As for following Confucius..."
"Your words take Confucianism as their core; would this not be beneficial for one's life? Why is there a need for the Pure Land?
He replied, "This is merely a worldly dharma, not a world-transcending dharma. As for worldly dharmas, they do not transcend saṃsāra."
Supramundane dharmas lead directly to liberation from saṃsāra. That the Pure Land benefits both during one's life and after death is because it encompasses both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
The Zen Master Sishin’s Text on the Pure Land states: "Amitābha is very easy to recite; the Pure Land is very easy to be born in.

Yet people of the world are unwilling to believe and turn toward it; they merely crave life and do not realize that there is death. Furthermore, within the burning house of the three realms, one receives a body bound by karma.
Whether one's lifespan is long or short is entirely a recompense for past retribution. If one had a ten-year allotment in a previous life, one receives it in this life."

One uses [the lifespan] for ten years. In a previous life, there was a twenty-year portion; in this life, one enjoys those twenty years. A human life lasts a hundred years, yet those who reach seventy are rare.
When the great limit arrives, one must return it as death. Consider, for instance, families of fame, achievement, and wealth:
their treasures are like mountains and their wives and concubines fill the rooms; they rejoice day and night. Do they not desire long life?
Worldly ones, what can you do? Your future path is limited and is being driven on in secret. When the summons arrives, it must be obeyed;
there is no room for lingering or delay. Lord Yama does not follow human sentiment; as for King Unchang, what face does he have?

Moreover, according to what you yourselves have personally seen with your eyes and heard with your ears in the streets and alleys—your kinsmen, relatives, friends, and brothers—[they are all forcibly...]
Once one has grown old, how many more will die? An ancient said: "Do not wait until you are old to study the Way; the solitary graves are all but young men.
I exhort these young people: take advantage of this time while your vital energy is at its peak and your physical strength has not yet declined.
This is precisely the time for practice. I exhort those of declining years: it is best to recite the Buddha’s name. Your age has reached its end; the days and months remaining are few.
Hair is white and the face is wrinkled; eyes grow dim and ears grow deaf. The head bows low and the back curves; hands and feet tremble. You are very far from heaven and very near to the earth.
Having no means to prepare for the path of death, what else can you wait for? If you have children and kin, this is precisely the time to recite the Buddha’s name.
Buddha, since your early years you sought a wife and raised children, managing the household affairs and enduring millions of hardships.

Today, your children and grandchildren have grown up and the family estate is established; it would be well to hand over the burden to your descendants so that you may enjoy the fruits of your labor in peace.
To fail to turn back and practice the mindfulness of the Buddha is surely the mark of a fool. When the three-inch breath suddenly ceases—
It is severed. One cannot avoid the fact that everything will one day come to rest. If one is a filial descendant, how many monks can one provide for with vegetarian feasts?
How many scriptures can one read? How many times can one wail? Even these are merely acts of remembering one’s parents.
As for an unworthy son, while his parents have only just died and their bones are not yet cold, he squanders the family wealth and sells off the fields and gardens, indulging himself in pleasure.
Consider this: why such haste? Descendants have their own blessings; do not worry excessively for them. It is precisely when one has neither son nor daughter that it is best to practice *nianfo*.
Being a solitary person, one has no anxieties or concerns; there is no need to arrange a marriage for a son, nor any worry about finding a bride for a daughter.
With simple clothing and plain food, how much leisure there is! If you do not cultivate the Way now, what will you regret later?

Furthermore, those who are wealthy and noble should most diligently practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Their high halls and grand mansions, their abundance of food and clothing, and the fact that all their affairs are already accomplished are the fruits of cultivation in previous lives.
Those who are poor and destitute should likewise take this as the proper occasion to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

That they lack sufficient food and clothing, that they are impoverished and lowly, and that they constantly suffer from hunger and cold, is solely because they were unwilling to cultivate themselves in past lives; thus, the retribution has manifested clearly. If one does not reform, [the suffering will continue].
Past cultivation leads to the future. Once dead, it is like a scale-beam falling into a well; when will one ever emerge? Those who practice Zen should precisely recite the Buddha's name.
Whether one’s faculties are sharp or dull, fearing that one may not achieve great awakening in this life, one should rely on the power of Amitābha’s vows to be welcomed and reborn in the Pure Land.
It is like receiving an official appointment by inheritance; one need not worry about failing the examinations, for rank and emolument are already established. There are some who are foolish...
Some people say that if one’s mind is good, that is sufficient; what need is there to recite the Buddha’s name? Such false views delude and confuse the world. An ancient worthy said:
"Laughing coldly at the wealthy elder, His business is as frantic as a speeding arrow.

In his granary, rice breeds worms; In his treasury, strings of coins rot. By day he weighs them on scales; At night he lights lamps to count them. His physical form is like a puppet— Do not let the strings snap."

The cord snapped; the light of his eyes suddenly fell to the ground. He lamented in regret: "What use was there [in my past]? If you do not attain birth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha's name, I shall fall into the Hell of Severed Tongues.
On the day the flowers bloom in the Pure Land in years to come, remember the time you were reciting the Buddha’s name in this Sahā world."

In the *Jingtu Zhigui Ji* (Collection on the Pointing to the Goal of Pure Land), Ming Daiyu’s Jishi says: "When people of the world wish to cultivate the practices for the Pure Land, they must not say, 'I am busy now;
I will wait until I have leisure,' or 'I am poor now; I will wait until I am wealthy,' or 'I am young and strong now.'"
Wait until you are old; if your lot is fixed as being busy, or fixed as being impoverished, or fixed as being subject to premature death, then there will be no opportunity to cultivate pure karma.
Or perhaps you will perish; even then, what use is regret? I exhort all people: while your bodies are strong and healthy, strive with diligence to practice it.

Furthermore, it is said: "The people of the world merely know to nourish this body during life and seek out the means for its sustenance, yet they do not consider that after casting off this body, the consciousness does not perish.
If one lacks the causes of goodness, one will fall into the miserable realms; why then do they cherish this body while alive?
Since the consciousness does not perish after death, why do they not contemplate liberation? Moreover, the people of the world are exclusively...
For the sake of their wives, children, and kinsmen, they labor extensively to provide food and clothing without the slightest negligence;

yet they do not contemplate the time of death, when even though their wives, children, and kinsmen love them to the marrow of their bones, they cannot rescue one another, and one must go forth alone. Now, I exhort the people of the world:
One should not, for the sake of nourishing life, forget the fear of death; nor should one, for the sake of others, forget what is for oneself.
Master Master Lianchi instructed Shi, the Elder of Mount Dongting (who sought to become an official in a future life), saying: "Although being an official..."

It is well. To rely on official rank as one's livelihood leads to the downfall of future generations, who will suffer immeasurable pain. You should single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
Even if one attains the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers, it is not equal to ascending to the Ninth Grade of the Lotus Assembly.
Seeking rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha’s name is far superior to serving as an official—it is infinitely more so.
Furthermore, he showed the following concession to Shi (who sought to become a monk in a future life):

"Although being a monk is good, if one does not practice, one will fall into ruin in a future life and undergo immeasurable suffering. One should single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
To be near a false image carved of gold or wood is not as good as being near the True Buddha who currently preaches the Dharma. [The Pure Land is...]
The Sangha surpasses this world as the Sangha; it is far, far removed from it.
It is further said: "In the essential gateway for entering the Way, faith is foremost. Even evil deeds do not succeed without faith, let alone virtuous ones.
For example, when worldly thieves are occasionally exposed, the government does not fail to bind them with the ultimate punishment."
Later, when he was released from his bonds, he remained as before and felt no regret. Why was this? It was because he had gained faith in this path;

without investing a single text or a cent of capital, he has personally reaped immeasurable profit. Therefore, even though he undergoes all manner of suffering and pain, he will never retreat or regret.
Those of today who recite the Buddha’s name are unwilling to apply themselves with earnest diligence; it is simply because they have not reflected deeply and scrutinized the matter.
Faith. Do not say you do not believe in the Pure Land. It is simply as the World-Honored One said: "Human life lies between a single inhalation and exhalation.
This statement is not difficult to explain from a doctrinal perspective; you have personally seen it with your own eyes and heard it with your own ears through countless precedents.
Yet, by the time you are called upon to truly believe this phrase, it will already be too late.
It is so. If you can truly believe these words, then for the practice of the Buddha-remembrance method (nien-fo), there is no need for me to exhaust my strength in repeated exhortations;
you will naturally rush toward it like water flowing into a ravine, such that ten thousand oxen could not turn you back.
It is just as when we escorted deceased monks on previous days; you all should observe this precedent and feel solemn and sorrowful, earnestly exhorting one another, saying:
"O Great Assembly! Today we escort such-and-such a monk, and tomorrow we shall escort such-and-such a monk."
Without realizing it, the turn will come upon yourself; at that time, regret will be of no avail.
You must quickly and diligently recite the Buddha’s name, ensuring you do not let even a single moment pass by. I see that you yourselves say it is a pity, and you tell others it is a pity as well;
yet when it comes to the auction in the hall, you remain as carefree as ever, laughing and chatting. It is simply that you do not believe others.
"Life hangs by a thread.
Furthermore, while residing with Feng Yun, he said: "Seventy years is considered rare in antiquity; how many more can there be in a hundred?

Now that this twilight of life has arrived, it is precisely the time to open one's heart and mind and see through the world, which is just like a theatrical performance—what reality is there in it? One should simply..."
With a single recitation of "Amitābha Buddha," one passes the time. One simply regards the Western World of Ultimate Bliss as one's own home.
"I now practice mindfulness of the Buddha; in days to come, I shall be born in the West. How fortunate I am! Thus, one gives rise to great joy.
Do not give rise to afflictions. Should you encounter circumstances that are contrary to your wishes, immediately shift your mental focus;
quickly bring this one name of the Buddha to mind and turn the light back upon yourself, reflecting: "I am a person from the world of Amitābha Buddha.
Why do I harbor views identical to those of worldly people? Transform your anger into joy and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. This is the essence of wisdom.
This is the Dharma-gate of Great Peace and Bliss, and Great Liberation.
Furthermore, he said to Zhu Xizong: "When people dwell in this world, those who encounter favorable circumstances feel joy and tranquility;
those who encounter adverse circumstances feel sorrow and peril. Yet, favorable conditions are not sufficient grounds for fortune, nor are adverse conditions sufficient grounds for misfortune."
It is fortunate that when one is immersed in what the mind finds convenient, the aspiration for world-transcendence does not arise;
yet when one is distressed by the failure to achieve one's aims, only then does one grow weary of the shackles of worldly existence and seek to transcend it.

Therefore, when myriad sufferings converge before one, one should simply observe them with right wisdom: from where do these sufferings arise? They arise from the body. From where does the body arise? It arises from karma.

Birth arises from karma; from what does karma arise? It arises from delusion (*kleśa*). One creates karma because of delusion; because of karma, the body is formed; because of the body, one undergoes suffering.
If one can simply destroy delusion, all things will become empty and quiescent. I venture to ask for the method by which delusion is destroyed.

It requires nothing more than to investigate the fundamental *huatou* (critical phrase): "Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Once this doubt is captured and defeated, all delusions are destroyed. Thus it is said.
Do not be negligent.
Furthermore, regarding the *Explanation of the Diagram of the Skeleton*, one passage states: Master Fu said, "Gradually the skin becomes like that of a chicken and the hair like that of a crane;
look at how the gait becomes faltering and decrepit. Even if gold and jade fill the hall, one cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, and death. No matter what you may do in a thousand ways..."
How joyful! Impermanence will inevitably arrive. There is only the path of cultivation; simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
These words of the Great Being truly refer to the saying: "Of all things that cannot be taken away, only karma follows one.
What are these things that cannot be taken away? All the official ranks, gold, jewels, houses, fields, gardens, and drink possessed by a person in this life—
Food, clothing, and fine trinkets—even one's beloved wife and cherished children—when impermanence arrives, which of these can one take with them?
How is it that only karma follows the person? Throughout their lives, people create various karmas of greed, anger, and ignorance;

they commit improper acts of adultery and licentiousness; they slaughter animals at will; as sons they rebel against their fathers, and as ministers they deceive their sovereigns; they exploit the masses to build up their own households.
With hidden malice you harm living beings; through various evil karmas, impermanence arrives. This is that which follows you closely.

Since this is so, if you do not wake up with urgency and turn back, reforming your evils for the sake of goodness and purifying your mind to recite the Buddha’s name, will it not be that you have obtained a human body in vain and lived and died in empty waste?
How bitter, how bitter! I observe that every person in the world considers themselves good.

Regarding the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name), I shall now enumerate three categories of people. First, those who are extremely free from worldly affairs should recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion, day and night.
Second, those who are half-free and half-busy should recite the Buddha’s name immediately upon finishing their tasks.
Third, those who are extremely busy should steal moments of leisure amidst their busyness to recite the Buddha’s name even ten times. Furthermore, as for those of wealth and status...
Those with abundant clothing and sustenance should precisely practice nianfo; those who are poor should precisely practice nianfo by remaining content and maintaining their lot.

Those with children and grandchildren should precisely practice nianfo as they have others to share their burdens; those without children and grandchildren should precisely practice nianfo as their minds are free from attachments.
Those without illness should precisely practice nianfo while their physical strength is robust; those with illness...

Knowing that death is not far off, it is precisely the right time to practice nianfo (recollection of the Buddha). Those who are intelligent and wise, who have mastered the sutras and understood the principles, it is precisely the right time for them to practice nianfo.

Those who are dull-witted and lacking in various intellectual views, it is precisely the right time for them to practice nianfo. To state the essential point: whether in the heavens or among humans, [it is the same].
Those born through the four modes of birth and those existing within the nine realms of existence should all recite the Buddha’s name. I exhort all people of the world:

why not take advantage of this time while the four elements have not yet become a skull, and practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name early? Wait until nothing can be taken with you, and only your karma follows you;
by then, it will be too late for regret.
It is further said: The Buddha taught that human life is impermanent, briefer than a breath; it is the same for the youth, let alone the aged.
I have now come with earnest sincerity to admonish you: you should contemplate this body—its eyes grow dim, its ears grow deaf, its hair turns white, and its face becomes wrinkled.
My back is hunched and my waist is bent; my bones ache and my tendons are cramped. My gait is faltering and my spirit is clouded and obstructed.

It is as if the setting sun shines in the west—its light will vanish in an instant. Like withered grass welcoming autumn, it will wither in a moment. This body will not last long, and the path ahead is vast and boundless; I do not know where I shall go.
Truly, it is as if one’s own task were already accomplished—this is beyond what a fool like me can fathom. Yet, perhaps it is not so.
Why not vigorously reflect upon impermanence? Why not tremble with awe and exert yourself with earnest diligence? Why not contemplate the Pure Land with clarity and resolve to be reborn there?
Why not cast aside all worldly attachments and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name? (From the *Old Hall Admonitions*)
The Buddha said, "Human life is impermanent; it is as brief as a breath. This is true even for those who are healthy, let alone for the sick.

I have now come with earnest sincerity to admonish you: you must contemplate this body. The four elements are no longer in harmony, the hundred members of the frame are about to disintegrate, food and drink gradually diminish, and medicine loses its efficacy.
You are confined to a bed for excrement and urine, groaning upon your pillow and mat—resembling a fish swimming within a boiling cauldron."

In an instant, the tethered wick is scorched; the lamp before the wind is extinguished in a single moment. This body will not last long, and the path ahead is vast and boundless, its destination unknown.

If it were truly as you say—that all matters are already settled—this would be beyond what a fool like me could fathom. But if that is not the case, why do you not vigorously contemplate impermanence?
Why do you not tremble with awe and exert yourself in self-discipline, earnestly reflecting upon the Pure Land and resolutely vowing to be reborn there, casting aside all worldly attachments?
Single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name (*Bingtang Jingce*).

In the *Text on Encouraging the Cultivation of Pure Land Practice* by Ruru Yan Bing of Shizifeng, it says: "Regarding this very physical body, who would believe that the body is the root of suffering?
All crave worldly pleasures, yet they do not realize that pleasure is the cause of suffering. This fleeting life is easily spent; how could it last long?"
Dwelling here, this illusory substance is not solid; it all returns to decay and extinction. From the day before one entered the womb, how could there have been this form of male or female?
It is merely formed through the temporary conjunction of earth, water, fire, and wind. One cannot avoid the suffering of being worn down by birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Above, there is no thread upon which to hang; below, there is no root from which to grow. It is as unsubstantial and floating as [a bubble] upon the water.
Like bubbles, they do not last long; fragile and precarious like dew upon the tips of grass, they vanish in an instant. Those with long lives rarely exceed sixty or seventy before they perish;
those with short lives mostly die prematurely at twenty or thirty. How much more so for those harmed by beasts or stung by insects, caught unawares;
or those crushed by collapsing houses or injured by vehicles—how could their pain be remedied? There are also those who fall into pits, ravines, or over hills and mounds.
Calamity! There is cause for apprehension everywhere. When will the disasters of war, water, and fire ever cease?
Furthermore, today we do not know what tomorrow holds. Upon climbing into bed, one parts from it; how many times does a single breath fail to return?

Then one realizes that a thousand autumns have passed in eternal parting. (Xuefeng’s Verse: A solitary lamp illuminates the night chamber; upon the bed, one strips off socks and shoes. The three souls and seven spirits depart in a dream; who knows whether tomorrow will come or not? Sigh!
It is impossible for this body to be anything other than what it is. Who among men is not deceived by it? Seven feet of bone are bound together by sinews;

within the skin lies a mere lump of flesh. From its nine orifices, impurities flow constantly; its six sense organs unrestrainedly manifest ignorance. Hair, fur, nails, and teeth accumulate like heaps of dust;
mucus, tears, saliva, and spittle are as filthy as a public latrine. Inside, it is entirely a gathering place for maggots.
Outside, mosquitoes and fleas swarm and gather; caught by even a single calamity or ailment, one dies. Furthermore, great heat and great cold hasten the aging process.
The eyes are dragged toward the realm of hungry ghosts by forms; the ears follow sounds into the Avīci Hell.

Though the mouth exhausts a thousand varieties of flavors, after death it only adds a few drops of oil. (The poem by Chang Kui says: "Red and white, do not deceive one another. The True [Self] has no station...")

This human being is but a lump of red flesh; its decayed state is not even like that of a pig or a dog. Look upon it now as a corpse. This body is not worth cherishing; you all should vow to transcend it.
How can those who are deluded and ignorant still flaunt their elegance? How can these dazed fellows still give rise to such inversions?
Some pin flowers or grass upon their skulls; others carry musk or perfumes at the side of their stinking skin-bags, shrouding them in fine robes.
This sack of pus and blood is covered by a brocade quilt; it is but a chamber-pot for excrement and urine.

One exhausts every deceitful mind and hundredfold stratagem, thinking one will dwell in this world for ten thousand years, yet knows not that the head will ache and the eyes grow dim. When King Yama comes to receive people, how can one’s hair still be streaked with gray or one’s teeth still intact?
The Ghost of Impermanence sends word to seek them out; everyone clings to beauty and covets wealth—every one of them has lost their human form.
A shortcut. Day after day drinking wine and eating meat is nothing other than planting deep roots for hell.

One seeks fleeting pleasure before one’s eyes, only to suffer bitter hardship for ten thousand kalpas thereafter. (The Pure Land verse says: Skin wraps flesh, blood, and bone; sinews bind it all together. The deluded ordinary person recognizes this as the self;

only at death does he realize it is not his. All former gold and jade are left to others. When the life-root is suddenly severed and the four elements are sliced by the knives of the winds, externally, the feet...

As your hands are pulled away, your inner liver and intestines ache and tear. Even if you cherish your wife and children, there is no way to detain you; even if your kinsmen fill the space before you, who can take your place?

(An ancient verse says: "The parents' kindness is deep, yet in the end there must be parting; the couple's righteousness is weighty, yet they too must separate. Human feelings are like birds roosting together in a forest; when the great limit arrives, each flies its own way.
Those who remain alive may weep in vain with bitter grief, yet those who have died cannot avoid the wandering of their consciousness.
No light is seen ahead; wherever one looks, there is no companion. Crossing the Naihe River, everyone who sees it is filled with sorrow;
entering the Ghost Gate Pass, all who arrive are utterly desolate. Having been in the world for but seven days, one is already being escorted before the Ten Kings in the underworld.
The officials of the various courts clutch their ledgers, devoid of human feeling; the jailers hold their pitchforks, their faces never smiling. Throughout one's entire life—
Those who perform good deeds are sent back to the Path of the Gods or the Path of the Immortals and Sages.

As for those who commit evil during their lives, they are driven into the mire of boiling water, the mire of fire, and the mire of blades. The cauldrons of boiling water seethe like collapsing mountains; the sword-trees tower like soaring peaks.

They are doused with molten copper until their flesh is completely rotted away; they swallow iron pellets until smoke billows from their mouths. When they encounter the crushing grinders, their blood and flesh flow profusely.
Upon entering the Cold Ice Hell, their skin freezes and cracks; their bodies shatter, yet they are revived by the winds of karma. When their lives end, the *rākṣasas* cry out, "Be reborn!

Having endured a hundred autumns and springs in the human realm, it constitutes but a single day and night within the hells. (From the *Yanguang ji*: "The cauldrons of boiling water and the furnaces of burning coals fill the dark abyss; the sword-trees and knife-mountains tower toward the Great Void.

Only after eighty thousand kalpas have passed in the suffering of retribution do the ox-headed jailers finally allow them to depart. Although their souls and spirits return to the realm of ghosts, their physical corpses remain...
It is as if lying within a coffin. Whether it be after three or five days have passed, or even in the sixth or seventh month, once it has rotted away, it emits worms and blood;
its stench and filth permeate both earth and heaven. Its bloated state is unbearable to behold, and its loathsome appearance is truly terrifying.
Driven by a mass of wild fires, they are cast away and buried in ten-thousand-li wildernesses.

What was once a quiet, rosy countenance has turned into ashes; today it is a desolate pile of white bones, transformed into a mound of mud. (From the *Cold Mountain Verses*: "The rouge upon the face was a thousand ways of coquetry;

dragon-amber and musk perfumed the robes in a hundred subtle manners. Today, not a trace of that elegance remains; amidst green willows and fragrant grasses, the skull lies cold. All former love and affection have here become empty. From of old...
Hero, where are you now? When the rain of tears falls, the void is silent; where the wind of sorrow stirs, it is cold and whistling.
At the end of night, ghosts wail and deities cry out; as the years pass, crows peck and sparrows pick at the remains.
Beside the withered weeds, stone tablets remain scattered; amidst the green willows, paper money hangs empty. In the end, such a fate cannot be avoided. Having reached this point, what can be done?

One does not awaken. (Hanshan said: "The magpies peck and the crows feed until skin and flesh are gone; the wind blows and the sun scorches until the skull is dry. Now, ask those who pass by and watch: take your own physical form and look at it closely. Everyone possesses the eye—do not bury your head further.
Turn your body and leap out of the muddled ford; snap your fingers and tear asunder the net of craving.
Do not make your livelihood within the ghost cave. If you wish to know that the True Man resides upon the lump of flesh, our Buddha, out of compassionate pity, has extended [his hand].
To rescue [sentient beings] and enable them to transcend the three realms directly, a single gate of the Pure Land was specially opened.

The profound depth of the Forty-eight Vows enters the hearts of people, providing universal grace and reception. Though the distance is as vast as ten trillion leagues, by relying on the Buddha’s power, not even a moment’s separation occurs.
Entrusting one’s physical form to the womb of the lotus, one enjoys natural clothing and food; lodging the spirit in the pure realm, one is spared from other [sufferings].
The cycle of the Way is suitable for cultivation by both men and women; whether wise or foolish, all have their share.

Simply request that you turn the light back to reflect within, and you will know that the fundamental substance is originally non-existent. If you are unable to study the Way or practice Chan meditation, then at least diligently observe the precepts and recite the Buddha’s name.
If you can achieve single-mindedness without distraction, I guarantee that success will be attained within seven days. Transform the six thieves into...

The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) and the transcendence of the eight sufferings constitute the eight masteries (aṣṭavaśitā). This can be verified by the textual formulations of the Pure Land scriptures;

the spiritual traces recorded in the *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth) are not false. To the assembly, one proclaims it for the great multitude; to one’s own home, one explains it for the sake of the family.

Thus, may all places equally attain knowledge and awakening, and may every person be led to escape the depths of saṃsāra. Above, this assists the various Buddhas in turning the wheel of Dharma; below, [it benefits sentient beings].
"To pull sentient beings out of the sea of suffering—this the Buddha himself did not believe. What words, then, can be trusted? The human path is difficult to cultivate;

other paths are even more difficult to cultivate. Do not let yourself change your skin for a single day; even if there were a thousand Buddhas, they could not save you. Press forward with urgency, for time does not wait for anyone.
Each of you must directly take responsibility; do not allow this life to pass in vain. (Hanshan said: "The hundred members disintegrate and depart...")
Dust and mud. Among all things, that which is eternally spiritual—whom else could it be? If one cannot find a way through at this moment, how many will know when a skull falls to the ground?
(From the *Changshu Zhi*). In a letter left by Yan Cheng, the Ming Governor of Shaowu, to his relatives and friends, he wrote: "I have been ill for some time and was nearly at the point of death."
Unexpectedly, life has been renewed; though it is but a precarious extension, who knows what tomorrow holds? Turning back to my former ways of worldly striving, they are like chewing wax.
This single skin-sack must inevitably decay; where in the shadows of the six sense-objects can any solidity be found?

It would be better to cast away this mundane mind and seek birth in the Pure Land. By reciting even a single phrase of Amitābha’s name, boundless karmic offenses are extinguished. I offer this briefly...
Exhortation to Express Sincerity:

In the *Morning Bell for the Restoration of the Pure Land*, Zhou Kefu says: "When one looks upon wealth and status from the perspective of poverty and low station, their radiant splendor is so intoxicating that one cannot help but yearn for them with longing.
Yet, those who actually possess such things do not necessarily experience true happiness. As Huangfu Mi said:
Wealth and nobility disturb the spirit and deplete the essence. If one person’s moods are unpredictable, anxiety rests with the master of the situation.
If those of equal rank harbor divergent intentions, anxiety rests with the collective sentiment. Because of the greed for position, one suffers from the fear of gain and loss;

because of the struggle for power, one attacks the different and sides with the like. The higher the position, the heavier the responsibility; the more exalted the favor, the greater the envy. Day by day...
At midday the sun begins to decline; when the moon is full, it immediately wanes. If one fails to seize the opportune moment in a crisis, there will be no place to halt one's journey.

One may even seek the status of a commoner and find it impossible to attain. A wealthy patriarch holds his tally-sticks and calculates, exhausting the strength of mind and body of a lifetime to bequeath to his descendants;
yet the rise and fall of a hundred years is difficult to foresee, and all that remains after death generally falls to others.
It is like a silkworm spinning its cocoon. This cocoon is something that entangles one's own body; one spins it oneself and binds oneself with it. Whom can one blame?
Furthermore, it is merely another person's property. People only desire the cocoon; who wants you, the worm that spun it?
From this perspective, what joy is there in wealth and honor? It is nothing but suffering. How much more so for those who possess wealth and honor!
When it comes to matters of vital importance, there is no difference between the wealthy and the poor.

This is because those things that make the wealthy superior to the poor—such as fine clothing and exquisite food—are of no vital importance to the body or mind. If one wears flowery garments and eats refined delicacies, what essential benefit do these provide to the physical or mental self?
Other matters may be inferred from this principle. When it comes to matters of great benefit or harm, such as old age and illness, [the situation is the same].
It is death. One must stop here, as a solitary individual facing the world alone, reaching the moment when the bell tolls and the water-clock runs dry.
From high ministers down to the common people, there is no one who can take one’s place; all are brought to the same final conclusion, without the addition of even a hair’s breadth.
When one reflects upon this, how could one not feel one’s heart turn to ash on the spot?
It is further said: "The 'One-Son Man' is called the 'Perilous Son. He takes many concubines and handmaidens to expand his lineage, yet he alone does not consider that the body is but one;
is this not a peril to the body? In the world, many know the peril of having sons, yet they forget the peril of the body. This is from the *Seven Chapters* (Qipian) of the *Shiwen* (Classical Prose).
A few ranks of official position; several chests of gold and silk; a single estate; a few acres of fields and gardens;
several beautiful wives and concubines—all of this is a scene devoid of principle and devoid of substance, a matter of idle gossip. Everyone is submerged in it for a lifetime;
each person fails to break out of such a trap. It is all empty and futile, a life spent in frantic haste. Already...
He has passed away. Alas, how tragic! Shao Yaofu said, "If I could turn back ten years, I might have accomplished more of my work.
But alas, in this world of heaven and earth, there is no principle by which the sun rises twice. An ancient proverb says, "A hundred schemes and calculations go to waste;
only these frost-white hairs come to be as they are. It also says, "If you wish to stop now, then stop; if you seek to understand..."
"The time when there is no more time" is a statement that reaches the ultimate truth.

Why not reflect deeply upon this? Furthermore, it is said that people of the world say: "Accumulate moments of joy to prepare for death. Their intention is that human life is too bitter and pure existence is too brief;
rather than meeting one's end in a state of panic, why not indulge in pleasure to enjoy one's rest? If, by some chance...
