As our transformations shift together, I recall my life’s journey and find it filled with many joyful events. Compared to those who spend their entire lives in poverty and distress, am I not surely superior to them by a single stroke?
This is of the same category as what the ancients said: "Ten times I listen to spring cries, changing the warbler's tongue;

three times I loathe old ugliness, exchanging it for a silkworm-brow. I replied: "If that were truly so, then the burden on one's shoulder would grow heavier, and the cauldron would boil even more violently."

Fuel. This is called "premature death. What is meant by "preventing death"? As the Buddha said, that which is received is itself empty. When one sets out various flavors of food, it is empty the moment the chopsticks are laid down.
When one departs with a large retinue of attendants, it is empty once they have arrived. Though one may spend the entire day wandering in sightseeing, it is empty once one has returned.
When one has finished performing good deeds, the diligent effort is immediately empty, yet the white karma remains fully present.

When one has finished performing evil deeds, the gratification of the mind is immediately empty, yet the black karma remains fully present. In the world, those who perform white karma are few, while those who perform black karma are many.

Thus, for the sake of a momentary gratification, one creates an ocean of karma that stretches boundlessly. Is this not the very strategy for preventing death? Indeed, preventing death is the foremost task of a great man;
it is the primary move in the defense against mortality. Nothing surpasses the thorough understanding of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
To understand birth and death, nothing surpasses the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) to seek rebirth in the Western Land. Furthermore, there is a certain class of people in the world...

There are those who take lofty principles as their ambition and leisurely detachment as their disposition; they may cultivate their spirits through poetry and wine, or exchange the mundane world for a game of chess.
Or they may settle their minds upon the Five Peaks, chanting and sighing amidst the mists and clouds. These are all merely those who waste their time in vain.
As for those superior to them, there are the ten classes of flying immortals and the feathered guests of the Three Mountains; they are not without the freedom of the phoenixes.
The crane prides itself on its soaring flight, yet it cannot help but remain ignorant of its true nature and unresolved regarding birth and death. Poet Bai Juyi said:
"Even if one were to attain longevity, it would merely surpass premature death. Longevity is spoken of only in contrast to brevity;
as long as one has not departed from the track of birth and death, it is better to study non-arising. Non-arising is precisely non-ceasing. Truly well said!
Furthermore, it is said that Dongpo remarked: "The other day, Wang Shi, the son-in-law of Han Chiguo, came to visit me.

He told me that Chiguo considers himself already decrepit and old, and intends to amuse his remaining years with music, song, wine, and women. Dongpo said: 'Precisely because they are his final years, one ought not to act in such a manner.
Recently, there was an elderly man who hosted a banquet for his relatives and friends. When the drinking ended, he spoke to the assembly, saying: 'I am now frail and..."

He departed. The sons called out after him, saying, "We pray you will leave us one word as an instruction. The old man said, "Simply rise at the first watch of the fifth watch [dawn]. The sons did not understand.
The old man said, "Only during the fifth watch can one attend to one's own affairs. One's own affairs are those which one can take with oneself at the time of death.
Furthermore, while I have been managing my livelihood in ordinary life, today I am about to pass away; what can I take with me?"

"What is it that departs? The sons were somewhat enlightened by this. They entreated their father to speak to Citragupta regarding the affairs of their own household, saying, "Rather than exhausting our minds with wine and sensual pleasures, it would be better to devise a plan for what must be taken at the time of death."

Tú Chìshuǐ further said: "The reason why people of the world do not practice mindfulness of the Buddha with sincerity and earnestness is simply that they regard the two words 'birth and death' with negligence.
Throughout their lives they are busily preoccupied, casting their very lives and spirits into the void as if they had no concern with them at all.
Even if they might momentarily lament and feel their hair stand on end in the face of such reality, after this moment they remain as before, mired in a drunken dream."
It is said: Worldly wisdom is in disarray; one is clever within the arena of fame and profit. The conscious spirit is in turmoil; one is muddled on the path of birth and death. Alas!
Who understands that the four elements are not solid and that impermanence is exceedingly swift? The three miserable realms and eight difficulties are most painful.
How few are those who are willing to go to what is essential and truly practice the Buddha-remembrance—perhaps one or two in a hundred. Long ago, there was a monk who visited a lay friend.
The monk exhorted him, saying, "The matter of birth and death is grave; you must urgently recite the Buddha’s name. His friend declined, saying, "I have three matters that are not yet settled.

The monk asked his old friend, "Your parents' coffin has not yet been moved, and the marriages of your sons and daughters are not yet complete. Not long after the monk departed, the friend suddenly passed away.
When the monk went to offer condolences, he composed a poem, saying: "My friend's name was Zhang Zuliu. He urged me to recite the Buddha’s name, Saying that 'three heads' would suffice."
How strange that Lord Yama lacks discernment! Before his three heads have even finished, he comes to summon [the deceased]. Although these words are simple, they are sufficient to awaken the worldly.
I wish that all people in the world would rouse their vigor and, with a single stroke, sever the cycle of saṃsāra.
If you can believe this word of the Buddha, then proceed with courage and recite it. This single thought is the bright lamp that destroys darkness.
This is the great ship for crossing the sea of suffering; it is the excellent remedy for escaping birth and death; it is the path for departing from the triple world.
Whether its efficacy is verified or not, whether one attains awakening or not—none of these are taken into account. One simply holds the single phrase of the Buddha’s name within the mind.
One recites it when there is nothing to do, and one recites it when there is something to do; one recites it in peace and happiness, and one recites it in illness.
One must be mindful of suffering; one must be mindful of birth; one must be mindful of death. If one is earnest in this way, there is nothing that will not be accomplished.
In *Jingtu chenzhong*, Qian Xiaozhi further states: "From of old, the cycle of birth and death within the three realms has been compared to a prison.
Thus, as long as one has not escaped from birth and death, all are prisoners within the jail of the three realms. There are three kinds of prisoners."

The first person says to himself, "I shall certainly have no way to survive," and thus merely seeks a precarious comfort within this state. Yet, one day the executioner arrives, and he is led to his death in a state of trembling fear.
The second person prides himself on being the son of a man worth a thousand pieces of gold; he does not spare his wealth as he prepares for his livelihood, yet his resolve is not firm.
On one hand, he indulges in the pleasures of the cauldron for the time being, while on the other, he fears that the path to rebirth may be cut off.
This too is simply a matter of following the Way to its end with a willing heart. Yet there are those of a rebellious and stubborn nature who cannot endure restraint;
they watch for a moment’s lapse in the guard's vigilance and struggle to break their shackles, surging forward without looking back.

Given such a resolute rupture, how could they possibly be content to savor the remainder of their life in stealth before death? Whether they emerge or not, their fate hangs in a state of indecision. Alas! This, too, is my [concern].
Such people are a prime example within the prison of birth and death. The first type of person is as common as flowing water;
they set their words upon fame, achievement, wealth, and honor, laboring to acquire them and indulging themselves in the ultimate luxuries of palatial dwellings, wives, and concubines.
When spoken to of birth and death, they remain unconcerned; when told that there is another way beyond birth and death, they merely respond with a silent, dismissive laugh.
[A smile. This is because they lack the faculty of faith entirely. As for the second type of person: from birth they possess latent roots;
they prostrate to the Buddha and discourse on Chan, protect and uphold the teachings, build temples and provide offerings to the Sangha, and are not stingy with their wealth.

Yet, they remain entangled within the net of worldly affairs; the tether of fame and the shackles of profit are like a thicket of eight-pointed thorns, binding them so that they cannot attain freedom. O people!
To fail to apply oneself single-mindedly to this one great matter of leaving the world, while hoping to accomplish it with only spare effort—how can there be such a thing as a crane from Yangzhou?
Though one may have performed meritorious deeds throughout one's life, they will not transcend the realms of humans and devas;

at the critical juncture of birth and death, one will still fail to leap free. This is because their fear of birth and death was originally not sincere and profound. As it is said: [The text continues: "If..."
The third type of person does not seek wealth or nobility, but exerts diligent effort; this is truly one who can seek birthlessness and deathlessness.
Now, seeing those in fetters calling out to heaven for their lives, everyone pities their folly and mocks them for not seeking life earlier.
I say that these condemned prisoners seek life too late; compared to our own kind, they are still...
This is a prudent calculation. A death prisoner is sentenced for execution during the autumn; such a case takes no more than a single day.

Before and after that one day, everything can be easily arranged and settled. Yet we, who dwell within the prison of the three realms, may die year after year, month after month, day after day, and moment after moment.
The lowly die, and the noble also die; the old die, and the young also die; the wicked die, and the virtuous also die.
There is no ranking by noble title, no ranking by virtue, and no ranking by age. If for a single breath one does not come [to the end], then present and past are divided.

If you do not prepare yourself early on, and merely wait for another moment, then should that very moment arrive when the warrant of execution is delivered and the executioner stands face-to-face, you will be flustered and bewildered;
how could you resist it? Furthermore, Yuan Zhonglang said: "Sentient beings dwelling in this world of five turbidities are like prisoners."
Regarding prisons: those who enter them are all offenders, for those dwelling among humans and devas possess bodies that are merely segments of karmic retribution.
Yet, when offenders enter a prison, they seek release at every moment, because they know that beyond the thorny walls there exists a vast world of great peace and happiness.
Now, sentient beings take afflictions as their home and birth-and-death as...
They treat it as a garden and grove, unaware that the Great Iron Ring Mountains are their thorny walls. Beyond the Dharma-field of the triple world, each has their own native land and place of joy.
Out of compassion for this, the Buddhas distinguish between the pure and the defiled, pointing out the path for returning to liberation.
Yet those who have long abandoned their karmic duties find no place of refuge; thus, the Buddhas further construct great dwellings for them.
They provide for their safety. On one hand, they come and go through the gates of the prison to serve as guides for the path;
on the other hand, they constantly wait outside the prison to maintain and decorate the guest lodgings. For such kindness, what body could ever repay it? As the Sūtra says:

"The Tathāgata appears in the world for one great matter. This "great matter" is precisely this very thing. Since the Buddhas do not begrudge extending their hands [in compassion], sentient beings [should likewise respond].
Yet you continue to cling to these trivial matters of a mere hair’s breadth, exchanging the small for the great; why is it that you do not awaken even at the point of death?

Having already recognized the path of delusion through the gateway of Easy Practice, and desiring to seek transcendence from the world, you must know that there are many gateways to entering the Way, yet none surpasses the recitation of the Buddha’s name for rebirth in the Pure Land.

The Pure Land is an easy path. There are many such pure lands; however, rebirth specifically in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is particularly easy to practice. This is because Amitābha Buddha made forty-eight great vows.

Having brought all sentient beings to liberation, his karmic affinity with this world is pervasive and profound, and his majestic power is likewise supreme; thus, he gathers all beings without exception.
If a person can place their faith and inclination in him, upholding his name with a sincere heart, there is none who will not receive his guidance and deliverance.
This is what is called "relying on another's power," which differs vastly in terms of ease and difficulty from those who rely solely on their own strength. Thus concludes the *Easy Practice Door*.
The *Lungshu Jingtuwen* states: "In general, throughout the Great Canon, there are more than ten sutras that speak of the Western Pure Land.
Their general outline describes that place as being adorned with the seven treasures and lacking the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, birds, beasts, and animals."
Even down to the classes of creatures that fly or crawl, all are eternally pure and spontaneous, free from all defilement and confusion;

therefore it is called the Pure Land. Its inhabitants are all born from within lotus flowers; they enjoy eternal life without aging. Their clothing, food, and dwellings manifest spontaneously according to their wishes.
The seasons are perpetually spring, with no further cold or heat. They experience great bliss and are entirely free from all suffering and affliction. Therefore...
It is named the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). The name of its Buddha, Amitābha, is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Immeasurable.

Because the light of this Buddha illuminates the worlds of the ten directions without limit, and because there are no sentient beings who recite his name whom he does not know, he is also called the Buddha of Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).
The lifespan of this Buddha, as well as that of the people within his land, is likewise immeasurable.
His lifespan is entirely without limit; even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it never comes to an end.
For this reason, he is also called Amitāyus Buddha (Buddha of Immeasurable Life). This Buddha possesses great vows to deliver sentient beings, and his majestic spiritual power is inconceivable.

Therefore, those who with a sincere heart place their faith and devotion in him, and who recite his name, will certainly have their calamities eliminated and their grievances against ghosts averted in this present life, and shall abide in peace.
It stills the body and spirit, increases blessings and prolongs life. Within the Western Seven-Jeweled Pond, a single lotus flower shall grow;
one day, one will be reborn therein and directly escape beyond the cycle of saṃsāra. Such instances all have documented precedents;
they are not empty words. This teaching is extremely easy to practice. Among the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates within the entire Tripitaka, there is none like it.
This essential and swift method is something that people often do not know—how lamentable! Even more lamentable is to know it yet fail to practice it.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "Innumerable and incalculable kalpas ago, there appeared a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja, who manifested his transformation."
To deliver sentient beings. At that time, there was a great king who went to listen to the preaching of the Dharma and subsequently attained awakening.
He then renounced his royal status to go forth and practice, becoming known as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara—this is none other than Amitābha Buddha.
Before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, he made forty-eight great vows, each vow being for the purpose of saving and delivering sentient beings. Thus he made his resolve.
Having made this vow, one then applies diligence to bring an end to birth and death. Next, one enters the stages of a Bodhisattva (*bodhisattvabhūmi*).
To "bring an end to birth and death" means that birth and death are naturally as they are. To "enter the stages of a Bodhisattva" means to cultivate wisdom internally and cultivate merit externally.
As for cultivating wisdom, it causes the nature of wisdom to expand day by day; by the time one attains Buddhahood, the nature of wisdom encompasses empty space.
In this world, there is nothing he does not know and nothing he does not see. Those who cultivate merit are thus entrusted with rebirth among all sentient beings;
taking on their same physical forms and mastering their languages, he establishes his teachings. Therefore, from the celestial lords above...
Down to the most minute insects and ants, all take birth within it. Thus, throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, they have been transforming sentient beings.
Now, in the transformation of sentient beings, there is none that does not result in the acquisition of merit.

Having acquired this merit yet not consuming it, their merit accumulates ever more and becomes ever greater; after a long time, it will pervade the world-systems of empty space. When the merit is great—

Thus, their majestic spiritual power (*vīrya*) is great. It is like people in the world: when one’s official rank is high, one’s influence and power are great. Therefore, there is nothing that this majestic spiritual power cannot accomplish;
only then can one fulfill one's aspirations and enter the stage of Buddhahood. This refers to the period from the initial generation of the vow until the attainment of Buddhahood.

There is nothing that does not benefit sentient beings. Therefore, when people wholeheartedly place their faith and turn toward him, recollecting his name, they will surely receive blessings and protection in the present life, and after death, they will surely be born directly in the World of Ultimate Bliss. If one can single-mindedly contemplate his physical form, one will surely behold the Buddha’s true body in this life;
for the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is omnipresent, and it is through the power of the human mind’s recollection [that this occurs].
When one becomes thoroughly matured with the Buddha, there is spontaneous communion; thus, the Buddha manifests his body.

Furthermore, it is said in the *Jingtu zhuan* (Biographies of the Pure Land): "Amitābha Buddha, together with the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, board the great vessel of the vow and sail upon the sea of birth and death.
Within this Sahā world, they call out to and lead sentient beings onto the great vessel of the vow."
They shall be sent to the Western Land. If one is willing to go, there are none who will not attain rebirth there.

Contemplating this, it is clear that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of compassion for sentient beings who are submerged in the sea of suffering and have no means of escape, employ their own power of vows.
It is like a boatman who entices travelers to board his vessel and delivers them to the other shore.
People only fear that they will not believe; if they have faith and are willing to go, then even those with sinful karma will surely attain birth [in the Pure Land].
Indeed, the Buddha cannot be compared to ordinary people. Ordinary people do not associate with others unless they are driven by power and profit, or unless it benefits themselves;
this is what makes them ordinary. The worthy and the noble are not like this, let alone the Buddha.
For one who lacks compassion is insufficient to be a Buddha, and one who does not deliver sentient beings is insufficient [to be a Buddha].

To be a Buddha, one must possess great majestic power; without it, one cannot be a Buddha. Because he possesses compassion, he sees sentient beings submerged in the ocean of suffering and desires to deliver them.
Because he possesses great majestic power, he is able to fulfill his heart's desire to deliver them.
Thus they accomplish the merit of salvation; this is why they are called Buddhas. A sutra says:
"The Great King of Physicians can cure all diseases, yet he cannot cure one whose life has come to an end. The Buddha can deliver all sentient beings, yet he cannot deliver those who lack faith.
To compare the lack of faith to the exhaustion of life is indeed the ultimate analogy. For faith is but a single thought-moment.
Furthermore, when a person is alive, if the mind intends to go, the body follows; if the mind intends to stay, the body follows. Thus, this body always follows the mind.
Yet, there are times when the mind desires to depart while the body remains bound by attachments.
At the moment the body perishes, there is only a single thought. Wherever that single thought reaches, there is nowhere it does not arrive. Therefore, with a single thought one is present.
If one is destined for the Pure Land, one will certainly be reborn there; how much more so for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who further invite and lead people toward rebirth?
Furthermore, it was said: "The layman Yang Jie, courtesy name Cigong, attained high honors in his youth and clarified the essential tenets of the Chan school.

He held that because the faculties of sentient beings vary—some sharp and some dull—that which is most accessible, easy to understand, simple, and easy to practice is none other than the Western Pure Land."
Simply focus the mind on contemplation; by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows, one will go directly to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).

In the preface he wrote for Wang Minzhong’s *Direct Pointing to Resolve Doubts Concerning Pure Land*, he said: "The light of Amitābha Buddha is like the great full moon, shining universally throughout the ten directions.
When the water is clear and still, the moon appears in its entirety. The moon does not hasten toward the water to come there suddenly. When the water is turbid..."
When it moves, the moon has no fixed light; yet the moon does not abandon the water and depart in haste. While in the water, there are clarity and turbidity, motion and stillness;
yet within the moon, there is no grasping or rejecting, no coming or going. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* records the words of the Elder’s Son Vimokṣa:
One knows that all Buddhas are like reflections and one's own mind is like water; those Tathāgatas do not come here.
If I wish to see the Tathāgata Amitābha in the Land of Peace and Bliss, I see him at will.

Thus, one knows that when sentient beings focus their minds with concentration, they surely see Amitābha. If one is born in that land, there will be no sufferings whatsoever. This is the Pratyutpanna Samādhi.
The Sūtra states: The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla asked Śākyamuni Buddha, "How can sentient beings of the future come to see all the Buddhas of the ten directions?
The Buddha instructed him to recollect Amitābha Buddha, whereby they will immediately see all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Furthermore, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If sentient beings from other regions hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitāyus..."

Even those who can give rise to a single thought of pure faith, who rejoice with delight, and who dedicate all their roots of goodness with the vow to be born in that land—such as these shall be reborn there according to their wish and attain the stage of non-retrogression. These are all the words of the Buddha. To disbelieve the words of the Buddha is [unwholesome].
How can such words be trusted? [If one] is not born in the Pure Land, what land could one possibly be born in? Dongpo said: "In his later years, Cigong served as a regional inspector and a prefect.
He frequently painted images of the sixteen-foot Amitābha Buddha to carry with him for offerings and contemplation.
When his life came to an end, he was moved by the Buddha’s arrival to welcome him; he passed away while sitting upright."

From the *Wenlei of the Land of Bliss*, Yang Cigong said: "The light of Amitābha shines universally throughout the Dharma-realm, embracing and never forsaking those sentient beings who recite his name.

Holy and ordinary beings are of one essence; when the capacity and the response coincide, the sentient beings within the hearts of all Buddhas are the ultimate bliss (*sukhāvatī*) in every dust mote, and the pure land within the minds of sentient beings is Amitābha in every thought-moment. Observing it from this perspective, the wise..."
It is easy for those who can sever doubt to be born there. It is easy for those in meditative concentration to be born there, because they are not distracted.

It is easy for those who maintain the precepts to be born there, because they are far removed from all defilements. It is easy for those who practice generosity to be born there, because they have no sense of "mine.

It is easy for those who practice patience to be born there, because they are free from anger. It is easy for those who practice diligence to be born there, because they do not regress. It is easy for those who neither create good nor commit evil to be born there.
Because their mindfulness is single-minded, those who have already committed various evils and whose karmic retribution has already manifested can easily be reborn there.
However, even if one possesses many good deeds, if they lack a sincere mind of faith and a mind of dedication and aspiration, they will not be able to attain rebirth.
Alas! Amitābha is very easy to invoke; the Pure Land is very easy to reach. Yet sentient beings are unable to invoke him or reach it. What can the Buddha do for them?
Now, to commit evil karma and enter the realms of suffering, and to recite the name of Amitābha and be born in Sukhāvatī—both of these are words of the Buddha.
It is truly delusional for worldly people to fear falling into hell while doubting rebirth in the Pure Land.
Zheng Qingzhi, Chancellor of the Song Dynasty, said: "Everyone says that practicing the Pure Land is not as good as Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya.

I alone say that among the Dharma-gates of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, none compare to practicing the Pure Land. For it is truly pure, luminous, and wondrous; it is empty, penetrating, and spiritually responsive."

Whether wise or foolish, all beings possess this nature. Yet, as the sense organs, objects, and illusory environments mutually entangle one another, the cycle of birth and death continues without end throughout kalpas.
Therefore, the Śākya-muni established expedient means through Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, enabling practitioners to enter by various gates and all attain transcendent awakening.
Only Amitābha Buddha has opened a singular gate, called the Cultivation of the Pure Land, as follows:
This single method for curing illness is concise and direct; with single-minded devotion, one reaches the other shore. It may be practiced by both the ordained and the laity alike.
While it is known as a shallow teaching intended to transform the ignorant and the common folk, in reality, it is the swift path to attaining Buddhahood.
Among those who study Buddhism today—be they in Chan, Teaching, or Vinaya—none surpasses this in its ultimate, perfect, and sudden nature.

As for Chan: unless one possesses sharp faculties and is a superior vessel who understands through spiritual intuition and mental resolution, one cannot avoid the error of falling into a stagnant emptiness.

As for studying the Three Vehicles: nothing compares to the Teaching; unless one forgets the trap upon catching the fish and sees the moon by following the pointing finger, one cannot avoid the malady of poring over old paper.
As for protecting the good and warding off evil: nothing compares to the Vinaya; unless one’s body and mind are pure and one’s inner and outer states are as one, then [one will fail].
One cannot avoid the suffering of self-entanglement. Viewing them as a whole: if one discusses the gateways entered, there are Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya;

if one considers their ultimate destination, they are Precepts, Samādhi, and Prajñā. Is it not the single gateway of the Pure Land alone that allows one to attain precepts, samādhi, and prajñā without relying on Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya?
At the very moment of reciting the Buddha’s name, chanting with the mouth and contemplating with the mind—does this not mean "committing no evil"?

Observing the precepts and binding one’s mindfulness to the pure realm—when illusory dusts are extinguished together, is this not concentration (*samādhi*)? Contemplating that there is truly no-thought, and the mental flowers are serene and still—is this not wisdom (*prajñā*)?

If a person can eliminate myriad concerns and direct their single mind toward the Western [Pure Land], then they will awaken to the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden Teaching without the need for staffs or shouts;
they will obtain the True Dharma Eye without reading the Great Tripitaka; and they will not merely maintain themselves within the four dignified postures (*īryāpatha*).
One attains great sovereign mastery. There is neither defilement nor purity; there is neither bondage nor liberation. At such a time, what constitutes precept, concentration, and wisdom?
What constitutes dhyāna, teaching, and discipline? My own mind and the Buddha-mind are entirely without distinction. This is the ultimate consummation of the cultivation of the Pure Land.
As for the water of eight virtues and the golden lotus pedestals—why should one harbor any doubt regarding them? This is the essential pivot of the Pure Land.
This has been diligently composed.
From *Master Yuantianru’s Questions on the Pure Land*: Question: There are many types of "Pure Lands of Common Residence.
Why is it that you now point specifically to Sukhāvatī, and further praise its environment and its superior conditions? Answer: The Sūtra says: "That..."

The sentient beings of that land have no manifold sufferings, but experience only various joys; therefore, it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī). Now, if we compare this by contrast with the Sahā world:
here, one possesses a physical body of flesh and blood, and birth is entirely suffering; there, one is born through transformation from a lotus flower, and thus there is no suffering of birth.
Here, the seasons shift and change, and the infirmities of old age encroach daily; there, cold and heat do not alter, and...

In this [world], there is the suffering of old age; here, the four elements are difficult to harmonize, and illnesses frequently arise. Therein, however, the transformed body is fragrant and pure, free from the suffering of illness.
In this world, those who reach seventy are rare, for impermanence is swift. Therein, the lifespan is immeasurable, free from the suffering of death.
In this world, there is attachment to kin and loved ones, and where there is love, there must be separation. Therein, there are no parents, wives, or children. Free from...
This is the suffering of separation from what one loves; these are enemies and bitter foes, and where there is enmity, there must inevitably be a meeting.
That, however, is a gathering of the most virtuous, free from the suffering of encountering those one hates. This [life] may involve hardship, hunger, and cold, with insatiable craving and seeking;

that [life], by contrast, has clothing, food, and precious treasures, all ready for enjoyment. This [life] may have an ugly and filthy physical form, with many impaired and deformed faculties; that, however, is upright...
This [world] has a stern appearance; its substance possesses radiance. This involves the cycle of birth and death; that is the eternal realization of non-arising.
This has the sufferings of the four realms of existence; that lacks even the name of the three evil paths.

This has hills, ridges, pits, and hollows, with forests of thorns and brambles, mountains of earth and stone, and is filled with filth and impurity. That has the ground of pure gold, with jewel-trees reaching to the heavens, and multi-storied pavilions.
[In this world] the Seven Treasures rise high and flowers bloom in four colors; yet here, the Twin Trees have already withered and the Dragon Flower [Buddha] has not yet appeared.
There, the Honored One of Immeasurable Life currently preaches the Dharma; here, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta merely look up to their illustrious names.
There, those two superior beings personally serve as one's supreme friends; here, hosts of demons and heterodox teachers disturb and confuse one’s correct cultivation. There, the Buddha...
In this world, there is a single unification through transformation; the traces of Māras and heretics have been severed. Here, seductive forms and licentiousness delude practitioners;
there, the retributive reward is pure and truly no women exist. Here, evil beasts and *chimei* (goblins) mingle and fan the flames of perverse sounds;

there, water birds and forest trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma. When these two lands are compared, their environments and conditions are vastly different, yet the excellence of the Land of Bliss [is manifest].
Their number is infinite; I have not yet had the leisure to enumerate them all. As for those whose lands are most excellent, they can gather in sentient beings who possess a longing for purity.
As for those whose conditions are most excellent, they can assist those who are born there in the power of their practice.
Although there are many such pure realms, only in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are the conditions for practice fully complete; therefore, it is pointed out universally.
Again, it was asked: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are all capable of being approached; why then do you single out Amitābha? The answer was:
"There are three reasons for singling out Amitābha: first, the profundity of his vows; second, the existence of a karmic affinity with the Sahā world;
and third, the relevance of his transformative path. Regarding the profundity of his vows: the sutra states that in the past, during his causal stage, Amitābha once made various kinds of [vows].

The vast and great vow is summarized as follows: "If, since my attainment of Buddhahood, there should be any sentient beings who wish to be born in my land, or who hear my name, cultivate various roots of goodness, and recite my name even ten times, yet do not attain birth therein—I vow not to realize perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, once born in my land, if there should be any regression or lack of certainty regarding their attainment of Buddhahood, [I vow not to realize perfect enlightenment]."

"I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment [until this is accomplished]. Thus, the *Huayan chao* states: "The Vows of Amitābha are profound; he specifically receives in his grace the sentient beings of this Sahā world.

Those with the karmic affinity: during the time when our Buddha Śākyamuni was present in the world, there were already many sentient beings who, hearing the Buddha’s teachings, turned their hearts toward Amitābha.
Let us consider those after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—sentient beings of the final age, whether monastic or lay, male or female.
Whether noble or base, rich or poor, those who have heard even a little of the Buddha’s teachings believe in and incline toward them;

even those who have not heard the Buddha’s teachings likewise invoke his name. Even among the stubborn, foolish, violent, evil, and faithless, when they encounter calamities or perilous situations, [they do so].
Some utter sounds of praise or lamentation; unconsciously, they find themselves calling out Amitābha Buddha’s name.
Even when children and women are at play—piling sand, kneading mud, or drawing on walls and partitions—they fashion images of Amitābha Buddha.
This extends even to those whose gait is not yet steady and whose speech is not yet formed; they are naturally able to chant "A-mi-tuo."
Amitābha Buddha. All of these arise without being exhorted and are accomplished without being taught; how could this be anything other than due to having a karmic affinity?
Furthermore, as the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* says: "I have spoken this sūtra so that you may now see Amitāyus Buddha and his land.
Whatever you ought to do, you may seek therein. Do not harbor further doubts after my parinirvāṇa. In the future..."
In that age, when the Way of the sutras has been extinguished, I shall out of compassion specially preserve this sutra for another hundred years.
Any sentient beings who encounter this sutra shall all attain liberation according to their wishes. Furthermore, the sutra states:
after this sutra has perished, the Buddha-dharma will be entirely absent; only the four-character name of Amitābha Buddha shall remain to save and deliver sentient beings. Its...
There are those who, lacking faith, slander and revile [him]; they shall fall into hell and undergo all manner of suffering. Therefore, the *Tiantai* [school] says:
"One should know that that Buddha has a particular affinity for this degenerate age. Regarding those who are connected [to him]:

the "Awakened Ones" refers to the sages of the two lands, who manifest dwelling in both pure and impure realms to subdue sentient beings through the two gates of "breaking" (*dharṣaṇa*) and "gathering" (*saṃgraha*). This is by means of the impure and the suffering...
He urges them on by means of many demonic afflictions to break them down, so that they may come to know weariness [with saṃsāra].
He gathers them in through purity, bliss, longevity, and non-retrogression, so that they may know what to rejoice in. Once they both feel weary and rejoice, the path of transformation proceeds.
Furthermore, among those for whom I, Śākyamuni, have not yet completed their deliverance beyond the teachings bestowed in the Three Vehicles, their deliverance lies with Amitābha.
Therefore, throughout the various Mahāyāna sūtras, there is repeated and earnest exhortation to praise [this teaching] and encourage its pursuit;
this is because it is intimately related to the path of transformation. For these three reasons, it is uniquely promoted.

The *Da yu jingtu zhigui ji* (Collection on the Pointing to the Goal of the Pure Land by Da-yu) states that the *Yuan tong fan fa shi hui zong ji* (Anthology of the Essential Teachings of Dharma Master Yuantongfan), citing the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, speaks of three powers for rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo*).

First is the power of the inherently existing Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), which refers to the Tathāgatagarbha within the mind of afflictions. Second is the power of compassionate light-gathering, which refers to the radiance of Amitābha.

It is immeasurable. It is the power of the Buddha’s vow to embrace and never abandon sentient beings who mindfully recollect him. Third is the power of the *nien-fo* samādhi (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
This means that by recollecting and mindfully reciting the Buddha’s name, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.

These three powers are like three strands of rope joined together to form a great cord, capable of pulling heavy objects. They are also like water, fire, and a mirror; if these are brought together and directed toward the sun with moxa, [fire will surely arise].
If one takes it up, fire can be obtained; if one holds it toward the moon and uses the bead to collect it, water can be obtained.
Here, the mirror possessing the natures of both water and fire serves as a metaphor for the power of the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by sentient beings.

The necessity of the light of the sun and moon coming to illuminate it represents the power of Amitābha’s compassionate light to gather and sustain them. Just as the bead and the moxa can draw forth water...
Fire is the power of faith and mindfulness of the Buddha. These three things are indispensable; one cannot be missing.
When these three factors harmonize, fire and water are produced. When these three powers mutually support one another, rebirth in the Pure Land will certainly occur.
The Great Master Lianchi’s *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* states: "To further clarify the path of practice—the shortest path among paths—there are two meanings.
First, while the study of the Way through other gates is a journey of ten thousand miles, the recollection of the Buddha for rebirth is what has been called 'the shortcut' since antiquity.
Yet within this single method of recollecting the Buddha, there are many approaches; now, specifically taking up the recitation of the Name is what constitutes the shortcut."
The path within the path, and yet the path. The crane soars and the Peng bird takes flight; the steed gallops like a soaring dragon.

Moving without haste, arriving without speed—it is the path within the path. The commentary states: These two meanings are first, a comparative evaluation among the various pure practices (*śukla-karman*);
second, a discernment of the primary text within this specific division. Therefore, it is called the "path of the path. Path.
A path that is narrow yet swift is called a "shortcut" (*kai*). "Narrow" is a metaphor for the simplicity and ease of the power of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection);
"swift" is a metaphor for the rapidity with which success is achieved through *nien-fo*. As Master Shandao’s verse says: "There is only the shortcut of practice;

simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Therefore, it is said that practicing the Way through other gates is called "ascending out of the triple world," whereas *nien-fo* leads to rebirth [in the Pure Land].

This is called "transversely exiting the triple world. It is like a worm inside a bamboo stalk: if it moves vertically, it is difficult to pass through the nodes; if it moves transversely, it can break through all at once.

Comparing other methods to the recitation of the Buddha's name (*nien-fo*), the recitation of the Buddha's name is the swiftest. Furthermore, there are many gates within the practice of reciting the Buddha's name.

There are four kinds of mindfulness of the Buddha according to the true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), extending even to the dedication of the myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti-pariṇāmana*) and so forth.

Although it is said that the Buddha of the true nature is inherently possessed [by all beings], sentient beings have heavy afflictions and those who attain realization and understanding are rare. Below these are several methods: In the contemplation of the image (*bimba-vipaśyanā*), once the image has departed, there is nothing more;

thus, the practice becomes interrupted. In the contemplation of the visualization (*saṃjñā-vipaśyanā*), the mind is coarse while the object is subtle, making the wondrous contemplation difficult to achieve. As for the myriad practices...
The practices to be performed are numerous; one inevitably falls into that which is most burdensome. Only this single dharma of holding the name is concise, direct, and straightforward.
If one can merely maintain mindfulness, one will attain rebirth. As the ancients said: "Once you have seen Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?

Thus, without even seeking the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one accords with it. Therefore, reciting the Buddha's name is the shortcut for spiritual cultivation, and it is through holding the name that one achieves this.
Furthermore, it is the shortcut within the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.

The *De yuan ji* (Collection from the Garden of Virtue), Appendix, states: "Yu Chunxi, an official of the Ministry of Rites during the Ming dynasty, requested leave to return to Tianmu Mountain and sat before the 'Deadly Barrier' at Gaofeng.
Day and night he exhorted himself with diligence; by the twenty-first day, he was so exhausted that he wished to lie down on his pillow. Suddenly—"
He saw Chan Master Gaofeng sever his left arm; having attained sudden enlightenment, he hurried to Yunqi to seek certification. Master Hong said:
"One who awakens from sleep will surely fall back asleep if they return to their pillow and bedding without first washing their hair or combing themselves.

One who awakens from delusion will surely return to delusion if they return to defilement and impurity without first adorning themselves. A lotus born of fire withers easily; a young bamboo shoot [is easily broken]."
Zhe said, "I shall devise a plan for myself. Do not let the light of a single moment obstruct the path of your own cultivation.
He thus exhorted him to dedicate his merit toward the Pure Land to continue their former causes. Consequently, Chenxi practiced this throughout his life.
Preface to the *Wenlei of the Land of Bliss* Chen Zan, a Court Gentleman of the Ming Dynasty, resided at home with a single-minded devotion to the practice of Pure Land.
A guest once visited him and rebuked him, saying: "Have you not heard the discourse of the Great Mirror [Huineng] regarding 'mind-only'?
Why do you loathe the defiled and rejoice in the pure? He replied: "The Pure Land of Mind-Only was proclaimed by the Great Mirror, yet it did not originate with the Great Mirror alone. This mind..."
"One becomes a Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The Buddha certainly spoke these words beforehand. It was because he feared that people would seek the Pure Land with an impure mind;
it was not that the land itself lacks both defilement and purity.
The Preface to the *Ten Essentials of the Pure Land* by Ming Cheng states: "In the method of reciting the name in the Pure Land, there are three essential points.

First, regarding the six-character Great Name: in every moment of thought, one must possess both aspiration and revulsion—like escaping a dark prison and hastening to entrust oneself to a royal house;
at every step, one must possess both aspiration and revulsion. Second, Chan meditation cannot be practiced without the Pure Land."
To prevent falling back into decline, how could one not feel a chill in one’s heart? The Pure Land must certainly not be entered through the mechanisms of Chan meditation;
if one relies on intellectual views, both paths will be ruined. If you can truly cultivate pure karma in the temple, you need not for a moment involve yourself in other schools.
Third, as for the single phrase "Amitābha," it cannot be fully brought forth by those of great penetration alone, yet even the most ignorant lack nothing of it. Should there be even a trace of it...
To engage in conceptual discrimination leads to the calamity of the great Dharma-māra. One should value single-mindedly upholding [the practice];

how could one envy a vague, superficial understanding? *The Direct Pointing to Nianfo* states: During the Yuan and Ming dynasties, the monk Miaoye authored the two volumes of *The Direct Pointing to Nianfo*.
Within it, the essay "Directly Pointing to the Essential Heart" refutes the false and reveals the true, being the most refined and profound work. It says: "Amitābha of Ultimate Bliss..."
When the marks and signs appear, they are the manifestation of one's own mind; when one's own mind manifests, that Buddha appears.
My mind is the Buddha’s mind, and the Buddha’s mind is my mind. Since they are of one essence and not two, it is said: "The Pure Land is Mind-only; Amitābha is one's original nature."

It is not that there are no lands or Buddhas in the West such that one need not seek rebirth there; rather, it is within your own arising-and-ceasing, conditioned reflections that what is called the "nature of the mind-only" resides.
To seek that Buddha is to seek one's own mind, and to seek one's own mind is to seek that Buddha.
Even a simple village couple, though they do not understand this principle, because they believe with sincerity that that land truly exists, at the end of their lives—

At that time, one may instead attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. I fear there are those who fall into the void because they mistake the shadow of conditions for the mind and claim that there is no external land;
thus, even though they practice the Way, they still undergo birth and death. Human life is impermanent; with each breath, one turns toward the next world.
Worldly affairs form an unbroken chain and lock, never ceasing. If one cannot, amidst the oppressive entanglements of worldly toil, set aside one's ambitions and cease from action—

Regarding the place of rebirth: with a single cut, one severs [the bonds]; through the power of aspiration and practice, exerting oneself with a single leap, how could one not be reborn there in accordance with one's thought?
*Jingzhongjing youjing* Scroll One;
*Jingzhongjing youjing* Scroll Two.
Regarding the *Awakening of Faith*,
doubts and errors have led disciples to hear teachings on "easy practice" and often hesitate to cultivate them; even those who have already practiced for a long time [fall into this state].
If one wavers on the Middle Way, doubts will arise daily; one may either lose previous merit or fall into external paths.
To err because of doubt leads to endless calamities, resulting in the loss of rebirth in the Pure Land. Originally, this does not mean one can immediately attain Buddhahood;
rather, what is relied upon is that one never departs from the Buddha, remaining forever without regression. Only after one is certain of attaining Buddhahood can one be considered secure.

This concludes the section on the life [of the Master]. Regarding the *Ten Doubts of the Wise*, the *Oral Questions of Tianru*, and the *Forty-eight Questions and Answers of Yunqi*, I have not spared effort in engaging in repeated debates upon them;
their arguments are most illuminating and most incisive. These three works are currently planned for exclusive publication.

Occasionally, a few passages from them have been excerpted and included in other sections; this present section, however, draws exclusively from the various questions, challenges, and miscellaneous discourses of past worthies.
This is appended to the present work to sever doubts and rectify errors. The Section on Doubts and Errors is compiled as follows:
Chan Master Yongming Yanshou of the Wudai period asked: "If one merely perceives one's nature and awakens to the Way, one immediately transcends birth and death.
What need is there to fix the mind upon that Buddha and seek rebirth in another land? He replied: "..."
A true practitioner of the Way should examine themselves with scrutiny; as one who drinks water knows for themselves whether it is cold or warm.
Herein lies a mirror for the heart to shatter many delusions. You virtuous ones, you should observe your own conduct and understanding: have you seen your nature and awakened to the Way?

Have you received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the Tathāgata and succeeded to the rank of the Patriarchs? Are you able to equal Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna? Have you attained unimpeded eloquence and realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

Can one’s samādhi compare with that of the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai? Can one’s mastery of both doctrine and practice, as well as the cultivation of both conduct and understanding, compare with that of National Teacher Huizhong?

These great beings all clearly bestowed their teachings and deeply exhorted rebirth in the Pure Land. This was surely for the sake of benefiting themselves and others; how could they have intended to mislead others or deceive themselves?
Moreover, the Great Hero [the Buddha] praised this and spoke with solemnity from his golden mouth. One should hope to follow the example of the ancients.
Worthy one, you have respectfully received the Buddha’s command; it shall certainly not be in error.

The biographies of eminent persons from past and present recorded in the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Those Reborn) are numerous and well-known; you should diligently encourage others to read them and examine them for yourself.

Furthermore, you must consider whether, at the time of death, you will attain mastery over life and death, departure and remaining. Have your heavy karmic obstructions from beginningless time certainly been... [removed]...?

Is this present *saṃbhogakāya* certainly liberated from saṃsāra? While traversing among the various classes of beings within the three miserable realms and evil paths, is it certain that there is no suffering or affliction as one appears and disappears with ease?
Throughout the heavens, the human world, and the worlds of the ten directions, can one dwell wherever one pleases?
Is there truly no obstruction? If you have attained clear and confident realization, what could be more excellent than this?
If you have not yet done so, do not be arrogant for a moment, lest you cause yourself to sink into eternal samsara and lose the benefit of the Dharma;
whom else will you blame then? Alas! How tragic! What lamentation can avail now?

The Master Cizhao’s *Ten Gates of Admonitions on the Pure Land* states: "For those who recite the Buddha's name at the time of death, the three doubts must not arise for rebirth in the pure land to be assured.
The first is the doubt: 'I have committed extremely heavy karmic deeds since birth, while my practice has been shallow for only a few days; I fear I shall not attain rebirth.'"
Second, one may harbor doubt, thinking: "Although I recite the name of Amitābha, perhaps my heart's vows are not yet fulfilled, or my greed, anger, and ignorance have not ceased;
I fear I shall not attain rebirth. Third, one may harbor doubt, thinking: "Although I recite the name of Amitābha, at the moment of death I fear the Buddha will not come to welcome me.
With these three doubts, one creates obstacles through doubt, loses right mindfulness, and fails to attain rebirth. Therefore, one must recite...
O person of the Buddha’s school, it is of vital importance to faithfully believe the clear intent of the Buddhist sutras and not give rise to doubt. The sutra says:
"A single recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

From the highest level of single-mindedness without distraction down to the successful completion of ten recitations, one is ushered toward the nine lotus ponds and bid farewell to the five turbidities. If you can maintain this mindfulness in every thought without obscuration, then...
If mindfulness is without deviation, then emotional doubts will be forever severed, and one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
The *Longshu Jingtuwen* states: "When people suddenly hear of the scenery of the Pure Land, many do not believe it;
this is not surprising. It is because they are constrained by what they see before their eyes that they conclude that what is not seen before their eyes must also be like this."
And so it is. For instance, one who dwells in a humble alley amidst filth and mire—how could they know of the purity of a grand mansion?
One whose vessel is small and whose food is but coarse herbs—how could they know of the square-chamber feasts served before a meal?

One whose tattered chest holds but a few grains—how could they know of the overflowing abundance of the imperial treasury? Thus, dwelling in this turbid world of Saṃsāra, one does not believe that there exists purity.
They purify Buddha-fields. Thus they are born from a womb, unaware that there is the transformation-birth from a lotus;
their lifespan does not exceed a hundred years, unaware that there is a lifespan as vast as the sands of the Ganges; and their clothing and food must necessarily depend upon labor.
One does not know that they possess natural clothing and food; one’s happiness is constantly intermingled with sorrow and affliction, and one does not know that they possess singular, pure happiness.
Thus, what the Buddha has spoken cannot be disbelieved simply because it is not seen with one's own eyes.
Moreover, since the Buddha strictly admonishes people against false speech, he would certainly not speak falsely to deceive others. The world...
When people speak falsely, they do so either to seek profit or to avoid harm. The Buddha has no desires for the world; how could he seek profit?
The Buddha regards birth and death as a sword cutting through empty space; how could he seek to avoid harm? Thus, the Buddha has no occasion to employ false speech.
Among those in the world who are superior to the average person, even they would not be willing to speak falsely to their own detriment.
If even the words of a mere mortal can be trusted, how much more so those of the Buddha? His words are credible and leave no room for doubt. Thus, the sages of old said:

"If the words of the Buddha cannot be believed, what words can be believed? In the past, there was one who branded a loyal minister as a member of a treacherous faction and had this inscribed upon stone;

yet a thunderbolt from heaven struck it down. Today, we use gold, jewels, and vibrant colors to engrave and decorate the scriptures, creating wheel-storages (*dharmacakra-kośa*) to enshrine the Buddha’s teachings.
It was offered with incense and flowers and adorned by divine dragons. If its words were false, they would be even more egregious than the stele of the treacherous faction;
why then has it not been struck down by heavenly thunder for thousands and hundreds of years? It is because its words are sincere.
If one’s words are sincere yet not believed, what can one wait for? Therefore, there is nothing further to doubt regarding the teaching of the Pure Land.
Moreover, from antiquity to the present day, those who have practiced this have experienced many instances of spiritual response; thus, it is especially impossible not to believe in it.
Furthermore, it is said: Some Confucians, because they perceive that followers of the Śākya school lack preceptual conduct, disparage their teaching and consequently do not believe in the Pure Land.
This is not so. How could one disparage Laozi because some practitioners are unworthy, or disparage Confucius because some scholars are unworthy?
A wise person does not reject words because of the person; how much less should one [reject the teaching] because of its followers?
Is it that you slight their teachings? The teachings of the Śākya [Buddha] comprise both worldly dharmas and supramundane dharmas.
As for those worldly dharmas that are identical to our own Confucianism, they cannot be enumerated in detail; let me briefly cite their principal points.
That which the Śākya followers diligently instruct the world with is nothing other than the prohibition of evil and the encouragement of good—yet how has our Confucianism ever failed to do so?
To refrain from evil and encourage goodness—let us consider this in terms of the present. The Buddha identifies killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the three karmas of the body;
yet Confucius spoke of overcoming brutality and abolishing killing, and the poet said that King Wen’s virtue extended even to birds, beasts, and insects.
Is this not, indeed, refraining from killing? As for stealing, it certainly was not mentioned by him. Confucius said: "I..."
It has not been seen that anyone loves virtue as much as they love beauty. The poet of the *Shijing* satirized those who do not love virtue but delight in beautiful forms;
does this not serve as a warning against sexual misconduct? The Buddha regarded false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh words as the four karmas of the mouth.
Confucius said, "If a person lacks trustworthiness, I know not how he can exist"; does this not serve as a warning against false speech? He further spoke of "clever words and clever commands."

The vibrancy of colors is the manifestation of benevolence; does this not serve as a warning against frivolous speech? The Book of Documents says, "Do not follow others' faces in public, only to speak otherwise behind their backs";
does this not serve as a warning against double-tongued speech? Malicious speech refers to the sounds of hatred and anger, yet it has not yet reached the level of foul language.
Xunzi said that words that wound others are more piercing than spears and halberds; this was his constant warning against the mouth of malice and anger.
The Buddha further identifies greed, anger, and delusion as the three karmas of the mind. Confucius said, "When one sees gain, one should reflect upon it," which is a warning against greed.
He said of Bo Yi and Shu Qi, "They did not dwell on past wrongs," which is a warning against anger. He said, "When in distress..."

If one does not learn, such a person is among the lowest of the people; this is precisely what constitutes the admonition against delusion. From this perspective, it can be said that Confucianism and Buddhism have never been different.
The only point of difference is that while Confucianism is limited to worldly dharmas (*laukika-dharma*), Buddhism possesses both worldly and transcendental dharmas (*lokottara-dharma*).
Because Confucianism is limited to worldly dharmas, it speaks only of a single lifetime and attributes [the outcome] to Heaven. As for Buddhism—

The Śākya [tradition] further possesses supramundane dharmas; thus, one knows that over successive lifetimes they perceive the beginning and end of the karmic conditions of sentient beings—this is precisely where they differ.

If one wishes to know the strengths of the Śākya tradition, one must examine the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi Sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Sūtra Asked by the Bodhisattva Anāvaraṇajñāna*, as well as understand the principles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. [Without these], one cannot [truly understand them].
To take what is right and instead condemn it as wrong—this is precisely what Confucius called "acting without understanding. Should one not be cautious of such?
If this is indeed the case, then the teachings of the Śākya clan are worthy of trust. How could one fail to believe his words regarding the Pure Land?
What is called the supramundane Dharma—Pure Land is particularly essential among these; one must not fail to exert oneself in it.
Furthermore, it is said: In the world there are those who specialize exclusively in Zen meditation, claiming that since the Pure Land is "mind-only," how could there be any further Pure Land?
"The nature itself is Amitābha; there is no need to see Amitābha further. This statement seems plausible yet is incorrect. Why?
Because the Western Pure Land possesses both principle (*li*) and manifestation (*ji*). If one discusses its principle, it can purify the mind; therefore, everything is pure.
Truly, this is the Pure Land of Mind-Only. As for its actual manifestation, there is indeed a world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*);

the Buddha has explained this with repeated and detailed earnestness—how could it be a false word? That every person can attain Buddhahood, which is what is meant by the so-called "Amida of one's own nature" (*svabhāva-amitābha*), is certainly not false.
Nevertheless, one cannot suddenly reach this state; it is like fine timber that can be carved into a Buddha.
An image may be exceedingly magnificent, yet it can only be accomplished through the labor of carving;
one cannot point to fine timber and immediately claim that the magnificence of the object has been realized. This is what is meant by the "Pure Land of Mind Only."
It is not the case that there is no longer any Pure Land, nor that one need not see Amitābha, for his very nature is Amitābha.
Furthermore, some may believe in the existence of a Pure Land yet cling to the doctrine of "mind-only," thereby claiming that the Western Realm is unworthy of being reborn in.
This refers to those who, through Zen meditation, claim to have awakened their nature, surpassing even the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and asserting that Amitābha is not worth seeing;
all such people have missed the mark. Why is this? Such talk is exceedingly lofty, and I fear it is difficult to reach.
In that Western Pure Land, there is no greed, no attachment, no anger, and no delusion. Is my own mind capable of being free from greed, attachment, anger, and delusion? In that Western Pure Land...
If one thinks of clothing, one obtains clothing; if one thinks of food, one obtains food. If one desires stillness, one attains stillness; if one desires to depart, one attains departure.
Yet, when I think of clothing but have no clothing, cold distresses my mind. When I think of food but have no food, hunger distresses my mind.
When I desire stillness but cannot attain stillness, the multitude of distractions distresses my mind. When I desire to depart but cannot depart, the bonds and entanglements distress my mind.
The mind—this so-called "Pure Land of Mind-Only"—is indeed not easily reached. That Amitābha Buddha possesses blessings as vast as mountains and seas, and power that upholds heaven and earth;
he transforms the hells into lotus blossoms as easily as turning over his hand, and beholds infinite worlds as if they were before his eyes.
Yet my own power of merit cannot even accomplish this for myself, and I am constantly fearful of my past karma.
How much more so for one who has fallen into hell? How much more so for one who has been transformed into a lotus flower?
One cannot even perceive what occurs on the other side of a wall; how much less can one see the infinite worlds? This is what is called the "Amida of self-nature"—truly not easy to reach.
Nevertheless, my own mind *can* be the Pure Land, yet it has not suddenly become the Pure Land; such is my nature.

One ought to be able to become Amitābha, yet suddenly one is unable to become Amitābha; how then can one neglect the Pure Land and fail to cultivate it, or abandon Amitābha and refuse to desire to see him?
Therefore, by cultivating the Western Paradise, one sees the Buddha and attains the Way with extreme ease.

If one remains only in this world, desiring to practice Chan to awaken the nature and transcend both Buddhas and patriarchs is extremely difficult. How much more so for those who cultivate the Pure Land;
since practicing the Pure Land does not hinder the practice of Chan, why must those who practice Chan disparage the Pure Land and fail to cultivate it?
The *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states: "In the ten directions there are immeasurable bodhisattvas who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
If even those bodhisattvas are reborn there while still remaining as ordinary beings, what person am I that I should not wish to be reborn there? Would I then be superior to all those bodhisattvas?
From this it is clear that the teaching of the "Pure Land of Mind-Only" and the "Amitābha of Self-Nature" is grand in theory but unnecessary in practice.

To speak loftily without being practical, or to practice without reaching the essential point, has misled many people. It is better to tread firmly on the ground, engaging in recitation and cultivation;

then every person will surely be born in the Pure Land and directly escape the cycle of saṃsāra. This stands as far apart from those who offer empty words devoid of substance as heaven and earth do from one another.
It is further said: "The Buddha-eye perceives events across immeasurable kalpas; therefore, from antiquity to the present, there is nothing it does not see.

Furthermore, one who observes the precept against false speech will certainly not themselves speak falsely to deceive others. Moreover, one who observes the precept against the notion of self will certainly not themselves maintain a sense of self to boast before others.
Thus, their words are truly worthy of being followed as a model. According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*).
They all have a lifespan of ten million years; when their numbers are exhausted, they re-enter the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).

Because they have never realized the true nature (*dharmatā*), they share the same name as the sentient beings of the six realms—namely, the "seven destinies" (*sapta-gati*). These are all people within the cycle of rebirth. As for those among the world’s people who study the path of the immortals (*ṛṣi*):

Out of ten thousand, not one succeeds. Even if one were to succeed, they would still not escape the cycle of saṃsāra, because they remain attached to form and spirit and are unable to relinquish them.
Furthermore, form and spirit are but delusions manifested within the true nature; they are not reality. Thus, Hanshan’s poem says:
"Even if you attain the status of an immortal, it is no different from guarding a corpse. This is not like the [views of] the Buddhist school.

Their coming and going in birth and death are as they please, and they are not constrained by anything. In recent centuries, those who have attained the state of an immortal are only Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin;
yet those who study the methods of Zhongli and Lü surely number in the tens of thousands, among my own personal acquaintances alone.
Their numbers were not few, yet in the end they all died and were buried beneath the earth; this was a lifelong, empty expenditure of mental and physical energy that ultimately yielded no benefit.
If you wish to seek long life, nothing compares to the Pure Land. Those born in the Pure Land enjoy an immeasurable lifespan.

The significance of this for attaining long life is immense. To fail to understand and cultivate this dharma-gate while instead studying the ways of the immortals is like discarding a fine jade present before one’s eyes to seek a *wǔfū* stone whose acquisition cannot be guaranteed—is this not delusion?

Someone may say, "Pure Land is a matter for after death; what proof or verification is there? The answer is: the *Jingtu zhuan* (Biographies of Pure Land) fully records such spiritual responses; how could it be otherwise?

There is no evidence [for such claims]. How much less so for the case of immortals (shenxian), who, upon attaining anything, keep it extremely secret and do not transmit it, believing that to reveal the celestial mechanism (tianji) would incur sin.
The gates of the Buddha-dharma, by contrast, fear only that its transmission may not be widespread;
they desire nothing more than to deliver all sentient beings before ceasing their efforts. This vastness of compassion is unfathomable and cannot be compared to that of the immortals.
It is further said: "There are those who do not believe in cause and effect, and consequently do not believe in the Pure Land.
Now, how can one possibly disbelieve in cause and effect? A sutra says: 'If you wish to know the causes of your previous life, look at what you are experiencing in this life;
if you wish to know the effects of your future life, look at what you are creating in this life. If you do not believe these words, why not observe the matters before your very eyes?"

The reason why human life includes poverty and wealth, nobility and meanness, suffering and joy, toil and ease, honor and disgrace, longevity and early death—such diverse varieties of fortune—is said to be the mandate of Heaven (*tianming*). Yet how could Heaven be partial toward individuals?

It is simply because the actions performed by people in their previous lives were different; therefore, the retributions they receive in this life are also different, and Heaven merely presides over them.

For this reason, this body is called the retribution body (*vipākakāya*). As for the retribution body, it arises because it is the recompense for what one did in previous lives; thus, this body is born.
What part does Heaven have in this? It is like a person who, having committed merits or offenses, must receive rewards or punishments from the government offices.
How could government offices act with partiality toward individuals? They simply preside over the principle that merit must be rewarded and transgression must be punished.

How could they impose rewards or punishments upon people without cause? If even worldly governments do not inflict rewards or punishments on people without justification, how much less would Heaven and Earth, in their creative transformation, bestow calamities or blessings upon people without cause?
Thus we know that because of the good and evil deeds committed in previous lives, one is recompensed with misfortune or fortune accordingly.

Since one cannot be purely virtuous, one cannot receive purely fortunate retributions; consequently, there are those who are wealthy and noble yet suffer from misery and premature death, those who are poor and lowly yet enjoy happiness, and those who possess honor and favor yet endure decline and disgrace. Such are the various ways in which karmic fruits and retributions manifest.
According to what one does, the result follows like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound; there is not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy.

Thus it is said: "Planting peach trees, one obtains peaches; planting apricot trees, one obtains apricots. It has never happened that by planting hemp one obtains beans, or by planting millet one obtains broomcorn millet.

Only the time of sowing is brief, while the time of harvest is long; therefore, the time spent performing good or evil deeds is very small, yet the retribution for receiving misfortune or fortune is very great.

It is great. Thus it is said: "In spring one sows a single grain of millet; in autumn one reaps ten thousand seeds. In human life, whether one performs good or evil, the retribution is just like this.
This is indeed the natural principle of the transformative power of the universe (*dharmatā*). If this principle can be trusted, then the teaching of the Pure Land must necessarily be trusted.
Why? Because both are the words of the Buddha. Since the Buddha’s words regarding cause and effect are sincere, they are certainly not false.
It is said regarding the Pure Land: thus, those who do not believe in cause and effect consequently do not believe in the Pure Land;
this may serve to resolve their delusions.
Furthermore, it is said that when people see good or evil deeds before them without immediate retribution, they consequently do not believe in cause and effect. And because...

Because they do not believe in the Pure Land, they fail to realize that when good and evil have not yet received their retribution, it is not that there is no retribution; it is merely a matter of whether it is swift or slow.
The Buddha once said to Ānanda: "There are those who perform good deeds in this life but fall into hell upon death, and those who commit evil in this life but are born in heaven upon death.
Ānanda asked why this was so. The Buddha replied: "Those who perform good deeds in this life and die..."
Those who fall into hell are such that the good karma of their present life has not yet ripened, while the evil karma of their past lives has already ripened.

Those who commit evil in their present life but are born in heaven after death are such that the evil of their present life has not yet ripened, while the goodness of their past lives has already ripened.

Where the karma has ripened, one first receives its retribution; it is like a debt, where what is most urgent is repaid first. The Master of the Left (Zuo Shi) said that Lord Luan Wu possessed virtue.
Because [the father] can provide shelter for his son, even though his son Yan committed evil, he was able to escape calamity.
Yet, when Yan’s son Ying practiced goodness, the evil of Yan instead brought misfortune upon him; thus, despite being virtuous, Ying met with disaster.
Speaking of what is visible before our eyes in this world, such is the retribution for good and evil. How much more so when separated by time?

O world! The Book of Documents says: "The Way of Heaven blesses the good and brings calamity upon the licentious. Laozi says: "The net of Heaven is vast and wide; it is coarse-meshed, yet nothing escapes it.
Thus, all three teachings speak of this principle; there is only a difference in the speed with which it manifests.
How can one fail to believe in cause and effect simply because the retribution is not seen before one's eyes? And on that basis, how can one fail to believe in the Pure Land?

Furthermore, it is said: Someone may doubt this, asking, "When a person here in this world recites the Buddha’s name, how can a single lotus flower immediately arise in the Western Seven-Jeweled Pond?
I reply to them: This is not difficult to understand. It is, for example, like a great bright mirror;
whenever an object comes before it, its reflection appears. How could the mirror ever harbor a conscious intention? It is simply because of its clarity that this occurs spontaneously.
In the land of Amitābha Buddha, it is pure, clear, and bright, naturally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions as clearly as one beholds one’s own reflection in a bright mirror.
For this reason, when one recites the Buddha’s name here, a single lotus flower will naturally arise in the western pond of the seven treasures;
of this there is no doubt. Yet some may still harbor doubts, saying: "As for those who recite the mantra for rebirth..."
"Amitābha Buddha constantly dwells upon the crown of that person's head to protect them.

If there are immeasurable sentient beings in immeasurable worlds who recite this mantra, how could Amitābha Buddha possibly go to the crown of each and every one of their heads? [The answer is: "It is said:"
This is also simply natural. It is like the single moon in the sky appearing universally in all bodies of water;
how could this not be natural? Some who practice with diligence may doubt this, saying: "Furthermore, at the time of death, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas come to welcome one.
Yet, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there are immeasurable sentient beings practicing with diligence; how could [the Buddhas] possibly know them all?"

When asked, "Does he go there to welcome them at the appointed time? [the Buddha] replied, "It is simply natural. For example, when the sun shines upon the heavens, it universally illuminates immeasurable realms;
how could this not be natural? How much more so the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, which far surpasses that of the sun and moon!
Thus, it dwells everywhere upon their crowns and knows their times everywhere—how can there be any cause for doubt?"
