Master Huìjué Yù said: "Some claim that the Pure Land is merely a skillful means (upāya) of the sages, intended to guide those of dull faculties and transform those with ordinary capacities.
If one were able to transcend directly and enter the stage of the Tathāgata all at once, what need would there be for the power of another?"
The answer is: Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra during the Buddha’s lifetime, and after his parinirvāṇa, Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna;
in this land, Zhizhe and Zhijue—all of them made vows to be reborn there. Are they all to be considered of dull faculties?

Śākyamuni, in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, exhorted his father King Śuddhodana and sixty thousand members of the Śākya clan to all be born in the Pure Land. Are they all to be considered ordinary vessels? Such as these...

Would the sages and worthies of old all have been inferior to those of sharp faculties and superior capacity found today? Moreover, if this were treated as a mere expedient (*upāya*), what then could be considered the reality?
The distinction between the expedient and the real does not follow a single path; were it not for one whose eye of the teachings is clear, how could one discern them?
You who possess discernment should believe the words of the Buddha; the retribution for [disregarding them] is no light matter—do not treat this with levity. Formerly, Sun Xin...

The Old Scholar (Lao Xueshi) initially harbored doubts on this account. Consequently, at a gathering with Yang Cigong and his guest, Minister Wang Minzhong, they discussed the Way until their views were in perfect accord, whereupon the scholar’s doubts were resolved. Both Cigong and Minzhong were Confucian scholars who studied Chan;
as they were now diligently seeking rebirth in the Pure Land as their refuge, one can know that the Pure Land is not a mere provisional device of the Sage, but is indeed true Chan.
Regarding the dwelling of his companions, Master Baiting said: "Those who cultivate the practice of Pure Land are always many, yet those who find its gate and proceed directly are few.
Those who discourse on the Pure Land are always many, yet those who grasp its essentials and point directly to it are perhaps rare. I have never heard of anyone who...

Regarding those who obstruct and conceal themselves for the sake of preaching: that which most obstructs oneself is nothing other than craving; that which most conceals oneself is nothing other than doubt.
If one can ensure that these two minds of doubt and craving are entirely free of obstruction, then the single gateway to the Pure Land will never be interrupted.

The preface to *The Treatise on the Ten Doubts* by the Son of Non-action states: "If craving is not profound, one will not be born in Saṃsāra; if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī."
Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty established a religious society on Mount Lu. He invited Yuanming because he valued his ability to attain realization and sever worldly attachments;
yet he rejected Xie Lingyun because his mind was muddled and his thoughts could not be focused.
Was this not precisely because these two individuals represented the essential gateway to the Pure Land?
Wuwei Yang Cigong said: "In this world, there are virtuous gentlemen who harbor three kinds of faithless thoughts regarding the Pure Land and refuse to seek rebirth there;
these are truly lamentable. The first is: 'I shall transcend both Buddhas and patriarchs; the Pure Land is no place for me to be born. The second is: 'Everywhere is the Pure Land;
I need not necessarily go to the West. The third is: 'The Holy Realm of Ultimate Bliss is for those of us who are ordinary [beings]..."
Indeed, one cannot fail to be reborn there. For those who traverse the ocean of practice, it is inexhaustible; for Samantabhadra, he vowed to see Amitābha;

though the Buddha-lands are empty, Vimalakīrti constantly cultivated the Pure Land; the Tathāgatas of the ten directions offer praise with their broad tongues, and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions share the resolve to go together.
Try to reflect upon this yourself: as for saying that one is insufficient to be reborn, how can such a claim be made? How self-centered!
How deceptive! Take for instance Nāgārjuna, the patriarchal master; the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* contains a prophetic text concerning him. Take also Vasubandhu, the founder of the doctrinal school;

the *Treatise on the Rebirth in the Pure Land* contains verses on seeking rebirth there. Ci’en [Xuanzang] praised him in his *General Praise*, first citing his "ten excellences," while Zhiyi analyzed the principles, clearly resolving the "ten doubts.
These were all men of supreme wisdom who diligently practiced for rebirth in the Pure Land. How can one say that rebirth there is unnecessary?
How self-deluded you are! The fiery chariots of hell may be extinguished; the boat upon the rocks may not sink.

Among those who manifest the retribution of their present deeds, none was more extreme than Zhang Kui, yet he transcended through ten recitations of the Buddha’s name. Among those dwelling in the depths of hell, none was more urgent than Xiong Jun, yet he revived and realized the wondrous cause.
The transgressions of worldly people may not necessarily be like this; to say that rebirth is impossible—how is it that you so utterly abandon yourselves?
Deceiving oneself, being self-conceited, and abandoning one’s own spirit, one flows into the cycle of saṃsāra—whose fault is this?
From *Master Tianru’s Questions on the Pure Land*: Question: The human mind is easily advanced and easily regressed; upon hearing a single word of exhortation, it may progress. Yet...

Though one is courageous and diligent, if suddenly an obstacle or difficulty should appear before one's eyes, one may immediately shift one’s thoughts and seek other expedients, claiming that pure practice is merely a matter for after death and offers no benefit in the present moment.
Consequently, body and mind both withdraw and slacken; is this not indeed understandable? The answer is: what you perceive is not yet...
It is extensive. Have you not seen it stated in the sutras that those who receive and uphold the names of the Buddhas shall obtain ten kinds of benefits in the present life?
First, day and night they shall always be protected by all the great powerful divine generals of the heavens, with retinues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, remaining invisible.
Second, they shall always be accompanied by twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, and one...
First, all bodhisattvas will constantly follow and protect them. Second, they will always receive the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas day and night;
Amitābha Buddha will constantly emit light rays to gather in and sustain such a person. Third, no evil spirits—whether yakṣas or rākṣasas—will be able to harm them;
no venomous snakes, poisonous dragons, or toxic drugs will be able to take effect upon them. Fourth, fire...
They shall not encounter the calamities of water, nor the threats of enemies, bandits, swords, or arrows; they shall not suffer imprisonment, shackles, or untimely and unjust deaths.

Sixth, all previously committed karmic deeds shall be completely extinguished, and the lives of those enemies they have killed shall find liberation, such that no further retribution or opposition remains.
Seventh, their dreams at night shall be upright, or they may dream of the sublime and wondrous form of Amitābha Buddha. Eighth.

First, their minds will always be joyful; second, their complexions will be radiant and lustrous; third, their physical strength and vigor will be abundant; fourth, all their undertakings will be auspicious and successful; fifth, they will never encounter calamities or adversities; sixth, they will always be protected by heavenly beings; seventh, they will not fall into evil realms;

eighth, their hearts will always be filled with joy, their countenances will be bright and glowing, their energy will be full and flourishing, and all they do will be prosperous and fortunate; ninth, they will always be honored, venerated, and provided for by all the people of the world, who will joyfully prostrate before them as if worshipping the Buddha;
tenth, at the time of death, their hearts will be free from fear, right mindfulness will manifest before them, and they will behold Amitābha Buddha and...
The assembly of holy ones, holding golden lotus flowers, will welcome and lead those reborn in the Western Pure Land, where they shall enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss until the end of the future.
These ten kinds of benefits, as recorded in detail in the sutra, were proclaimed by the Buddha’s own mouth.
Since this benefits both the present life and future lives, there is no dharma-door more essential for both the mundane and supramundane realms than the practice of Buddha-recitation.
You should simply apply yourself with diligence; there is no need for doubt.

Chan Master Changlu Ze said: "Now, although the World-Honored Tathāgata employs the two gates of *saṃgraha* (attraction) and *vidhāna* (repression), and manifests his residence in both pure and impure lands, the original intention of the Sage was not that the Sahā world—with its hills, mounds, pits, and gullies;
its five realms of rebirth living in intermixture; its mountains of earth and stone; and its abundance of foul impurities—is simply to be loathed. Nor was it because the world of Ultimate Bliss..."
The realm has the ground of pure gold; its rows of trees reach toward the sky, and its towers soar with the seven treasures. Flowers bloom in four colors—this alone is truly cause for joy.
This is because those who first enter the Way have not yet perfected the power of patience (*kṣānti*); they must rely upon pure conditions as a superior support. Why is this?
In the Sahā world, Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet been born. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Amitābha...
While the Buddha currently dwells preaching the Dharma in this Sahā world, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta can only be admired from afar for their illustrious names.

In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, however, those two sublime beings personally serve as one’s supreme spiritual friends. In this Sahā world, various demons vie with one another to harass and disturb practitioners;
in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, amidst its great radiance, there is certainly no such demonic interference. In this Sahā world, corrupt sounds are intermingled...
Turbulent is this world, where women’s beauty is seductive and licentious. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, however, the water-birds and forest trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma;

their primary retribution is pure and serene, and there are truly no women there. Thus, for the cultivation of practice, nothing compares to the Western Realm in terms of having all necessary conditions.

Yet those of shallow faith rashly give rise to doubt and slander. Allow me to discuss this earnestly: among the people of this land, there is none who does not weary of the clamor and bustle of the secular home and long for [the peace of the West].
Because of the tranquility of the *araṇya*, those who abandon their homes to leave the household life are praised with earnestness.

Yet, how could the manifold sufferings of this Sahā world be limited merely to the clamor of a secular dwelling? And how could the leisurely ease of Sukhāvatī be limited merely to the stillness of an *araṇya*?
To recognize the excellence of leaving the household life yet not wish for rebirth there—this is the first delusion. To toil with hardship over ten thousand *li* to seek knowledge from afar...
The "wise one" (zhishi) is one who illuminates the Great Matter and resolves the questions of birth and death.

Since the World-Honored One Amitābha possesses supreme physical and mental karma and his power of vows is vast and profound, every utterance of his perfect voice brings clarity and accord with reality. To wish to associate with such a wise one yet not desire to see the Buddha—this is the second delusion.
As for the vast assemblies in monastic groves, all delight in dwelling there; yet they do not wish to [enter] a small community or a place of practice (daochang).
To rely [on worldly attachments] while the number of those in the Land of Ultimate Bliss who are in their final birth before Buddhahood is exceedingly great,

and where all such superior virtuous people assemble in one place— yet, desiring to frequent forest hermitages while not admiring the pure assembly of the ocean-like multitude— this is the third delusion.

The people of this land rarely exceed a hundred years in their maximum lifespan; yet they are beset by childhood ignorance, senility, and chronic illness, with the eyes of stupor and sleep closing for the greater part of their lives.

If even Bodhisattvas remain obscured by the "darkness between states" (*antarābhava*) and Śrāvakas still lack clarity upon emerging from the womb, then a mere inch of jade or a moment of time—nine-tenths of which are lost—before reaching the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), is truly cause for heartache. As for those in the Western [Land]...
The lifespan of such persons is immeasurable; they rest within a lotus calyx, free from the suffering of death, continuing in an uninterrupted succession until reaching Bodhi.
Thus, they immediately attain the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), and the rank of Buddhahood can be expected with certainty.

Yet, while wandering through the transient life-span of this Sahā world, they remain unaware of the long-lasting years in the Pure Land—this is their fourth delusion. As for those whose rank has reached the stage of non-retrogression and whose fruition is realized...
Being unborn, they are without desire amidst desire; dwelling in the dust of the world, they are not defiled by it.

Only then can they give rise to unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) and exercise coessential pity (*sahaja-karuṇā*), returning to enter the realm of worldly toil and harmonize their light with the five turbidities. As for those who have heard but little and possess only single-minded wisdom, or who correspond to a small degree of goodness—
They then claim to have forever emerged from the four currents and transcended the ten stages; they revile the Pure Land while remaining attached to this Sahā world.

Thus, with eyes blindfolded, they return empty-handed, wandering aimlessly as they were before, side by side with oxen and horses, following in the footsteps of hell-beings, unaware of who they truly are.
This is comparable to a Bodhisattva of Great Power; such is the fifth delusion. Thus, the Sūtra says: "One should make this vow:
'May I be born in that land. To fail to believe the sincere words of the Buddhas and not wish to be reborn in the Pure Land—is this not utterly deluded?
If one believes the Buddha’s words and is born in the Pure Land, then one cannot be constrained by the bonds of successive existences, nor can one be affected by the kalpas of time.

They cannot cause harm. One repents the eight sufferings of the human realm and lacks the five signs of decline in the heavens. Since even the name of the evil realms does not exist, how much less could they have reality?
Only the Dharma of the One Vehicle is revealed; there is certainly no third. Taking refuge in the Three Jewels of the One Essence, one serves the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
The Buddha’s light illuminates the body, and the myriad delusions silently vanish. The flavor of the Dharma nourishes the spirit, and the six...
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are fully perfected; one should bring them to completion through mindfulness.

The thirty-two manifestations of bodies according to various types pervade all lands as numerous as motes of dust, circulating through the five realms of existence and universally benefiting all faculties.

Without wavering from a single mind, one universally practices samādhi, sprinkling the water of meditative concentration throughout the trichiliocosm and delivering sentient beings from the burning house. Thus, both self-benefit and the benefit of others are entirely perfected.
It is full. Thus, the Pure Land of Mind-Only and the Amitābha of Self-Nature are truly the essential gateway to liberation and the swift path for cultivation.
For this reason, there is no definitive Mahāyāna teaching that does not point toward the Pure Land;

from the sages of the past to those of the present, both self and others have all vowed to be reborn there. This is because, in wishing to deliver others, one must first deliver oneself. Alas! Among men...
To be heedless is certain to bring near sorrow. Once one loses this human body, there will be deep regret for ten thousand kalpas.

Therefore, leading the great assembly of the ocean-like multitude, each should recite the name of Amitābha Buddha—whether a hundred times, a thousand times, or even ten thousand times—and dedicate these merits toward the same aspiration: the vow to be reborn in that land.
I earnestly hope that this sublime assembly at the Lotus Pond and the Dharma-light of the Golden Land will mutually support one another in exquisite harmony, so that this vow may surely be fulfilled.
Like a boat sailing with the current, if the labor of oars and poles is further applied, then even a journey of a hundred thousand li will be reached without toil.

Master Lianchi said to Wu Dajun: "Do not concern yourself with whether you have attained awakening or not; do not concern yourself with existence or non-existence, nor with the internal, external, or intermediate;
do not concern yourself with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; do not concern yourself with whether this dharma-gate is the same as or different from others.
Since doubt has not yet arisen, do not concern yourself with who is right and who is wrong. Simply hold fast to the Name, with single-minded devotion and undivided attention."
Practice with uninterrupted continuity, acting with pure singleness and without distraction.

It is further said: Nowadays, many people are fond of talking about "investigation and awakening" (cankewu) and fond of speaking of "transcending birth and death. They do not realize that realization in this land is extremely difficult;
it is called "vertically transcending the three realms. Even a Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner) must still come back once more—how much more so for an ordinary person?
The sentient beings of this land mostly first take birth in the Western Land and subsequently attain awakening.
This single gate of being born in the Western Land is called "transcending the three realms horizontally"; it is without fail in ten thousand cases.
Furthermore, he replied to Wu Jili, saying: "There is no need to worry that your karmic offenses are deep, nor is there any need to doubt that your spiritual capacity is dull. A sutra states:
'A single sincere invocation of the name of Amitābha Buddha extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
How can one then doubt that one's karma is deep? Moreover, the ancient sages said: 'There is only the shortcut of practice: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.'"
"What need is there to worry about dull faculties? Seeing his companion, he told him this. He further said:
"There are those who claim that the Pure Land is solely within the mind, and that beyond the ten million billion lands there is no further Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This doctrine of 'mind-only' originally derives from the words of the sutras; it is truly not erroneous. However, as for those who cite and rely upon it..."
You have misunderstood its essential meaning. Indeed, mind is identical to objects; ultimately, there are no objects external to the mind.
Objects are identical to mind; likewise, there is no mind external to objects. Since objects are entirely mind, why must one rigidly cling to the mind while rejecting objects?

To negate objects in order to speak of the mind is not yet to have attained a thorough understanding of the mind. Others may further say: "The Pure Land seen at the moment of death is all [a projection of] oneself..."

Therefore, there is no Pure Land [external to the mind]. When considering those who have practiced *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) throughout past and present and attained rebirth, they were met by the holy assembly at the moment of death, accompanied by celestial music, exotic fragrances, banners, pennants, and palatial towers.

While it might be said that these were seen only by that single individual as manifestations of their own mind, at that time the entire great assembly saw them as well; some even heard celestial music resoundingly fading away toward the west.
Furthermore, there was a rare fragrance that remained in the room for many days without dispersing. Now, celestial music does not travel toward other directions; yet it departed facing west.
Since that person has already passed away, this fragrance still remains. How can this be called a lack of a Pure Land?
As for Master Chan Master Yuanzhao, people see his name designated as being in the "Lotus Grade" (Sukhāvatī); how could one take the mind of another and treat it as if it were Master Yuanzhao’s own?
"Is it the mind? Furthermore, let me ask you: when the signs of hell appear at the moment of death, is that not the mind? He replied, "It is the mind.
"Does that person fall into hell? He replied, "Yes, he falls. "Now, since he has fallen into hell, the existence of hell is clearly established."
Is it that the Pure Land alone does not exist? For one whose mind manifests hell, they fall into a truly existent hell;
for one whose mind manifests the Pure Land, do they not arise in a truly existent Pure Land?

Furthermore, it is said that among scholars there are those who slight the Pure Land and do not practice its cultivation, saying: "For people like us, we ought to enter official service through the imperial examinations;
why should we instead accept an office as a 'yearly tribute' (sègòng) candidate? One scholar remarked: "This analogy is a great error. The lotus pedestals are themselves divided into nine grades.
Why do you not take the highest, but instead content yourself with being of the lower grade? Now, to advance [the argument]:
The scholar-rank (shike) comprises three hundred positions, which may also be divided into nine grades—high, middle, and low.

Why do you not take the vanguard of those ranks, but instead content yourself with being at the very end of the list? Those of the highest grade attain rebirth above; they are the very leaders of the Lotus rank. Thus, the verse praises them:
"The three minds are fully developed, and the profound principle of truth is clearly understood; they proceed to the Golden Terrace, where they immediately realize non-arising."

Within the School of the Gate (the Chan/Zen tradition), this refers to that which is called "passing the imperial examination with one's mind empty and returning home" after achieving great penetration and great awakening.
Upon hearing this, the scholar sighed and said, "My doubts have melted away like ice."
Furthermore, it is said: Someone asked, "The Tathāgata Śākyamuni pressed the earth with his toe and it immediately became a golden world.

Since the Buddha possesses such supernormal powers, why does he not immediately transform this Sahā world—this place filled with mountains of earth and stone and impurities—into the Land of Ultimate Bliss adorned with the seven treasures? Why must sentient beings instead be made to run about [in search of it]?"
Regarding the vast distance of hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-lands—alas! The Buddha cannot save those with whom he has no karmic affinity;
do you understand this? A pure affinity invokes a pure land. If the minds of sentient beings are not pure, even though a pure land exists, by what means could they be born there?

It is like the ten wholesome deeds that lead to rebirth in heaven; one might transform a hell into a heavenly realm, yet for those sentient beings who commit the ten unwholesome acts, the Tathāgata...
He extended his golden arm to pull him [up], yet the man was ultimately unable to cross even its threshold.

For this reason, in an instant, the world of Golden Color vanished through the Buddha’s withdrawal of his supernormal power, and it returned once more to being the Sahā world. Furthermore, one person asked:

"The sutra states that a single sincere recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. What do you say to this statement?"
Is it a matter of facts? Or is it a matter of principle? Alas! A scripture says: "A single invocation of 'Namo Buddha' has already established one upon the path to Buddhahood. It further says:
"In a single prostration to the Buddha, from the heels of the feet up to the Diamond Realm, every speck of dust represents the attainment of the rank of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*).
Now, there is truly no need to debate whether this refers to facts or principles; one must simply apply oneself with utmost sincerity (*zhìxīn*). This is the only thing to be feared.
If the mind does not reach [the truth], do not worry that your transgressions will not be extinguished. As it is with phenomena, so it is with principle;
as it is with principle, so it is with phenomena. What cause for doubt is there?
Furthermore, it is said: Someone asked Miaoxi, "Fools spend their entire days counting prayer beads, seeking pure karma.

Is the practice of reciting the Buddha's name something that fools do? Alas! I have previously debated this. Miaoxi merely stated that fools spend their entire days counting prayer beads while seeking pure karma;
he did not say that fools spend their entire days seeking pure karma with a single, undistracted mind.

He asked again: "An ancient master’s verse says: 'Those who achieve Buddhahood are rare; those who practice nianfo are many. If one practices for a long time, it may instead turn into demonic activity.
If you now wish to easily achieve Buddhahood, a mind of non-thought is not too much. This refers to 'nianfo without thought.

How can one practice nianfo with a mind of 'having' [thoughts]? [The Master] replied: "This is an exhortation intended for those who practice nianfo with a distracted mind and do not contemplate the mind."
Furthermore, it is not said that one who has practiced for a long time yet remains undisturbed in mind becomes a demon.

To have no thought of Buddha at all, yet first to worry about having such thoughts, is like a hungry person who wishes to eat but first worries about a bloated belly and so does not eat. He asked again:
"The Sixth Patriarch said, 'If people in the East commit evil, they should recite the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the West. What was the intent of this? He replied: "The Sixth Patriarch..."

To say that evil people recite the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, while not saying that good people recite the Buddha’s name with single-mindedness and without distraction, implies they are seeking rebirth.
Furthermore, an evil person would certainly not recite the Buddha’s name; if there were one who did, it would be a pretense and not true recitation.
It is like an evil person practicing the ten wholesome deeds to seek rebirth in heaven: an evil person would certainly not practice the ten wholesome deeds; if there were one who did...

Such "goodness" is merely a pretense; it is not true cultivation. There has never been a truly good person who recited the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion and was not reborn in the Western Land.
He asked again: "The ancient masters said that 'discarding the defiled to seek the pure' is the karma of birth and death.

How then can one discard the Sahā world to seek Sukhāvatī? He replied: "When they said that discarding the defiled to seek the pure constitutes the karma of birth and death, they were not speaking of [the practice of] single-minded..."
To fix the mind on grasping for a pure land while remaining distracted is itself an action of birth and death. You have not yet abandoned the defiled, yet you already worry about grasping the pure;

this is identical to the previous worry regarding having thoughts. Furthermore, it was asked: The Chan school says, "I do not like to hear the single word 'Buddha,'" and they also say, "Kill even if the Buddha comes;
kill even if a demon comes. If that is so, why practice the recitation of the Buddha's name? Alas! As for their speaking of the Buddha...
As for this single word "one" (之), I do not like to hear it. As for the four characters "single-mindedness without distraction" (一心不亂), I do not like to hear them either.
When he says, "If the Buddha comes, kill him; if the Mara comes, kill him," he does not say, "If 'single-mindedness without distraction' comes, kill it too."
Now, returning to the source is non-dual, yet the expedient means are manifold. Therefore, while the home to which one returns is one, the boat and the carriage each follow their own path.
To mock the carriage with the boat, or to mock the boat with the carriage, results in nothing but frivolous discourse. This principle is self-evident; there is no need for redundant words.
He asked again: "Recently someone said, 'I do not practice mindfulness of the Buddha, because internally there is a mind that can contemplate, and externally there is a Buddha who is contemplated.
As long as this duality of subject and object is not forgotten, how can it be called the Way? Alas! Does he consider solitary abiding in empty stillness to be the Way?
Internally there is a mind capable of stillness, and externally there is an object of stillness—is this not yet the duality of subject and object?"
Is it not so? Why not simply say "the single mind is undisturbed"? Then who is there to act, and upon what object? What is internal, and what is external?
Since you and I have already cultivated the Pure Land, we need only worry about failing to reach the state where the single mind is undisturbed.

If the single mind is undisturbed, then let him face a thousand kinds of ridicule and ten thousand kinds of slander; one shall remain as majestic and immovable as Mount Tai. What more is there to say?
How perplexing!
Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* (*Wangsheng lun zhu*) states: Question: When Yao dwelt in a thatched hut, Ji Fu admonished him regarding the use of jade ornaments.

Among the kings and ministers of the world, even the most exalted value simplicity and plainness; why then do the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Land prize such precious adornments? Answer: There are two meanings to this. First:
The man of superior wisdom knows that when the mind is pure, the land is naturally pure; when one is upright and victorious, the foundation is necessarily strong.
This is indeed the natural principle. The mind is truly free from attachment. It is like Shun while he was in the furrows of the fields, personally bearing the plow and hoe;

once he received the abdication from Yao, the ceremonial halts and the ceremonial cap with its hanging jade discs were provided spontaneously without being sought. What did Shun have to do for his own pleasure? Therefore it is said: "Though he possessed the world, he did not regard it as his own."
Second, for the sake of ordinary beings of dull faculties who are bent [toward worldly things], it is necessary to demonstrate suffering and pleasure so that they may give rise to joy and aversion.

First, one leads them by means of the hook of desire, and later causes them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom. This is analogous to a country currently afflicted by famine and cold suddenly hearing of the prospect of fullness and warmth.
Having been submerged in the precipice of profound darkness, one suddenly beholds the realm of radiant light. How could one’s body and mind not leap with joy?
Shedding the old for the new, one attains rebirth there and ultimately achieves liberation. Such is the manner in which one is skillfully guided and received.
It is further said: There are approximately four obstacles that cause people today to refuse to uphold the teachings upon hearing of the Buddha. These four obstacles are:

first, the notion that "the mind itself is the Buddha," leading one to wonder why one must abandon one's own thoughts to contemplate another; this arises from not realizing that while the Buddha is indeed the mind, this does not preclude the practice of recollecting the Buddha.
For if the mind is the Buddha, how could it not be that the Buddha is the mind? Yet, they cling only to contemplating the mind and do not permit the recollection of the Buddha.

If one were to say "Buddha" and "the mind-Buddha" are two, then the meaning would not be established. Therefore, one recollects the Buddha and recollects the mind, for the two do not obstruct each other.
Why does one not universally recollect all Buddhas but instead recollect only a single Buddha? It is because one does not know that by concentrating the mind on a single object, one achieves samādhi.
This is truly because the wisdom of sentient beings is shallow; they cannot bear complexity. Thus, ordinary intelligence cannot distinguish [between them].
The spirit must be concentrated. Those who employ the mind on many divergent paths lose their merit. As the Bodhisattva Puguang asked the Buddha:
"If there are buddha-fields in all ten directions, why do you praise only the Western Land? The Buddha replied: "The people of Jambudvīpa have minds that are largely distracted and chaotic;
by causing them to focus the mind on a single object, they may attain rebirth there. Since all Buddhas possess the same Dharma-nature body, to recollect one Buddha is [to recollect them all]."
This is because one should be mindful of all Buddhas. Third, it is said that every Buddha is worthy of mindfulness;
why then does one not follow the mindfulness of any single Buddha, but must specifically be mindful of Amitābha? This is because that Buddha has a special affinity with sentient beings.

It is truly due to the fact that his name is what people delight in reciting; even an evil person, at times when they do not notice it, will involuntarily lose their voice to call out the Buddha’s name. Thus...
When a person of supreme attainment encounters auspicious matters, they do not consciously think of the Buddha, yet they joyfully praise him.

When people encounter evil matters or suffer hardships, they do not consciously think of the Buddha, yet their grief and pain are most poignant. Such karmic conditions and causes are never brought about by anyone else; they occur spontaneously.
Fourth, why is it that one does not contemplate the Buddha’s merits, wisdom, marks and signs, and radiant light, but instead contemplates only his name?

It is because one does not know that holding the name is most suited to the capacities of beings in the Dharma-ending age, and because it is inconceivable. Regarding "suited to capacities," the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra* states:

"Sentient beings are dull and ignorant; they cannot understand through contemplation. One need only cause them to maintain the continuity of the sound of recitation, and they will naturally attain rebirth."
It is further said: "The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is difficult for all the world to believe. Regarding what is called "difficult to believe," ten points may be briefly cited.

First, dwelling now in this defiled land, one has long been accustomed to it and feels at ease; upon suddenly hearing of that land’s pure adornments, one suspects such a thing does not exist—this is the first difficulty in belief.
Second, even if one believes in that land, one may still doubt whether rebirth can be attained in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.

First, there is the difficulty of believing that one will certainly be born in Sukhāvatī. Second, even if one believes that one will be born there, one further doubts how one can go to that land when it is ten thousand *koṭis* of lands away from this Sahā world; thus, there is the difficulty of believing that such a vast distance can be traversed.
Third, even if one believes it is not far, one further doubts how an ordinary person of the mundane stage, burdened by deep and heavy karmic obstructions, could suddenly attain rebirth in that land.

Fourth, it is difficult to believe. Even if one were to gain faith, one would further doubt that birth in this Pure Land must necessarily involve wondrous and marvelous Dharma-gates and manifold meritorious practices;
how could one simply by holding the Name achieve rebirth? This is the fifth difficulty of belief.
Even if one were to believe and hold the Name, one would further doubt that holding this Name must necessarily span many kalpas before success can finally be achieved; how could it be otherwise?
"One day or seven days, one shall then attain rebirth there"—this is the sixth point of difficult faith.

Even if one believes that rebirth occurs after seven days, one may still doubt that birth in the six destinies does not involve the womb, egg, moisture, or transformation; how then can it be that in that land all are born by transformation from lotus flowers?

The seventh difficulty in belief is this: even if one believes that [the Buddha] is born from a lotus, one further doubts that those who have newly entered the Path will encounter many conditions for regression;
how then can they attain the stage of non-regression simply by being born in that land? This is the eighth difficulty in belief.

Even if one believes in non-regression, one further doubts that this is merely a means to attract sentient beings of dull faculties, and that those of superior wisdom and sharp roots need not necessarily be born there. This is the ninth difficulty in belief. Even if one believes...
Those of sharp faculties also give rise [to doubt]. They harbor uncertainty regarding other sutras, wondering whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, or whether there is a Pure Land or no Pure Land;
thus they remain in indecisive hesitation. This is the tenth difficulty of faith. Therefore, it is said that "all the world" finds it difficult to believe;

this implies that it is not only those in the evil realms who find it difficult to believe, but even humans and devas may still harbor doubts. It is not only the ignorant and deluded who find it difficult...
Even those who are faithful and wise may still harbor doubts about it; it is not only beginners who find it difficult to believe, but even those of long-standing cultivation may still doubt it.
It is not only ordinary beings who find it difficult to believe, but even those of the Two Vehicles may still doubt it.
Therefore, it is said that this is a teaching difficult for all the world to believe. To now proclaim this Dharma in this world is like entering a land of naked people and attempting to...
To manifest majestic deportment and point out black and white to those born blind—this is called a "difficulty.
This is what is meant by the inconceivable merit of benefiting others.
Furthermore, the preface to the Forty-Eight Questions and Answers states: "The teaching of the Pure Land originated with Dharmākara at its causal ground and began with Vaidehī.
It was proclaimed as the golden words of the Teacher on Vulture Peak and spread through the Lotus Society of the Great Being at Mount Kuang-lu.
By focusing the single mind in aspiration, one transcends the three realms horizontally; truly, this is the essential path for the Dharma-ending age."
It is indeed so. Those of superior capacity accord with the principle through the very facts; they are firm in their conviction and do not turn back.

Those of inferior capacity follow upon hearing [the teaching]; they likewise have no cause to give rise to delusion. Only those of neither superior nor inferior capacity, situated in the middle stream, desire to follow their desires yet deviate from them, having no fixed direction in their will.
For this reason, the ten doubts are common even among the wise; some seek instruction from Master Ze, while others are admonished by the Celestial Drum.
Zhuán. With a heart of profound compassion and lingering affection, how could this be called mere verbosity?
These words were simply unavoidable. Master Ouyi clearly stated: "As for the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation, there is nothing particularly marvelous about it;

its essential requirement is simply deep faith and diligent practice. The Buddha said: "If a person merely recites the name of Amitābha Buddha, this is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous Chan."
Tiantai said: "The four kinds of samādhi are all equally named 'Buddha-remembrance. The Buddha-remembrance samādhi is called the king among samādhis.
Yunqi said: "A single phrase of 'Amitābha Buddha' encompasses the Eight Teachings and perfectly subsumes the Five Schools.
It is a pity that people nowadays regard Buddha-remembrance as a shallow matter, claiming it is merely the practice of foolish men and women."
Because their faith is not deep, their practice is likewise not vigorous; they spend their days in idle indolence, failing to achieve any merit in purification.
Some may skillfully devise expedient means, wishing to deeply clarify this *nien-fo samādhi*, yet they invariably take the investigation of the word "Who" as the ultimate goal.
Little do they realize that the mind manifesting in a single thought is fundamentally beyond words and transcends all conceptualization, requiring no deliberate mental effort.
It is free from all attachments. That Buddha who is the object of one's present mindfulness is likewise fundamentally beyond the reach of emotions and conceptual calculations.

Why labor over speaking of "subtlety" or "the source"? It is simply a matter of being able to believe and maintaining a steady composure. Proceed directly with the recitation—whether ten thousand times by day and night.

Whether it be fifty thousand or thirty thousand [recitations], one should take the standard of fixed and unerring practice as the measure. Having completed this for the duration of one lifetime, one vows never to change or alter it.
If one were unable to attain rebirth despite this, the Buddhas of the three periods would be speaking falsehoods. Once rebirth is attained, there shall be no further regression;
all various Dharma gates will manifest before one. One must by all means avoid being like Zhang San today and Li Si tomorrow.

Fourth: When encountering those of the Teaching School (Dharma-character), one again thinks of examining chapters and extracting phrases; when encountering those of the Zen School (Gate of the Patriarchs), one again thinks of investigating questions and answers;
when encountering those who uphold the Vinaya, one again thinks of donning the robe and using the alms bowl. Thus, at every turn, there is no resolution.
If every aspect is not clear, how can you know that your recitation of Amitābha Buddha has reached maturity?

Because these thoughts are manifold, they interrupt right mindfulness. Thus, a single moment of interrupted mind is itself the shackle of the three miserable realms.

This is karma. Furthermore, while guarding the roots of the precepts, if one’s resolve is not firm, or if one pursues objects of desire through body and speech at every thought-moment, the scriptures teach that it would be better to pour molten copper down one's throat than to receive food or drink with a mouth that has broken the precepts.
It would be better to wrap one’s body in glowing iron than for a body that has broken the precepts to receive the robes of others;
how much more so when, due to a lack of strictness in the various precepts, the deviant mind moves recklessly, and because of this reckless movement, one interrupts dedicated cultivation?
Thus, a single thought of interruption is not merely the karma of glowing iron or molten copper. Furthermore, one must sever both hatred and attachment, yet the will remains undetermined.
Concentration: Whenever you encounter empty fame or fleeting profit, if you cannot examine yourself and break through them, then when fame and profit belong to you, greed and attachment arise;
when fame and profit belong to others, hatred and jealousy arise. As the ancients said: "To crave fame and profit is to hasten toward the realm of ghosts;
to pursue love and hate is to enter the pit of fire. Yet you, because of this love and hate, sever your connection to the Pure Land. Thus, in a single thought-moment—
A distracted mind is itself the karma of the hungry ghosts' fiery pit. Third, regarding seeking spiritual efficacy: having studied the primary practice, one must seek its miraculous efficacy.
Now that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled, the signs of death are manifest before you; you know how much more time remains until your end.
You must attend to this in the present moment and seek to see the Buddha immediately. For instance, Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu—once...
During his lifetime, he was thrice graced by the Buddha’s hand upon his head. Furthermore, as the Dharma Master Huai-gan testified, by reciting the Buddha’s name, he immediately beheld the Buddha.
Likewise, when the Dharma Master Shao-kang chanted the Buddha’s name once, the assembly saw a Buddha fly out from his mouth;
when he chanted it ten times, ten Buddhas flew out from his mouth like a string of pearls. Such are these numinous [accounts].
This has been verified countless times. If your mind is without interruption, it is not difficult to see the Buddha; if an interrupted mind arises, you will certainly not see the Buddha.
Since you do not see the Buddha, you lack the affinity for the Buddha. Lacking the affinity for the Buddha, it is difficult to be born in the Pure Land.
If you are not born in the Pure Land, you will inevitably fall into the evil realms. Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the suffering of the three miserable paths.

This is the path of practice. Be cautious, be cautious! Regarding the three aforementioned strategies, you should personally lash yourself with remorse so that your mindfulness does not depart from the Buddha, and the Buddha does not depart from your mindfulness.
When resonance and the Way meet, you will see the Buddha before you. Having seen the Buddha of the Land of Bliss, you will see all Buddhas of the ten directions;
having seen all Buddhas of the ten directions, you will see the Buddha of your own innate, true nature. Once this is achieved—
Upon seeing the Buddha of the innate, natural self-nature, one immediately attains the manifestation of great function.
Thereafter, one dedicates their compassionate vows to extensively transform all sentient beings. This is called Pure Land Chan, and it is also called Chan Pure Land.

The *Da you zhiguī jí língzhī guān jīng shū* states: "There are those who make a vow, wishing that before attaining the Way, in every place where they are born, they may encounter a Buddha and hear the Dharma, and leave home as a *kumārabhūta*.
Now it is said that if one is born in the Pure Land, one will spontaneously encounter Buddhas and become a monk;
it is only because they do not know of the Pure Land that they harbor such a vow. This applies to the masters of the Chan and Lecture schools alike.
Such views are numerous. I have attempted to say to them: "Now that you have already attained birth as a male and entered the Sangha, you ought to seek liberation immediately.
Why do you instead seek to be a man again before wishing to renounce the world? Is there not even the slightest progress?"
It is further said: "Sentient beings are deluded and inverted; they are addicted to the five desires and do not seek liberation.
None among them have yet been able to give rise to a resolute mind-vow to be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss.

It is only when they encounter enemies and those they hate, suffer from parting from loved ones, face the signs of old age, sickness, and death, and are oppressed by dangers and tormented by unbearable, agonizing suffering, that they finally weep with grief and cry out."
One takes refuge in the Buddha Jewel in the hope of escaping death. Furthermore, those who are wealthy and noble often lack the leisure to cultivate Buddhist practices;
those who do have such leisure fail to develop faith; and even those capable of faith suffer from an inability to sever their doubts.

As for those who resolve to practice only when driven by hardship and suffering, they mostly lose the opportunity due to their advanced age. Thus, one knows that one must give rise to right faith and arouse right mindfulness while still alive.
Furthermore, for one who cultivates the conditions for goodness, how could this not be a difficult undertaking?
Great Master Xian Shengchan composed the "Exhortation to Arouse the Bodhicitta," wherein he elucidated ten kinds of causes and conditions.

It states: "When these ten conditions are fully understood and the eight factors are thoroughly known, one has a gateway through which to proceed and a ground upon which to develop [the aspiration]. Only..."
I pray that the great assembly will take pity on my ignorant sincerity and compassion for my earnest resolve. May we together establish this vow and together give rise to this mind:

may those who have not yet given rise to it do so now; may those who have already given rise to it cause it to increase; and may those whose resolve has already increased cause it to continue in succession.
Do not be intimidated by what is difficult and retreat in cowardice; do not view what is easy and become frivolous; do not desire quick results and fail to be enduring; and do not be indolent.

Do not lack valor. Do not remain entirely without resolve because of dullness; do not disparage yourself as having no share [in the path] because your roots are shallow. For example, it is like planting a tree:

the longer one plants, the deeper the roots become despite their initial shallowness. Or it is like sharpening a blade: the longer one grinds it, the sharper the blade becomes despite its initial dullness.
How could one, because the roots are shallow, refuse to plant and allow the tree to wither of its own accord? Or, because the blade is dull, refuse to grind it and leave it as it is?
...of its being useless. Furthermore, if one regards spiritual practice as suffering, one fails to realize that indolence is even more bitter.
Through practice, one exerts effort for a brief time to attain peace and joy for eternal kalpas; through indolence, one seeks comfort for a single lifetime only to suffer for many births.
Moreover, if one takes the Pure Land as one's rudder and helm, why worry about falling back? And having attained the patience of non-arising, then—
Why worry about hardships? Do not say that a single thought is insignificant; do not claim that empty vows are of no benefit. When the mind is true, the reality is achieved;
when the vow is vast, the practice becomes profound. Space is not the greatest; the Mind-King is the greatest. The diamond is not the hardest; the power of the vow is the hardest.
If the great assembly can truly not abandon my words, then the kinship of Bodhi shall from this point form a marriage alliance. Lotus...

We form a bond of alliance and friendship from this day forward. It is our wish that we may be born together in the Pure Land, behold Amitābha together, transform sentient beings together, and attain perfect enlightenment together.

In the *Xifang gongju nianfo shuo* (Western Paragon’s Proof on the Discourse of Mindfulness of the Buddha), it says: "O virtuous people! In this world there are a thousand paths and ten thousand ways;

why then do we only exhort people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha? The human mind is of paramount importance. It is that which leads the soul and guides the spirit, and through it, destiny is fashioned and the body is born.
Nothing proceeds from anything other than this. To think of good, one ascends to heaven; to think of evil, one descends to hell. A single thought [can determine all]."
As humans, if for a single thought one acts perversely, one becomes an animal. What makes one a hungry ghost? It is simply because one’s thoughts are not right.

When one thinks of demons, one becomes a demon; when one recites the Buddha’s name, one becomes a Buddha. If you wish to escape the six realms of existence, there is no way other than to recite the Buddha’s name alone.
If you do not yet recite the Buddha’s name, once you lose this human body, it will be difficult to regain it for ten thousand kalpas. Therefore, Śākyamuni Tathāgata taught people:

Recite the Buddha’s name. Master Huiyuan taught people to recite the Buddha’s name. If reciting the Buddha’s name could not bring an end to birth and death, how could the Buddhas and Patriarchs have been willing to deceive people?

If one recites the Buddha’s name but does not attain Buddhahood, the fault does not lie with the Buddha. If you recite with your mouth but do not recite with your mind, though you recite, it is as if you have not recited at all.

Even if you spend your entire life doing so, it is not worth a single true utterance. The character for "recitation" (nian) is derived from the heart radical; it originally does not derive from [the mouth].
The mouth recites while the mind contemplates throughout one's life; the voice follows the mouth as naturally as an infant cries for its mother.
The mind-Buddha and the mouth-Buddha—neither can be abandoned. While there are thousands and tens of thousands of Buddhas, why do we recite only the name of Amitābha Buddha?
It is because he originally made forty-eight vows, vowing to deliver all sentient beings throughout the ten directions. Among them, it says: "If [there be ten..."

If, among all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions, there should be one who is able to invoke my name, Amitābha Buddha, yet does not take birth in my land, I vow not to attain Buddhahood.
That land has the ground of pure gold; its gardens, groves, and palaces are entirely adorned with the seven treasures.
It is surrounded by seven rows of trees, seven layers of jeweled nets, and seven tiers of railings. Within it...

There were pavilions made of the seven treasures, stairways of the seven treasures, bridges of the seven treasures, and ponds of the seven treasures filled with water of eight virtues and lotuses of nine grades.
There were white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, and kalaviṅka birds.
There were immeasurable great arhats, śrāvaka disciples, and bodhisattva retinues, including the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

The Bodhisattvas, the pure assembly of great ocean-like Bodhisattvas, countless emanation Buddhas, countless Bodhisattvas, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time,
as well as all devas and humans— every great sage and great worthy— gathered together at the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are no women in that land. When a woman gives birth here, she immediately becomes a man. All the people there are born with lotus flowers as their parents.
There are those of the highest grade who are born in the upper level, those of the highest grade who are born in the middle level, and those of the highest grade who are born in the lower level;

those of the middle grade who are born in the upper level, those of the middle grade who are born in the middle level, and those of the middle grade who are born in the lower level; and those of the lowest grade... [and so forth].

Those born in the superior grade of the lower level, those born in the middle grade of the lower level, and those born in the inferior grade of the lower level are all sentient beings from the ten directions;

their [differences] are brought about by the depth of their vows and their diligence or indolence. Those born within the lotus flowers possess bodies that are fragrant and pure, with features that are upright and handsome.
Their minds are endowed with wisdom and are free from afflictions. They do not wear clothes yet they are not cold, nor does clothing ever cling to them.
He was free from agitation; he did not eat, yet felt no hunger, and even when eating, he was never sated. He was without pain or itching, without sickness or aging.

Following the Buddha’s sovereign will, he wandered at ease and without concern. After every meal, he would simply join his companions, the bodhisattvas, to walk along the paths and terraces on all four sides.
There, he perceived only extraordinary fragrances striking his nose and wondrous music filling his ears; flocks of birds sang in harmony amidst lotus flowers and jeweled trees.
The brocade and embroidery fluttered about. Looking up into the sky, one saw *mandārava* flowers falling in profusion like rain.
The music of that land may be called the ultimate; the lifespan of its people is likewise immeasurable. This is named the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Alas! Human wealth and nobility become empty after a hundred years; celestial splendor ceases after a thousand years.
Once one enters the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, there is immeasurable life. Yet the method for rebirth therein relies solely on the single phrase of Amitābha.
There is such an exceedingly convenient and excellent matter in this world, yet people are unwilling to practice it. Furthermore—
Upon reaching there, one must wear iron shoes and inquire after the Ultimate Way. From this day forward, you must urgently bring forth a vow:

"If I do not practice the Buddha-recitation and do not seek rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, may I become a ghost and fall forever into the Fengbu Hell of the Northern Subterranean Realm.
Alas! Alas! Let the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures be left for others to awaken to.
There are eighty-four thousand gates [of practice]. Apart from the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha," not a single other word is required.

Each person shall go separately to sweep a quiet room, provide an image of the Buddha, burn a censer of fragrant incense daily, change a bowl of pure water, and light a bright lamp at night. [The image may be] drawn on paper or carved in wood.
He is then identical to the True Buddha. Love him as one’s own parents; revere him as a sovereign. Attend upon him morning and evening with absolute sincerity and respect.

His prostrations should be like mountains collapsing, and his rising should be like clouds ascending. He should inquire after [the Master’s] well-being upon departing and inquire after it upon entering, whether at five *li* or ten *li* [from the temple].
Always be as if before the Buddha. For every drink and every meal, you must first make an offering. Whether raising your eyes or moving your mouth, there is nothing that is not the Buddha.
Do not let a single string of prayer beads leave your hand; do not let a single invocation of Amitābha leave your mouth. Recite it loudly, or recite it softly.

Reciting the six-syllable mantra; reciting the four-syllable mantra; reciting with urgency; reciting slowly; reciting aloud; reciting silently; reciting with palms joined; reciting while kneeling with a low voice;

reciting facing the Buddha; reciting while facing west; reciting while striking the wooden board; reciting while striking the fish-shaped gong; reciting while counting on a rosary; reciting while walking the meditation path.
Recite while prostrating; recite alone; recite with the assembly; recite at home; recite abroad; recite in leisure; recite in busyness; recite while walking; recite while standing;
recite while sitting; recite while lying down; recite even in dreams—this is true recitation. Recite until the heart is moved to tears;
recite until the fire is extinguished and the ashes grow cold; recite until the gods revere you and the ghosts tremble.
With reverence, one attains the joy of the devas and the delight of the spirits. One utterance of "Buddha" causes the palaces of the Māra kings to tremble;
one utterance of "Buddha" shatters the sword-trees and knife-mountains. One utterance of "Buddha" eliminates karmic obstructions accumulated over hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes;

one utterance of "Buddha" opens the conditions for the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence. This is truly like pressing oil from seeds—the sound of the striking increases its efficacy.
Fierce! As the boat tosses upon the rising waves, the sound of its trembling grows ever more mournful. The cauldron of boiling water lies behind, while the lotus pond lies ahead.
Though there may be thousands or tens of thousands of people obstructing me, I do not take them to heart; it cannot be otherwise.
Regarding the vow to extensively deliver others through the gateway of practice: one should benefit oneself and likewise benefit others.

To seek to deliver others before having delivered oneself would cause both self and others to drown together; this is certainly inappropriate. Yet, to seek only to deliver oneself without delivering others is to fall [into a narrow path].
The shallow views of the two vehicles are particularly inconsistent with the Buddha’s mind. Although their power is not yet sufficient, their minds lack nothing.

The Confucian texts speak of "renewing oneself and renewing others" and "establishing oneself and establishing others"; these are all principles. Thus, I have compiled this as the Gate of Universal Salvation.

The *Pure Land Text of Longshu* states: "I have composed this discourse on the Pure Land with the desire to exhort all who see and hear it to broaden their minds, taking the mind of the Buddha as their own mind, so that every person may come to know this and be reborn entirely within the Pure Land."
One should give rise to this thought: "If people were to know this Dharma-gate as I know it, would that not be joyful?

If people do not know it as I know it, would that not be painful? If one stops at personal cultivation alone, then one is a follower of the Śrāvakas, known as a Hīnayāna practitioner—like a small vehicle that can only save oneself. This...
The Buddha says that such a person severs the seeds of Buddhahood. One who can widely exhort others is called a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva;

this is like a great vehicle, meaning one who brings salvation to both self and others. Such a person attains immeasurable merit and retribution, and is therefore able to reach the stage of Buddhahood.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, together praise Amitābha.
The merits of the Buddha are inconceivable; that is to say, they cannot be fathomed by the mind nor discussed in words.
Such are his merits—they may truly be called ultimate. What, then, could he not accomplish? Thus, he is able to exhort even a single person to cultivate the Pure Land.
By means of these wholesome conditions, it is possible to dissolve and eliminate evil karma, it is possible to increase and exalt blessings and longevity, and it is possible to bring about adornment.
It is likewise appropriate for the merit of rebirth in the Pure Land, and it is also appropriate for the posthumous dedication for the deceased.
However, if one offers prayers with utmost sincerity, there will be no failure to obtain its karmic fruits. One can see a brief account of this in the biography of Fang Zhu.
How much more so when encouraging from one person up to five or ten people? And how much more so if those who have been encouraged, in turn, encourage others, passing it on to one another?
If one continues in this way without ceasing, then the teaching of the West may spread throughout the world, and sentient beings in the ocean of suffering may all be born in the Pure Land.
To exhort others toward the path of goodness is called the gift of Dharma; such is this Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
This is the greatest of all Dharma-gifts; it leads one to transcend saṃsāra, surpassing all other forms of Dharma-giving.
Therefore, its meritorious retribution is inexhaustible. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāmaitrī said in his verse on exhorting the cultivation of the Western Land:
"To encourage two people to practice is superior to one's own diligent effort; to encourage ten or more people brings merit that is already immeasurable; if one encourages a hundred..."
One who [recites] a thousand times is called a true Bodhisattva; furthermore, one who exceeds ten thousand recitations is Amitābha himself.
Contemplating this, how could those who proclaim the Western Paradise not broaden their minds, so that everyone may come to know this path and accumulate immeasurable karmic rewards?
It is further said: To give a single meal to one suffering from hunger, or a single garment to one suffering from cold, is already a great kindness.

How much more so for those who are submerged in the six realms of existence with no prospect of escape—to point out this Dharma-gate to them, enabling them to directly transcend saṃsāra and receive infinite and boundless longevity and bliss; how could such kindness ever be exhausted? *Vajra*.

The Sūtra says: "If a person were to give their body in alms as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, it would not equal the merit of someone who hears this sūtra and, with faith, does not oppose it; the latter's merit surpasses that of the former.
This is because those who give their bodies in alms do not escape receiving worldly rewards of fortune, which eventually come to an end; however, if one believes in this sūtra, then..."
There is a gradual realization of the true nature; as for its merit, it is never exhausted. This is why it surpasses the former.

As I observe it, this is not only the case for those who believe in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. If one encourages others toward the Pure Land, the karmic reward is likewise inexhaustible.
Why is this? In the Pure Land there is no further cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*); once there, one has attained non-retrogression and proceeds directly to Buddhahood.
Only then does it cease. Those born there, though not yet Buddhas, are nonetheless on the阶梯 (staircase) to Buddhahood.
Thus, to exhort a single person to cultivate the Pure Land is to bring one sentient being to the realization of Buddhahood.

Since every one who becomes a Buddha must necessarily deliver immeasurable sentient beings, and since those beings delivered by them all originate with me, how could their merit and retribution not be so?
This is superior to the merit of giving away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

Furthermore, it is said: whenever one receives instruction from teachers and friends, is uplifted by those who have been kind to one, or is treated with courtesy by associates, one should inform them all of the Pure Land and take this as one's repayment. This extends even to when one shares a single meal with any person.

Regarding the grace of tea: whether it be a single word or a brief sitting together, down to the labor of a servant attending to my needs, and all those who exert themselves in every aspect of my enjoyment—I inform them of this [the merit of tea] so that they may be delivered from the sea of suffering.
It is not only these people; I desire to transform everyone—whether known or unknown, recognized or unrecognized—by means of this.
He causes them to be born together in the Pure Land. Moreover, it is not only this instance. During the time when Śākyamuni Buddha was in the world, there was a country that was difficult to convert.
The Buddha said that Maudgalyāyana had a karmic affinity with it and sent him to convert the people. All the inhabitants of that country followed his teachings.
Someone asked the Buddha, "What karmic connection did they have with Maudgalyāyana? The Buddha replied, "In a past life, Maudgalyāyana was once a woodcutter."
In the midst of the mountains, a swarm of bees was startled into flight. Maudgalyāyana then uttered these virtuous words: "After I have attained the Way, I shall deliver all these bees.
Those who are now the people of this city were, at that time, those very bees. Because Maudgalyāyana uttered these virtuous words, they became connected through karmic affinity.
Observing this, one should not merely encourage the practice of cultivation toward all people; [one should do so for all beings].

In the Pure Land, all birds and beasts, down to the smallest crawling and wriggling creatures—indeed, all that have form and can be seen—whenever I behold them, I shall recite the name of Amitābha Buddha several times for their sake and make this virtuous vow:
"May you all be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss. After I have attained the Way, I shall deliver you all. This is not in vain.
It is thus with those whose forms and features can be seen. As for those whose forms and features cannot be seen, I shall likewise form this thought and speak these words:
"In this way, my wholesome mindfulness is thoroughly matured; I have a karmic affinity with all sentient beings.
It is certain that I shall attain the highest grade of the highest birth. At another time, when I transform and deliver them, there will be none who do not joyfully follow."

Master Lianchi said: "When a filial son serves his parents with diligent labor and provides for them so as to bring them peace, this is filial piety. To establish oneself in character and practice the Way so as to bring glory to them is great filial piety.
To further exhort them toward the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance, enabling them to attain rebirth in the Pure Land, is the ultimate expression of filial devotion."

This is the greatest of great filial pieties. I was born late and have only recently heard the Buddha-dharma; yet the sorrow of the wind-blown tree has already reached its ultimate pain, lasting for all eternity.
Though I wish to follow after them, there is no way to do so. I inform all people: while one's parents are still in the hall—
One should encourage the recitation of the Buddha’s name early on. On the anniversary of one's parents' passing, one should perform this practice for three years;
for those unable to do so, it may be for one year or for forty-nine days—either is acceptable. A filial son who wishes to repay the profound kindness of his parents must not fail to know this.
It is further said: there are three types of worldly filial piety and one type of supramundane filial piety. As for the three types of worldly filial piety:

first, to serve one’s parents with joy, attending to them and nourishing them with delicious food; second, to achieve success in the civil service examinations and enter government office, thereby honoring one’s parents with rank and emolument;
third, to cultivate virtue and exert oneself in conduct, attaining the status of a sage or a worthy to bring glory to one’s parents. These are the three.

This is what is called filial piety in the world. As for filial piety that transcends the world, it is to exhort one’s parents to observe the precepts and uphold the Way, to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, and to pray for rebirth in the Pure Land—thereby forever parting from the four modes of birth, bidding eternal farewell to the six realms of existence, entrusting their essence to the womb of the lotus, personally attending upon Amitābha, and attaining the stage of non-retrogression.
For a child to repay their parents, nothing is greater than this. When I was young...
I knew that I had entered the Path, yet my two parents had already passed away; I composed a "Text of Self-Remorse for Filial Neglect" to express my grief and resentment.

Now, seeing those among the assembly—both laypeople and monastics—who enjoy the blessing of both parents living, I am moved to even greater emotion, and tears flow profusely from my eyes and nose as I bow my head to the ground in prostration to exhort you.
Regarding the gateway of diligent practice and steadfast upholding:
once faith is sincere and vows are firm, if one does not encourage oneself with actual practice, then that faith is merely empty faith.
May this be a mere aspiration; empty words provide no benefit. How could one possibly obtain [the fruit] without effort?
In all matters, there must be ascetic practice before success can be achieved, let alone the great task of transcending the world. Now, it is not necessary to fully cultivate all myriad practices;
yet, even on this path of holding the Name—which is most simple and easy—is it possible to proceed without a focused mind and earnest effort? As for those who hold the Name:
One must recite with the mind; do not merely recite with the mouth. In ordinary times, deluded thoughts fly about like birds, making it impossible to observe them.

Only when one takes up the prayer beads does one first realize how difficult this mind is to restrain. My faculties are dull and my obscurations deep; therefore, I have long employed the method of forceful constraint.
With the hand grasping these beads, let the mind follow the hand, ensuring that not a single bead passes by in vain. In this way, may [the practice be fruitful].

Having gained some measure of confidence, I have here selected the admonitions of former sages and inscribed them by my seat to restrain the wandering mind and provide a basis for self-reflection and vigilance.
This concludes the "Section on Refining and Maintaining."
The Master of the West specifically pointed to Bodhisattva Jue-ming-miao-xing and said:
"In general, for those who practice the Pure Land, the greatest taboo is 'intermixture. What is meant by intermixture?

It refers to reciting sutras, chanting mantras, and organizing assemblies, while also being fond of discussing trivial Zen, prattling about omens of good and ill fortune, and claiming to see gods and ghosts."

This is what is meant by "intermingling. If one is intermingled with other concerns, the mind will not be single-minded. If the mind is not single-minded, it will be difficult to see the Buddha and attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

Will this not result in a lifetime spent in vain? From now on, do nothing else at all; simply and firmly hold fast to the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu," aspiring for birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Only when success is achieved after a long period of time— [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available.*
Not so. The verse says: The single phrase "Amitābha" is the dhāraṇī of all phenomena. Sound and mind depend upon one another; Mindfulness of this remains fixed upon this.
The response and resonance are inconceivable: The lotus blooms within the Seven-Jeweled Pond.
Furthermore, it is said: Someone asked, "If one is unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha with single-mindedness, what expedient means should be employed?

The Bodhisattva replied, "You need only cease fixed conceptualizations and recite slowly. You must ensure that the sound accords with the mind and the mind follows the sound. After reciting for a long time, all thoughts will naturally become clear and pure;
when the mind and its objects are extinguished and illumination is attained, you will enter the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. However, in your daily life, you must..."
One must recite many times, from a thousand to ten thousand, with the mind uninterrupted; then the faculties will most easily reach full maturity.
If one forces oneself to achieve single-mindedness, it will ultimately not become so. At that time, Da Ben was beneath his seat when he suddenly uttered several cries of "Gu!
The Bodhisattva said, "So it is, so it is."
It is further said: "The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* consists of twelve fascicles, and the names of the Buddhas number twelve thousand;

these must not be increased and must not be decreased. Simply follow my practice. As for the sutra, it must be recited with evenness and purity—neither slack nor hurried, neither too fast nor too slow.
The Buddhas' names must be recited with every voice and every thought—neither harsh nor wavering, neither floating nor sinking. Thus it goes.
Regarding the two characters for "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*): this is not merely reciting the established text once;

one must issue from within one's own heart a genuine vow of a great Bodhisattva, with utmost sincerity and earnestness, universally wishing that all sentient beings may together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Yet my mind is without attachment, equal to empty space; this is called dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Furthermore, when sitting in stillness, you should reflect inwardly and investigate deeply:
the Buddha is none other than my own mind, and this mind is the Buddha. There is no need to seek it externally; abide as the mind is.

If, at times when you are not reciting the Buddha’s name, they surge like billowing waves and do not cease for even a moment, how could you possibly perceive them yourself?
It is further said: "In the practice of nianfo (buddha-recollection), there is silent recitation, loud recitation, and vajra-recitation.

However, loud recitation may be perceived as too strenuous, while silent recitation easily leads to dullness. Simply maintaining a continuous and dense flow, with the sound residing between the lips and teeth, is what is called vajra-recitation.
Furthermore, one must not be dogmatic; if it is felt to be strenuous, there is no harm in practicing silent recitation."

If one perceives dullness or drowsiness, it is not improper to raise one's voice. Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha nowadays merely strike their hands like fish eggs while shouting along with their mouths;
for this reason, they fail to obtain benefit. One must ensure that every phrase leaves the mouth and enters the ear, and that every sound awakens the mind within.
It is like when one person is in deep sleep and another calls out, "So-and-so!"—then that person immediately wakes up.
Thus, it is that mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is most capable of gathering the mind.
It is further said: "It is difficult to achieve realization of the Dharma amidst the conditions of worldly dust; it is better to apply oneself directly to one's studies.

When one finds leisure from household duties, one should immediately and silently hold fast to the Name. One values only that each character be distinct and every phrase be intimate and personal. Mind—
Then you will naturally maintain composure. If, after a long time, you do not regress, samādhi will be accomplished;
this itself is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). It is further said: "If an elder has not yet attained clear realization, there is no need for alarm;

it is simply that his mental power has not yet been fully exhausted. Now that you have fallen ill, there is no necessity to exert yourself with forced vigor; simply rely on the instructions found within the sūtras.
Regarding the name: maintain single-mindedness without distraction. Unify your flavor by reducing external conditions; reduce them as much as possible.
Only respond to those things that cannot be avoided, and once you have responded, the power of your practice will naturally take hold.
