It is further said: "Distracted thoughts are the illness; mindfulness of the Buddha is the medicine. A chronic illness cannot be cured by a single dose, and accumulated delusions cannot be eliminated by a momentary thought.
The principle is one and the same. Do not concern yourself with the flight of distracting thoughts; it is simply essential that your mindfulness of the Buddha be precise and earnest.
With every syllable distinct and every phrase continuous, maintain this with all your might—only then will you have a direction toward liberation."

This refers to what is called "true accumulation through long-term effort," whereby in a single moment there is a sudden breakthrough. It is like the analogy of whetting a pestle to make a needle or forging iron into steel;
this is certainly not a falsehood. There are many gateways to entering the Way, but this one alone is the most direct shortcut.
One must not neglect it. One must not neglect it.

It is further said: "The Dharma gates are immeasurable, yet their essence lies in clarifying the mind. As for the essential gate to clarifying the mind, nothing compares to the recitation of the Buddha's name (*nien-fo*).

During intervals from reading and writing, or when the mind is troubled, sit quietly and recite the Buddha’s name; this brings great benefit. When a single thought is fixed upon the Buddha, distracting thoughts retire;
the mind becomes empty and the environment tranquil—how wondrous! I pray that you do not treat this lightly or neglect it."
Furthermore, he sent a letter to Wang Zhi, saying: "Your noble family has cultivated magnificent virtue for generations; why then does your honored person suffer such a severe illness?
Could it not be that past karma has brought this about? The causes of disease mostly stem from killing living beings; therefore, I have placed particular emphasis on the practice of releasing life.
Now I have something further to present: the difference between having an external monk perform repentance on one's behalf versus performing repentance within one's own mind."
The difference in merit is vast. I pray that you empty your mind and completely cease all external conditions.
Within this state of emptiness, single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha just once. As for what is called "recitation," it need not involve opening the mouth or moving the tongue;
simply reflect inwardly with the mind’s eye, making each character distinct and each phrase continuous, from morning until evening.
From evening until dawn, his thoughts were uninterrupted. Whenever he experienced pain or suffering, he endured it with patience, maintaining single-minded mindfulness.
As a sutra states: "Reciting the Buddha's name with a sincere heart once extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
Therefore, the merit [of this practice] is vastly superior.

Furthermore, Qian Guangzhan asked: "This mind has been dissolute for a long time. Although I use the recitation of the Buddha's name to restrain it, I regain it only temporarily before losing it again.
How can I maintain this practice? Answer: "A ground that has been inverted for a long time cannot have its success achieved in a single battle.
It depends solely on steadfast courage and non-retrogression until the ground of the mind is illuminated; then, once attained, it will be attained forever."

It is further said: "Quiescence (śamatha) remedies distraction; when distraction departs, dullness (styāna-middha) arises. Alertness (vipaśyanā) remedies dullness; when dullness departs, distraction arises.
When both quiescence and insight are maintained together, both dullness and distraction recede. Now, one need only practice mindfulness of the Buddha with clarity and vigor.

To be single-minded in mindfulness is called "clarity" (jing); to reflect back while mindful is called "vigor" (ming). Clarity is quiescence; vigor is insight. This is the singular mindfulness of the Buddha.
Thus, both cessation (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) are fully present.

Furthermore, it is said: "When people of the world possess even slightly sharp faculties, they tend to look down upon the practice of nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name), claiming it is merely the business of foolish men and women."
Those people merely see foolish men and women reciting the Buddha’s name with their mouths while their minds wander a thousand li away;

they do not realize that such practice is called "reading" the Buddha, not "mindfulness" (nian) of the Buddha. Mindfulness arises from the mind; when the mind recollects and does not forget, it is therefore called mindfulness.
To illustrate this by means of a Confucian analogy: if a Confucianist were to constantly recollect and keep Confucius in mind, would he not be drawing near to Confucius?
It is almost so. Nowadays, people constantly contemplate and recollect the five desires without considering them wrong, yet they instead regard the mindfulness of the Buddha as wrong.
Alas! To let such a life pass in vain—how does this compare to being a mere fool or a simpleton?
It is a pity that while wisdom is possible, folly is not.

It is further said: "In the past, when I was at the Refining and Grinding Hall (Ryōmaba), the Abbot addressed the assembly, saying, 'On the day of the Middle Primordial (Chūgan), we shall perform the Ullambana feast.
I took this to mean that offerings would be prepared; however, no offerings were made, and we did nothing but recite the Buddha's name for three days.
Furthermore, I heard that in the past, there was a temple administrator who was summoned by the authorities. The First Seat of the hall then gathered the assembly."
For protection, the multitude merely recites mantras; for mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*), they likewise do so only with a loud voice.

These two matters transcend ordinary sentiment and represent the strategic insights of great beings; they are truly worthy of being taken as models. As for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha today, it is called "exclusive cultivation" (*zhuanxiu*).

Yet, when it comes to praying for longevity, they rely on the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*; for resolving transgressions, they rely on the Liang Dynasty *Emperor’s Repentance Ritual* (*Liáng huáng chàn*); and for rescuing one from calamities and hardships...

If you seek to eliminate calamities, recite the *Dharani for the Elimination of Disasters*. If you seek wisdom, recite the text of Avalokiteśvara. As for the Buddha you have previously been mindful of, set him high upon a shelf;
if he does not benefit the matter at hand, do not think about it. Consider that the lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable—how much more so is the lifespan of a mere hundred years?
Reflect that that Buddha can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas—how much more so the defilements, misfortunes, and calamities before one's eyes!
How difficult this is! One cannot help but reflect on those words of the Buddha: "I shall illuminate the boundless realms with the light of my wisdom.

How much more so, then, regarding the wisdom extolled by people of this age? The *agada* medicine is the sovereign remedy for ten thousand ailments; yet, with their minds divided and wavering, none are willing to believe or accept it.
When faced with such divine and sublime craftsmanship, what can one possibly do?
It is further said: "The practice of forming societies for the recitation of the Buddha's name began with Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu.
Do those who lead the society today equal Master Huiyuan? Are those who join the society equal to the eighteen worthies? If so, they should be few rather than many;
for those who cultivate the Pure Land with sincerity are like the members of a monastic hall. As for the mixing of men and women..."

This is a rule common to our society and one that has never before existed on Mount Lu. Women should naturally remain at home to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; they should not join the ranks of men.

To distance themselves from worldly censure and to protect the True Dharma of the Buddha—nothing is more essential than this. I pray that you, my fellow practitioners, will together observe this precept.

Furthermore, regarding societies for the release of living beings (*fangsheng she*), it is better that they be small rather than large; for those who truly save sentient beings through compassion are like the members of a Buddha’s assembly.

It is my humble opinion that each person, according to their own insight and according to their capacity, should purchase and release them—whether at the end of a season or at the end of the year—and then gather at one place to account for those released and examine their merit.
When discussing karma, it disperses in an instant; one must not be extravagant with offerings for the *zhāi* (fasting/retreat), nor should one indulge in wasting time.
I pray that you, my fellow practitioners, will maintain this together.

Furthermore, the Preface to the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* states: "If one focuses on phenomena (*dharma*) while maintaining mindfulness, one can ensure continuity; thus, the merit of entering the stage [of non-retrogression] will not be in vain.
However, if one clings to principle (*li*) while the mind remains truly unenlightened, one conversely incurs the calamity of falling into emptiness.

The sub-commentary notes: "As for those who cling to phenomena yet lack earnest faith, there is certainly no need for discussion. Even if one were to single-mindedly recite the Name, with every thought succeeding the next in continuity," [the text continues].

There may be interruptions; though one might not yet clearly comprehend the principles of the Truth, if one has already been able to accomplish the purification of the body, then even if one’s rank is low, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is certain.
This is what is meant by the saying: "For a scholar, being at the very bottom of the list on the honor roll is still no disgrace;

one only fears not having one's name on the list at all. How can one condemn such a person for clinging to their ignorance? This remains true even for those who grasp the principle and whose minds are actually clear and enlightened. It is also...

This must be discussed. Even if one gallops with wild wisdom and becomes addicted to stubborn emptiness, yet has never attained awakening to their own fundamental mind, to then speak lightly of the Pure Land and hold in contempt rebirth therein does great harm.
This is what is meant by "expansively embracing emptiness and negating cause and effect," a state of vast indifference that invites calamity and disaster.

Furthermore, the preface to the *Shuchao* states: "To point directly at that which allows one with a mind of thought (*sanimitta-citta*) to enter the state of no-thought (*animitta*)—the mind is fundamentally without thought;
the arising of thought is a deviation from it. Yet, since beginningless time, sentient beings have been habituated to deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which is not easily dispelled all at once.

Teaching the recitation of the Buddha's name now is like using poison to counteract poison or employing troops to stop troops. Once the illness has healed and the enemy has been pacified, one abandons the medicine."
As for the essence: there is no separate self at all; they are merely marauders. Originally, they were my own infants. The commentary states:

The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* says, "The essence of mind is free from thought, yet it gives rise to thoughts of recollecting the Buddha. Is this not, rather, to disturb the mind? The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* says, "Without applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), this is called recollecting the Buddha.
Without ideation (*saṃjñā*) and without speech, this is called recollecting the Buddha. Yet, to give rise to thoughts of recollecting the Buddha—is this not...?

This is contrary to the Buddha’s teaching. Now, you claim that by extinguishing all discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), one practices the "Buddha-recollection of the true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-buddhānusmṛti*).

While this principle is indeed correct, although the mind may be free from conceptualization, the ignorance-tainted mind continues in an uninterrupted succession of moments. It is like a chronic illness of seven years’ duration or a long-disordered populace;

hence it is called "habitual conditioning. If one now attempts to forcibly suppress it and abruptly compel it toward emptiness and stillness, one merely halts its movement and returns to [the state of] cessation.

Cease! Ceasing only causes further agitation. Even if coarse thoughts momentarily subside, subtle thoughts still persist; to claim at such a point that one has attained "correspondence" (*yoga*) is a mistake of no small magnitude.

Since you remain on the level of ordinary beings, unable yet to sever deliberation and forget external conditions, why not cultivate progress by taking those very conditions and deliberations as the path?
Thus, use mindfulness to counteract mindfulness itself: recite the name of a single Buddha to replace those hundreds of thousands of millions of diverse [distractions].

It is mindfulness. Yet delusion arises from the True, like waves following the water; that which is thought is itself emptiness, the manifest fundamental substance. One does not attain Bodhi apart from thought;
therefore it is said that the myriad dharmas are illusory and there is only this one mind. To fully awaken to one's own mind is to find Bodhi at every turn.
It is just as when a sick body recovers, it is then called a healthy body; or when a turbulent people are settled, they are called a peaceful people.

These are indeed virtuous people. To abandon thought in order to seek the mind is like a physician who must destroy his own body to cure a disease, or one who intends to slaughter a nation to bring peace to its people. How could this possibly be reasonable?
It is further said: "Pure lands exist throughout the worlds of the ten directions; why then do you specifically point toward the West and instruct us to be born in that country?

This is truly because the Way is lost when there are many diverging paths, and the arrow hits the mark only through single-minded focus. The mind must not have two uses, and one's efforts must not be applied in a distracted manner."
The Great Master Youxi’s *Dharma Words on the Pure Land* states: "Reciting the Name is as taught in the *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*:

'If one recites the Name for seven days with a single mind and without confusion. There is the 'single mind of affairs' and the 'single mind of principle. If one recites the Buddha’s name orally, one should bind the mind to that object;
let the sounds follow one another in succession, and let the moments of mind remain undistracted. Even if the mind wanders toward external objects, one must gather it back. This requires...
Give rise to a mind of resolve. Sever thoughts of the future. Cast aside worldly affairs. Let go of the攀缘 (pān-yuan) mind.

Cause this mindful mind to gradually increase—from brief to long, from few to many—whether for one day, two days, or even seven days, until you have ultimately achieved single-mindedness without distraction;
only then will you stop. This is the matter of single-mindedness. If you obtain this...
Thus, the pure cause for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is accomplished; the right mindfulness at the moment of death will surely be attained.
One will be free from the suffering of physical illness, will not be entangled by evil states, and will know in advance when the time has come.

With joy in body and mind, one will pass away auspiciously—whether sitting or standing—and will personally behold Amitābha Buddha, who will extend his light to welcome and guide them. For those who practice with single-mindedness according to principle, there is no other method than simply [to focus] upon...

Within this single mind, in every thought-moment, one thoroughly realizes that the mind which is mindful and the Buddha who is being mindful are equal throughout the three periods of time and mutually interfused throughout the ten directions.
They are neither empty nor existent; neither self nor other; without going or coming; neither arising nor ceasing.
The single thought-moment of the present is itself the gateway to the Pure Land of the future. To contemplate while not contemplating;
to contemplate within non-contemplation; to arise within non-arising; to be non-arising within arising—within that which is beyond contemplation, one contemplates with fervor;
within non-arising, one fervently seeks birth. This is the realization of the principle within the single mind of practice.

The Ming Dynasty Master Hanshan Deqing was a devoted practitioner of Pure Land cultivation. A Zen practitioner from Haiyang requested to receive the precepts and asked about the essentials of practicing for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Deqing replied: "The Buddha taught that there are many expedient means for the practice of transcending birth and death.
Among them, none is more swift or essential than reciting the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. This dharma gate is such that the Buddha did not wait for a question before teaching it."

The Buddha himself declared that these three roots universally encompass all and equally include the fourfold assembly; it is not merely a provisional teaching established for those of inferior capacity.
As the Sūtra says: "If you wish to purify a Buddha-land, you must first purify your own mind. Thus, in practicing pure karma, one must take a pure mind as the foundation.

To purify one's own mind, the foremost requirement is first to ensure the purity of the root of precepts. Regarding the three actions of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind—these ten...

Evil karma is the cause of suffering in the three miserable realms. Now, regarding the essentials of upholding the precepts, one must first purify the three karmas; then the mind will naturally become pure.
Within this pure mind, one should cultivate a sense of weary detachment from the sufferings of Saṃsāra and resolve to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nourishment (An-yang).

One must then establish the correct practice of Buddha-recollection (nien-fo). However, for Buddha-recollection to be effective, one’s concern for birth and death must be urgent. First, sever all external conditions and single-mindedly maintain the one [Buddha-name].
Reflect: take the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" as the very root of your life. Be mindful of it without ceasing; let every thought be uninterrupted.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether lifting the spoon or taking up the chopsticks; whether turning, moving, bowing, or looking up;

whether in motion or stillness, in leisure or busyness—at all times, remain neither deluded nor obscured, and maintain no other mental objects. If you apply your mind in this way for a long time until it becomes pure and matured, then...
Even in dreams, one does not forget or lose it; when waking and sleeping are of one time, then the practice becomes continuous and unified—this is the moment of attaining efficacy.
Furthermore, there was a lay practitioner named Jingxin who asked: "I am unable to achieve a state of single-mindedness in my recitation of the Buddha's name."

"Please grant us instruction. He replied clearly: "The foremost requirement for practice is an urgent sense of the reality of birth and death. If the mind is not urgent regarding birth and death, how can one achieve the continuous, unbroken state of mindfulness of the Buddha?
Furthermore, since sentient beings have come from immeasurable kalpas ago, every thought has been nothing but deluded conceptualization."
The faculty of emotion is firmly obstructed. Although you have now entered the path of the supramundane, how has there ever been a single thought of earnest concern for birth and death?

Day after day, moment after moment, you follow after emotions and have never practiced introspection. Now, you wish to use this superficial faith to sever the cycle of birth and death accumulated over many kalpas—is this not like trying to extinguish a fire of piled firewood with a cup of water?
How could such a principle possibly exist? If it were truly a mind concerned with birth and death...
Urgently! Moment by moment, act as if your head were on fire. Fearing only that once a human body is lost, it will be difficult to regain it for a hundred kalpas.

You must bite down firmly upon this single invocation of the Buddha's name. You must certainly overcome delusive thoughts so that they manifest before you at every moment in all places, unobstructed by delusion.
If you apply such diligent and earnest effort, after a long time it will become pure and mature; then, naturally, there will be resonance. Do not...
Seeking to form a single mass, it spontaneously becomes one. This matter depends entirely on exerting effort oneself.
He further said: Whenever reciting the Buddha’s name, first set aside all the various distracted thoughts within your own breast at once.
Place it where there is nowhere to place it. Simply hold up the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" with vivid clarity, uninterrupted in the mind.
It should be like beads strung on a thread, or like the nocks of arrows fitted together, with not even a hair’s breadth of gap between them.
Exerting yourself in this way and remaining steadfastly fixed, you will not be led astray or lose your focus by any circumstances or conditions in any situation.
In daily life, whether moving or resting, remain unmixed and undisturbed; let it be as it is even in dreams and sleep.
When the moment of death arrives, if you can maintain single-mindedness without distraction, that is precisely the time of transcending birth into the Pure Land. Furthermore, it is said:

apart from the two periods of formal practice each day, simply fix the single sound of "Namo Amitābha Buddha" across your chest. Do not forget it from moment to moment; let every thought be nothing but this.
Be oblivious. Do not think of any worldly affairs at all. Take this single phrase "Buddha" as your very life-root;

clench your teeth with determination and never let it go. Even while eating, drinking, rising, resting, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, this one sound of "Buddha" must be ever-present before you.
If you encounter circumstances of adversity or favor, joy or anger, or when your mind becomes unsettled by the realm of afflictions—
As soon as one raises the single sound of "Buddha" and applies it with pressure, afflictions are seen to be extinguished instantly.

Since moment-to-moment afflictions are the very root of the suffering of birth and death, to now extinguish those afflictions through the recitation of the Buddha's name is precisely where the Buddha delivers one from the suffering of birth and death.
If one can extinguish afflictions by reciting the Buddha's name, one will be able to bring an end to birth and death; there is nothing else required.
Dharma: If you can maintain mastery over your afflictions through mindfulness of the Buddha, you will maintain mastery even within sleep and dreams.
If you maintain mastery within sleep and dreams, you will maintain mastery amidst the suffering of illness.
If you maintain mastery amidst the suffering of illness, then at the time of death, you will know your destination. This matter is not difficult to practice.
It simply requires that one’s single thought be intensely focused on birth and death, relying solely and steadfastly on the recitation of the Buddha’s name without seeking anything else.
After a long time of such pure cultivation, one will naturally attain great peace and joy, and achieve great benefit.
Zhang Shouyue of the Ming dynasty once composed three hundred poems in the style of Hanshan to exhort both monastics and laypeople, all of which take the Pure Land as their ultimate refuge.
One poem states: "The Great Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, The great power of Amitābha’s vows— After thousands of births and myriad kalpas, Only today have I finally recognized them.
One should conceive the thought that this is difficult to encounter; Be careful not to lose it again. Recite the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth; This is what is truly precious."
Keep the mind focused on one point. One version says: "Beyond all things, lodge your idle body; let all conditions subside of their own accord.
Without being stained by even a speck of dust, simply recite the name of the Buddha once. Let your nature be as soft as cotton, yet your mind must be as hard as iron.

If you are willing to engage in useless activities, you are reaching for the moon at the bottom of the water. Another version says: "Yesterday I entered the Lotus Society; my mouth is the Buddha and my mind is also the Buddha. Today..."
Within the burning house, affairs are manifold and thoughts are likewise manifold; unless one’s spiritual capacity is profound, one cannot avoid being submerged in the turbidity of worldly toil.

For this reason, the sages of antiquity cultivated the Pure Land practices in the mountains. One saying goes: those of the superior grade see the Buddha quickly, while those of the inferior grade see the Buddha slowly.

Though there may be differences in speed, there will never be a time of regression. In Zen meditation, the illness lies in attachment to forms; in the recitation of the Buddha’s name, it is vital to sever doubt.
Truly, truly, there is the Pure Land; truly, truly, there is the Lotus Pond. One says: "Seventy years are rare in antiquity; before us, there are not many days left.
Hurry to prepare your provisions for the journey, lest you fail to arrive in time. Whether horizontal, let it be horizontal; whether vertical, let it be vertical.
He was straightforward. How could he have had the leisure to distinguish between black and white?
Ming Zhang Guangwei’s discourse on the recitation of the Buddha’s name states: The sutra says, "Uphold the name with single-mindedness and without distraction.
As for "upholding," it is not something that can be grasped; it is what the Confucians call "earnestly wearing it upon one's breast," as described by Zhu Xi.

To instruct one to "reverently uphold" means that what follows in the text is not lost; this is the meaning of being undisturbed. The Confucianists also speak of "constantly bearing [the teachings] in mind.
Zhu Xi explained this as "always keeping it before one's eyes," which is precisely the meaning of "contemplating the Buddha" (*guanfo*). It is also the meaning of being undisturbed:

reciting the Buddha’s name with the mouth, contemplating the Buddha’s image with the eyes, and turning the ear back to listen to oneself as the sound flows from the tongue—this is the flavor of *dhyāna*.
The mind is gladdened. As the nose perceives fragrances, one knows them to be the mindfulness of the Buddha. Returning the six [senses] to the One, how could there be distraction?
Now, as I practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, I employ a skillful means: I observe this mind as being like a pure jewel vase. The names of the Buddhas are like grains of rice;
with each word and each phrase, they are like grains being poured into the vase, descending like a string of pearls. Since the grains are inexhaustible, the vase is never filled. I do not let go.

He cast a single grain outside the vessel and looked upon it; though not even a foot in diameter, it contained within it the Buddhas of a trichiliocosm, numbering as many as the atoms of ten billion worlds.
I, too, was gathered together with them in one place, sporting, enjoying ourselves, and resting.
"This is precisely where I find rest for my body and establish my life. He further said: "The verse of Master Shinan states: 'In reciting the Buddha’s name, do not greedily seek to recite too much;
simply recite one hundred times with an undisturbed mind. If you miss even one thought at the ninety-ninth recitation, you will have turned back the entire rosary and it will not count.
In this way, from one hundred to a thousand, and from a thousand to ten thousand, let them string together like beads on a cord. [He then drew] an arrow.
Arrows cannot pierce it, and blades cannot penetrate it; even a host of millions of māras shall all flee in retreat.

When I was reciting the Buddha’s name in the past, I did so merely by reciting it as a whole; only now do I realize that each word must emerge from within the heart, and each word must likewise enter back into the heart.
When reciting the Buddha’s name, one must first close the eyes and sit upright, concentrating the spirit and stabilizing the thoughts, without allowing for a single [distraction].

Free from even the slightest distracted mind, a restless and competitive mind, or a dull and indolent mind, open your mouth and let out sound, ensuring that the voice issues forth from the mind and the mind is transmitted through the mouth.
Regulate the breath so that the voice is harmonious—neither too slow nor too fast—with every syllable distinct and every phrase continuous.
If divided, a single character may form a sentence; if integrated, hundreds or thousands of sentences are as direct as a single sentence—continuous and dense.
From one sound to ten million sounds, from one moment to twelve hours, there is no interruption and no succession, neither deficiency nor omission.
After long practice until it becomes pure and mature, the flower blooms and the Buddha is seen.

Regarding the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*), the ancients observed that because the minds of sentient beings are distracted, it is difficult for them to achieve success in visualizing meditative objects (*guanxiang*). For this reason, they exclusively encouraged the single-minded recitation of the Name.

Now, the method of contemplation is also divided into two gates: the phenomenal (*shi*) and the principle (*li*). The subtlety of contemplation according to principle is as described in the so-called "one mind and three [contemplations]."
Contemplation is fundamentally subtle and profound; it truly cannot be achieved suddenly by an ordinary person at the beginning of their practice.

Regarding the method of contemplative cultivation, one should select any single visualization from among the sixteen contemplations and contemplate it repeatedly at all times, focusing the mind with unwavering concentration.

When the mind and its objects become empty and clear, the recitation of mantras will further enhance one's progress. Once one has become proficient in this regular contemplation, the objective realm will manifest when the time comes.
Manifest before you. This is the essential method for maintaining stability while riding a horse or using a staff; it must not be neglected as a practice to be cultivated concurrently.

Compiling this section on the Gate of Contemplation, the *Longshu Jingtuwen* says: "Purify yourself through fasting and precepts, clarify the mind and settle the thoughts, sit facing west with composure, and close your eyes."
Remain silent. Visualize the true golden-colored body of Amitābha Buddha seated upon a great lotus flower in the midst of a pool of seven treasures in the western direction.
His body is sixteen feet tall, and between his two eyebrows there is a single white tuft of hair pointing upward.
It has eight facets and is hollow within. It spirals to the right five times. Its radiant brilliance illuminates its golden face and golden body.
Next, settle the mind and fix one's attention upon the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa). One must not allow even the slightest thought of anything else to arise.

Whether closing or opening the eyes, one should see it clearly in both states. This is intended so that the mindfulness remains constant and unforgetting. Practicing in this manner for a long time, the mind of recollection...

Upon reaching maturity, one naturally experiences a response by beholding the entire body of the Buddha. This method is the most supreme; it means that when one visualizes the Buddha within one's own body, this very body is the Buddha.
Furthermore, it surpasses mere verbal recitation. After death, one will certainly attain birth in the highest grade of the highest level.
During the Tang dynasty, Qi Fang and Yuan Guo, two individuals who practiced the visualization method, felt themselves arrive in the Pure Land after only five months and beheld the Buddha.

Regarding the hearing of the Dharma, that which is called the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* provides a detailed exposition of various methods of visualization. Furthermore, it does not stop at this alone.

Master Lianchi said: "As for concentrating the mind through contemplation—whether sitting, standing, or forming mental images—all of these are flexible and lack fixed rules according to the occasion."

One should simply constantly observe the gap [between thoughts]. This is not something that can be accomplished by those whose engagement with sensory objects remains unresolved. Although one may not be able to observe it constantly, this too is a form of practice; do not worry about it.
It is further said that Han Zhuangbo Wei, every time at sunset, would face the northwest and visualize Mount Kunlun.

After doing this for a long time, he saw a celestial immortal from Mount Kunlun transmit the Dharma to him and enable his liberation. This is somewhat similar to the practice of "observing the sun" in the west.

However, those people merely belong to the realm of deluded thoughts; they have simply failed to cultivate right contemplation. Having long accumulated such delusions, even when their spiritual energy reaches its limit, they are still able to achieve what they see [in their visions].
How much more so, then, for one who single-mindedly practices right contemplation and achieves samādhi—how could such a person fail to attain rebirth?

Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* states: "Those who cultivate the Pure Land, when prostrating to the Buddha, should imagine themselves within a lotus flower performing the prostration, while the Buddha is within a lotus flower receiving their veneration.
When recollecting the Buddha, they should imagine themselves within a lotus flower sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), while the Buddha is within a lotus flower drawing them forth."
Thereafter, one should single-mindedly hold the Name. In the past, there were two monks who visualized lotus flowers opening and closing; they subsequently attained rebirth there.
How much more so for one who adds to this the single-minded holding of the Name—how could such a person fail to be reborn? Question: This sutra does not include [visualizations of] physical forms.

"Why is it now like this? [The Master] replied: "Because there is a primary focus, yet there is no obstruction to other practices. For example, when a Bodhisattva practices the six perfections with a particular emphasis on giving, it does not mean that the others are not cultivated;
they are simply practiced according to one's strength and capacity. Now, mindfulness of the Buddha is likewise."
Those who primarily focus on visualization should recite the name for a short time; those who primarily focus on reciting the name should visualize for a short time.

This is also the meaning of acting according to one’s strength and capacity. As for the statement that one does not combine both the name and the physical form, it is because there is a concern that if one is single-mindedly focused on holding the name while simultaneously being single-mindedly focused on visualizing the form, not only will the mind lack two simultaneous functions, but the two tasks will also conflict.
If one practices without distinguishing between the weightiness and lightness [of the practice], there will be no accomplishment at all.

If one clearly understands the meaning of the primary and auxiliary methods, then holding the name with a single mind constitutes the primary method, while even a brief period of auxiliary practice returns to that primary method. It is like adding fuel to a fire;
what obstacle could there be?
The Dharma Words on the Pure Land by Master Youxi state: Regarding visualization, it is as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.
There are sixteen objects of contemplation, yet the visualization of the Buddha is most essential.

One should visualize the body of Amitābha Buddha, sixteen feet in height, appearing like an image of purple-golden hue, standing upon a lotus flower made of the seven precious jewels, with hands extended downward in the gesture of welcoming and guiding. His body...

There are thirty-two marks of a great man, and eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). One who forms this visualization does so according to both phenomena (*vastu*) and principle (*tattva*).
As for the phenomena: one fixes the mind upon the Buddha and the Buddha upon the mind. First, one contemplates the level soles of the feet, which are like the base of a casket;
next, one contemplates the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel. Proceeding in this sequence, one traces the marks in reverse order up to the crown of the head.
The *uṣṇīṣa*. Furthermore, following the conditions from the *uṣṇīṣa* down to the soles of the feet, one perceives them with perfect clarity, without any distraction of mind.
Regarding "reasoning with single-mindedness," the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the body of the Dharma-realm; they enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings.
Therefore, when you contemplate the Buddha in your thoughts, that very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics."
Excellent! This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the right and universal knowledge of all the Tathāgatas arises from the mind’s conception.
Therefore, you all should fix your mindfulness upon that Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat.

The meaning of *Samyaksaṃbuddha* is fully elucidated herein. The subtle and wondrous threefold contemplation is explained in detail in the *Miaozongchao* (Commentary on the Essential Meaning) of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
Relying upon these two types of correct practice, one must necessarily advance by means of their mutual dependence.

Whenever one is walking, standing, sleeping, or reclining, one should single-mindedly recite the Name; whenever one is sitting cross-legged upon a meditation mat, one should contemplate with every thought. Thus one practices.
When weary, sit cross-legged to contemplate the Buddha; when rising from sitting, walk in meditation while reciting his name.
If one practices thus within the four modes of deportment without interruption, rebirth in the Western Land is certain.
Master Hanshan said: "While single-mindedly holding the name is certainly the correct practice, it must further be supported by visualization and contemplation to be seen as stable and secure.
When the Buddha taught the sixteen sublime contemplations to Vaidehī, she was able to achieve her goal in a single lifetime.
Now, one should select any one of these sixteen contemplations—either contemplating the sublime marks of the Buddha alone, or those of the Bodhisattvas."
Contemplate the realm of the Pure Land, as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* regarding the jeweled ground of lotus flowers and so forth, visualizing it according to your inclination.
If your visualization becomes clear and distinct, then throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, you will appear to be actually present in the Pure Land.

At the moment of death, you will be reborn there instantaneously in a single thought-moment. By applying the mind in this way and diligently maintaining the precepts, you will forever sever evil thoughts and afflictions. Through this purity—
The mind, with its continuous stream of contemplative awareness, is the true cause for the Pure Land; nothing surpasses this.

Ming Tang Yizhi said: "I have observed that in recent years, while periods for Chan, Vinaya, and doctrinal lectures are being propagated everywhere, the gate of Pure Land visualization has been neglected and left untaught.
Indeed, there are not a few people in the world who recite the Buddha’s name with their mouths, yet [the method for] generating..."

That the Pure Land is not numerous [in number] is because they do not cultivate the gates of contemplation (*guanmen*). For those who attain rebirth there, it is the mind that can go, while the mouth cannot go.
If one causes those who practice contemplation to be continuous and unceasing—such that whether dressing or eating, they are always within contemplation;

whether their spirit wanders through the sea of lotuses to prostrate before the Buddha amidst the flowers, or sits gazing at the golden countenance with its radiance shining in the four directions, or beholds him face-to-face—then [the land will be filled].
Amitābha’s body fills the void; sometimes one may quietly see his companions together at Lake Anavatapta.
One must not fail to know that what the ancients called "maintaining this single visualization" is intended to allow one to gradually ascend to its peak.
Zhang Cimin said: "The method of reciting the Buddha's name must be accompanied by visualization (*vipaśyanā*). Close your eyes and face west;

sit upright and contemplate silently that the spirit separates from the physical form and proceeds directly toward the West. Gradually, you will see forests, various waterfowl, and roads demarcated by golden cords."
Balustrades crisscrossed one another as he proceeded swiftly along the path. Before his eyes appeared jeweled ponds with exquisite lotuses, fragrant altars, and multi-storied pavilions.
There, the Tathāgata stood manifest in a body sixteen feet tall; Avalokiteśvara attended to his left and Mahāsthāmaprāpta to his right, emitting light from between his eyebrows.
He extended his hand to receive and guide us; I and the assembly of the ocean were all gathered within his light and led upward.

Prostrating at his feet with profound sorrow and earnestness, we suddenly beheld his golden palm touch our heads and nectar drench our bodies. This mind became vast and clear; we were protected and established in great peace and stability.

Gradually the spirit returns; once it has emerged and become stable, one will travel once through that world each day. When the path to rebirth is matured and the time arrives, one will not be deluded.
I pray that you convey this to all those who recite the Buddha’s name: you must understand that it is the mind that recites, and do not merely recite with the mouth.
Upon entering this gate, you are not far from the Buddha.
The Path within the Path, Part Three;
The Path within the Path, Part Four;
The Method for Encouraging Practice.
Regarding the practice of severing attachment through the gate of meditative visualization and upholding its power, there has never been a time when one was not diligent and earnest;
yet, if one cannot sever worldly conditions and is dragged along by affection, deluded thoughts will fly about in confusion. To have preferences and attachments is, in fact, love.
Anger, resentment, anxiety, sorrow, and fear likewise arise from attachment; it is because of this that the mind cannot remain upright.
Even if one has gained insight during ordinary times, one cannot avoid being moved by the heart when faced with actual circumstances, thereby failing to achieve the perfection of purity.

Truly lamentable! One must possess the power of firm endurance to sever the cords of craving. By examining this repeatedly and through diligent exertion, one may eventually reach the state of spontaneity;
this would be close to the goal. Thus concludes the Section on Severing Craving.
The Western Direction Explained. Bodhisattva Jue-ming-miao-xing said: "If there is a student who asks, 'How can one become free from worldly desires and attain non-obstruction?
the Bodhisattva replied: 'I shall deduce the great from the small and the internal from the external;
you all should understand its meaning well. Suppose someone here, for no reason at all, were to snatch away a single coin from you.'"

"Do you feel anger? He replied, "Though a single coin is insignificant, I would feel anger if I saw it taken from me. "And if someone were to give you that same single coin for no reason at all, would you feel joy?
He replied, "Though a single coin is insignificant, I would feel joy if I saw it given to me. Someone else answered, "A single coin is extremely trivial;
what is there to rejoice in being given, and what is there to be angry about being taken? The Bodhisattva said, "If you can be thus, then your mind—"
"You have been pure for a long time; why then do you still remain submerged in turbidity and defilement today? You should know that those who study fail to cleanse their minds with diligence.
Whether perceiving existence or non-existence, they are attached everywhere; in every thought-moment they are full of craving.

Consequently, their karmic consciousness rushes about in confusion, never stopping for even a moment. Even when they recite a single phrase of 'Amitābha Buddha,' their mental focus still wanders abroad."

That you can return to oneness in an instant is truly because, throughout immeasurable kalpas, you have never for even a single moment or day given rise to a mind that distances itself from worldly desires.
For this reason, these worldly desires have likewise, since beginningless kalpas, never for a single moment or day been willing to leave your minds.
Your bodies are entangled and your minds are bound; you have plunged deeply into the net of dust. How could you be like a lotus flower?

It emerges from the mud without being stained by it. Therefore, know that if one wishes to sever greedy attachment, one must first practice the contemplation of relinquishment and the contemplation of "this is not mine" regarding the taking away and giving of even a single word.
When it is taken away, do not give rise to anger; when it is given, do not give rise to joy.

In this manner, proceed until it concerns hundreds of thousands of millions of words, even up to billions of trillions of words, and even to one's own flesh, marrow, and bones, and even to the past and present.
From the future mind, thought, and consciousness, up to birth and death, karmic retribution, bodhi, and nirvāṇa—all are exactly like this;
there is no difference between the giving and taking of this single phrase. Spontaneously, habitual outflows will be extinguished, and obstructive conditions will be forever eradicated.

You shall gradually tread upon purity and accomplish the factors of enlightenment. You all should practice in reliance upon this; do not again harbor doubts regarding obstacles or hindrances. Furthermore:
He said: "Do you worry that your bodies are entangled in the worldly net and that your thoughts cannot be purified? I have a method for you:

simply make a vow to distance yourselves from the world and seek deliverance; turn your steadfast devotion toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss with a heart that seeks to behold Amitābha Buddha, replacing your persistent pursuit of fame and profit. In this way, you can immediately transcend the afflictions of the mundane world."
Thus he followed the path of awakening.

In the *Lèbāng wénlèi* (Classified Writings on the Land of Bliss), it is recorded that during the Song dynasty, Faying cultivated his mind through pure practices. When donors arrived, he would not refuse them; he accepted only a small portion of their offerings.
When those who lived with him urged him to renovate his quarters, he said, "If even this physical body is impermanent, why concern oneself with external things?"
In the eighth month of the fourth year of the Shaohui era, he manifested illness. While in meditative concentration, he beheld two bodhisattvas from the Pure Land.
The Great Master Youxi’s *Pure Land Dharma Words* states: "If one seeks sincere and earnest instructions for my sake, nothing is more essential than the two words of Yang Cigong:
'If love is not deep, one will not be born in Saṃsāra; if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in the Ultimate [Pure Land].'"
Joy! Indeed, in the practice of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*), one must unify the mind, earnestly uphold the Name, and maintain single-minded focus without distraction;
this is that upon which I must exert my utmost effort. Yet, there are times when one forgets and cannot recollect, or recollects but cannot remain unified.

This is due to nothing other than being led astray by emotional attachments. One must therefore diminish attachment to block such delusions, sever the root of emotion, and liberate oneself from craving.
This is what I must devote my whole heart to. Yet, there are times when one thinks of it but cannot forget it, or forgets it but cannot let go of it entirely.
This is due to nothing other than the inability of the mind to maintain single-minded focus.

Therefore, for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, if they habitually harbor even a slight attachment to this Sahā world, at the moment of death they will be obstructed by that attachment.
If one cannot be reborn when pulled [by a single thought], how much less so when there are many attachments?

That is, if there is even a single moment of inconsistency in the thought directed toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one will be turned away at the time of death by that thought and fail to be reborn; how much more so when there are many such thoughts?

Indeed, regarding the nature of attachment, there are those that are slight, those that are heavy, those that are profound, and those that are thin; there are those directed toward the primary retribution and those toward the secondary environment. These have been enumerated in succession.
As for these objects: parents, wives, children, brothers, friends; fame, achievement, wealth, and honor; essays, prose, and poetry; the Way, arts, and crafts;
clothing, food, and drink; houses, fields, and gardens; forests, springs, flowers, and plants; precious gems and playthings—such various wonders and excellencies are beyond counting.
Some are as massive and heavy as Mount Tai, while others are as light as a single hair from a goose’s down. There are...
To not forget a single thing is love. To not omit a single thought is love. If there is even one love remaining in the breast, then thoughts will not be unified;
if there is even one thought that does not return to oneness, then [true life] cannot arise. Alas!
"If love is not profound, one will not be born in Saṃbhava; if mindfulness is not single-minded, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī.

These two phrases may truly be called a golden probe for scraping away cataracts from the eyes and a sacred medicine for curing chronic ailments of the gallbladder and diaphragm. For all who are resolved to seek birth in Sukhāvatī, [these words are essential].
You should inscribe this upon the walls of your rooms and engrave it upon your skin. Recite it with solemnity from time to time, and maintain its presence in every thought.
Regarding the attachments of this Sahā world, seek daily to diminish them; regarding the mindfulness of Sukhāvatī, seek daily to cultivate it.

Lighten these attachments further and further until they gradually reach non-existence; cultivate that mindfulness further and further until it gradually approaches the ultimate. If you can truly do so—
In this way, although such a person has not yet escaped the Sahā world, they are no longer a long-term guest of the Sahā world;

although they have not yet been born in Sukhāvatī, they are already a distinguished guest of Sukhāvatī. When death approaches, right mindfulness will manifest before them, and rebirth in Sukhāvatī is certain.

Someone asked: "Is there a way to diminish attachment? He replied: "There is nothing more essential for diminishing attachment than a single thought-moment. The questioner asked again: "What about a single thought-moment?"
"Is there a Way? He replied, "In a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*), nothing is more essential than lightening attachment.
Someone smiled and said, "Your words, Master, seem to waver between two ends; they appear to lack a central principle. How can you lead those who study? He replied, "It is not a matter of two ends.
I wish to clarify the reason why a single thought-moment cannot be maintained as one. This is because the mind is scattered by diverse conditions."
However, the distracted mind has diverse objects of focus; this is brought about by its compulsive pursuit of sensory realms.
Thus, when there is one object in the Sahā world, there is one mind among sentient beings; and when there is one mind among sentient beings, there is one object in the Sahā world.

Therefore it is said: "Because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise. When conditions aggregate, the mind wavers within; when it pursues external objects, it rushes outward.
Dissipation: when the mind and its objects race together, they are as inexhaustible as the sands of the Ganges. If attachment is not forgotten, how can one’s thoughts be unified?
Therefore, those who wish to unify their thoughts have no better way than to diminish their attachment; those who wish to diminish their attachment have no better way than to unify their minds;

those who wish to unify their minds have no better way than to block off external objects. When all objects are empty, then all conditions are utterly stilled. When all conditions are utterly stilled...
Then, in a single thought-moment, one spontaneously achieves realization. If a single thought-moment is achieved, then the conditions of craving are exhausted. Therefore it is said:

"If you wish to unify your thoughts, nothing is better than lightening your cravings. If you wish to lighten your cravings, nothing is better than focusing on a single thought. For craving and thought cannot coexist;
they are like the sun and moon alternating in their courses, or like light and darkness turning away from each other. Someone asked: "Is there a way to block external objects?"
He said: "What I call 'blocking off the realm' does not mean eliminating all phenomena, nor does it mean closing one's eyes and not looking.

It means to realize their emptiness by engaging with the realm itself, and to empty the derivative by returning to the fundamental. This is because the myriad dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; their existence is a matter of mental construction (*citta*).
Thus, when the mind is present, objects are present; when the mind is empty, objects are empty. When objects are empty, the original nature [is revealed]."
Manifestation: when the original nature manifests, the myriad dharmas are empty; when the myriad dharmas are empty, emotional thoughts cease.

This occurs spontaneously and naturally, not through forced effort. As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "The seer and the conditions for seeing, along with the perceived forms, are like flowers in the sky—they have never existed at all.
This seeing and its conditions are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. How could there be [delusion] within this?"
This is not [the case]. Therefore, if one wishes to block off their sphere of influence, there is nothing better than embodying the emptiness of all things.

When one embodies the emptiness of all things, emotions naturally cease; when emotions naturally cease, craving does not arise. Since it is only the mind that manifests, once a single thought is formed, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says:
"To know it as an illusion is itself to leave it; no expedient means are required. To leave the illusion is itself awakening; this is also not a gradual process. There is neither going nor staying.
The transformation is as swift as the sound of a drum struck by a mallet. Those who study the Way should apply their whole hearts to this matter. Again, he asked:
"Are the lightening of worldly attachment and the single-minded focus on the Pure Land the same or different? He replied:

"One may be able to lighten attachment to this Sahā world, yet not necessarily be able to unify the thought of Sukhāvatī; however, one who can unify the thought of the Pure Land will certainly be able to lighten attachment to the Sahā world."
This is explained in terms of the distinction between those who lack resolve and those who possess it.

If one sets aside the lack of resolve and speaks only of possessing it, then loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is not a mindfulness that is not forgotten, and mindfulness is not a single-mindedness that does not forget loving-kindness; in these two practices, there is from the outset no interval or separation.
Master Lianchi cautioned himself, saying: "The ancients had a saying: 'Yu cherished every inch of shadow. As for the common people, they should cherish every minute of shadow.
Now that I am decrepit and worn out, it is not merely a matter of cherishing minutes; even for the duration of a single snap of the fingers, I must not allow my mind to be distracted.

'Not allowing the mind to be distracted' means that apart from the correct mindfulness of the primary inquiry (*ben-can*), if even a single thought of miscellaneous distraction arises, it must be immediately swept away."
Gather and return to right mindfulness; there must be no delay for even a moment. Now, I shall briefly set forth seven matters.

Having truly left the home life for the sake of birth and death, and desiring directly to achieve final resolution in this one lifetime, you must strive with all your might to maintain them and constantly admonish yourself.
First, you must not accumulate wealth, build houses, purchase fields, or keep any exquisite objects, including even scriptures, images, or other such items.
From antiquity, those who have emerged from noble families have all refrained from lingering attachment.

With single-minded right mindfulness, you must not engage in various non-essential matters that do not constitute immediate karmic conditions for merit. Wait for the time when the Great Matter has been clarified; it will not be too late to perform them then.
For now, let us temporarily set aside the gateway of the myriad practices.
With single-minded right mindfulness, one must not give rise to thoughts of greed or attachment toward pleasant forms or tastes, nor toward those who speak pleasant words in praise of me.
One must not give rise to thoughts of anger or vexation toward unpleasant forms or tastes, nor toward those who speak ill of me, who revile me, or who insult me. [One must plant...]

Whenever anything occurs that opposes or offends me, I shall give rise to a mind of anger and affliction; even regarding matters of the past or future, whether favorable or unfavorable, I shall entirely exclude them from my thoughts.
Maintaining firm walls and a steadfast defense, I shall keep my mind fixed in right mindfulness and refrain from composing verses or literary works.
One must not practice calligraphy in the true or cursive styles, compose inscriptions or couplets, polish formal letters, or peruse extraneous secular texts.

One must refrain from discussing the gains, losses, strengths, or weaknesses of others, and even more so from relying on mere subjective opinions to compose works with an arrogant mind, or attempting to offer critical evaluations of Chan while lacking thorough realization.
One must maintain silence and bind the tongue, focusing the mind one-pointedly on right mindfulness, and must not, under any circumstances, form intimate bonds with friends or associates.

One may attend invitations, travel to mountains to enjoy the scenery, engage in miscellaneous conversation and idle talk—indeed, all manner of worldly affairs—provided they are matters that ought to be done according to reason and cannot be avoided.
Aside from these, one must cease all other activities and maintain single-minded right mindfulness. One must not be greedily attached to them nor be negligent;
one must not indulge in excessive sleep. Until the Great Matter is clarified, one must exert oneself, endure hardships, and remain single-mindedly focused on right mindfulness.

Seventh, one should not compete with worldly people in talent or ability, nor strive for fame or power. One must not claim what has not been attained as attained, or what has not been realized as realized;

one must not deceive others by calling oneself a "spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) or falsely exalt oneself. Instead, one should maintain humility and embrace ignorance, remaining in the stage of a student throughout one's life to refine oneself.
One should always be diligent, ever-striving, and maintain single-minded right mindfulness.
Master Hanshan said: "To practice the recitation of the Buddha's name with the aim of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, one must first resolve the great matter of birth and death.
People nowadays only begin to recite the Buddha's name once they have resolved to end birth and death; they simply say that the Buddha can bring about the ending of birth and death."
If one does not know the root and trunk of birth and death, in the end toward what can one attain liberation?

If the mind that recollects the Buddha cannot sever the root and trunk of birth and death, how can one attain liberation from birth and death? What is the root and trunk of birth and death? An ancient said:
"If karma is not heavy, one will not be born in Saha; if craving is not severed, one will not be born in the Pure Land. From this we know that craving is [the root].
This root of death—tracing back this root of craving—it does not exist only in this present life, nor did it exist in one, two, three, or four lifetimes.

From beginningless time, through birth after birth and life after life, as we have cast off one body and taken up another, when has there ever been a single thought-moment free from this root of craving?
Because the seeds of such a root of craving have accumulated over vast eons and are profoundly deep, birth and death are without end.

It is truly pitiful. Only today have you finally resolved to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, yet you merely hope for rebirth in the Western Pure Land while remaining ignorant of the very root of birth and death.

How could you have ever severed even a single thought of attachment? Since you do not know the root of birth and death, you recite the Buddha’s name on one side, while the root of birth and death continues to grow unchecked on the other.
To practice such mindfulness of the Buddha is to remain entirely disconnected from the resolution of birth and death.
Related to this: when one reaches the moment of death, only the root of craving for life and death manifests before one.
It is only then that one realizes the Buddha has been of no avail at all; by then, it is too late for regret. Therefore, I exhort those who practice nianfo now:

first, you must understand that craving is the very root of birth and death. As you practice nianfo now, in every thought-moment you must sever this root of craving, even amidst the activities of daily life.

Previously, when practicing *nienfo* at home, whatever one saw with the eyes—children, grandchildren, family affairs, or property—not a single thing was not an object of attachment, as if one’s entire body were in a pit of fire.
Attachment was the master, while *nienfo* was merely a superficial veneer.
For instance, when the feelings for children and grandchildren manifest before you, turn the light back and look: is this one sound of "Buddha" truly [real]?
If you can overcome it, do you love it? If you can indeed sever it, do you love it? If you cannot sever it, how will you ever ultimately resolve the matter of birth and death?
Therefore, I urge those who practice Buddha-recitation: the foremost requirement is to have a sense of urgency regarding birth and death.
The resolve to sever birth and death must be urgent; one must, in every thought-moment, cut through the very roots of birth and death.

Then, every thought-moment is a time for resolving birth and death. If one is truly earnest in this way, with every stroke of the blade meeting blood, then if one does not emerge from birth and death, the Buddhas would be guilty of speaking falsehoods.
In *The Morning Bell for Returning to the Pure Land*, Zhou Kefu states: "The Buddha identifies greed, anger, and delusion as the three poisons.
When the poison of greed resides in the mind and manifests through the body, it becomes theft. Therefore, whether by daylight or in the dark, all such acts are termed 'theft.

Among the five desires, the desire for form (sensual lust) is the most potent. The Tathāgata has said: 'Suppose there were another matter in the world as grave as sexual desire; if a person were to obtain it...'"
The Way is indeed rare. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "All sentient beings, because of lustful desire, establish their very nature and life.

Through thousands of births and myriad kalpas, they have come from within this [desire]. Therefore, lustful desire is particularly heavy; as for the eight difficulties and the three miserable realms, one heads toward them from within this [desire], and among these, the calamity of lust is the most惨烈 (catastrophic).
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In your cultivation of samādhi, you originally seek to transcend worldly toil."

If the lustful mind is not eliminated, one cannot transcend the realm of dust. Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever lust, they will inevitably fall into the paths of demons.
Furthermore, it says: "If you seek the Buddha’s wondrous fruit with a lustful mind, even if you attain wondrous enlightenment, it will all be rooted in lust.
With lust as its fundamental basis, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape. This sutra begins by borrowing the setting of a chamber of lust.
This establishment of discourse takes the fundamental ignorance of sentient beings as its primary point of departure;
only thereafter does it address those with the karmic capacity for the Way. This is truly the "needle-method" of the Tathāgata’s crown. Furthermore, the Sutra in Forty-two Sections states:
The Buddha told the śramaṇas, "Be careful not to look at women. If you see them, do not look. Be careful not to speak with them. If you must speak with them, command your mind."
Regarding Right Practice, he said: "I am a śramaṇa dwelling in a defiled world; I must be like a lotus flower, unsullied by the mud.
To the elderly, I shall act as a mother; to those of middle age, as an elder sister; to the young, as a younger sister; and to the children, as a daughter.

I shall honor them with propriety, and my mind shall be exceptionally focused and attentive. I shall contemplate from the top of my head down to my feet, looking inward at this body: what is there within it?"

It is filled with the various impurities of decaying matter; this explains its significance. According to the words of this sutra, it is truly the most authoritative instruction of the Śākya clan, and not merely something that applies to śramaṇas alone.
Peng Chimu’s *Biographies of the Holy and Sages of the Pure Land*, in the section on Kings and Ministers, states:

"For kings and ministers to enter the Way is more difficult than for lay practitioners (*jushi*). Those who are preoccupied with fame and office prioritize advancement; those who indulge in ease and pleasure regard quiet cultivation as a hardship."
Were it not for those who have long planted roots of merit and firmly maintained their correct vows, how could they avoid falling back from the precipice?

As for these gentlemen, who do not abandon the toils of the mundane world yet together take refuge in the Pure Land, they may truly be called those who manifest in the bodies of officials to preach the Dharma.
This is especially true of such figures as Liu Zhitou, Bai Juyi, Su Shi, and Zhao Mengfu, whose praises [of Amitābha] are well known.
Alas! Though the pure cause for refuge exists, when the moment arrives to relinquish consciousness, such auspicious responses are rarely heard.

This is truly because the intellect is deluded by manifold paths and illness arises from attachment to existence. That literary men harbor such habitual tendencies has been the case since antiquity; yet when birth and death arrive, [one must face them].
It is impossible to rely on mere luck. Future gentlemen should take this as a warning and a lesson.

The "Preparation for the End" involves accumulating merit and practicing virtuous deeds throughout one's life, eliminating attachment and severing all that is non-virtuous; this is fundamentally intended as a preliminary arrangement for the final moment of death.

If, at the final moment when approaching death, one suddenly becomes fearful of dying and anxious, with the inner mind becoming confused and disturbed, would this not be a great betrayal of one's original resolve?
At that time, one must exert all effort to maintain composure; only by casting aside everything else and keeping right mindfulness clear can one truly proceed toward the goal.
While such meritorious practice is certainly maintained during ordinary times, it is especially critical at this juncture.
Finally, I have compiled the "Section on the End of Life.
Regarding the "Text on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at the Hour of Death" by the Tang Dynasty Master Shandao: The Disciple Zhiguizi asked:

"Among all worldly matters, none exceeds the reality of birth and death. With a single breath not returning, one belongs to the next world; with a single thought erring, one falls into the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*)."
Hui: "Your humble servant has repeatedly received your instructions on the method of rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo*).

The principle is very clear. Yet, I fear that when illness arrives and death approaches, my consciousness may become distracted; furthermore, I worry that others might disturb my right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), causing me to forget the pure cause.
I humbly hope you will again show me the way to the ultimate path, so that I may escape the suffering of the sinking wheel of saṃsāra. The Master said: "Excellent is your question."
Furthermore, for all people who wish to be reborn in the Pure Land at the end of their lives, they must not fear death.

They should constantly reflect that this body is full of suffering, impure, and entangled by various evil karmas. If one can cast off this defiled body and be reborn transcendentally in the Pure Land, one will experience immeasurable bliss and be liberated from the miserable realms of birth and death, attaining even those things most desired—just as if one had cast off a heavy burden.
Though my clothes are tattered, they may be exchanged for precious garments; you need only set aside both body and mind and harbor no attachment.
Whenever you encounter illness, contemplate impermanence and wait for death with single-minded resolve.

You should instruct your family members, caregivers, and those who come to inquire after me that whenever they approach me, they must recite the Buddha’s name for me and not speak of trivial or mundane matters.
Regarding matters of long or short duration within the family, there is no need for soft words of consolation or prayers for peace and happiness;
these are all empty, flowery words that provide no benefit. When one is gravely ill and approaching the end, relatives must not shed tears or wail.
They may also utter sounds of lamentation and distress, or their minds may become distracted, causing them to lose right mindfulness.
At such times, they should simply chant the Buddha’s name with one voice until their breath ceases; only then may they weep piteously.

If there is even the slightest attachment to this world, it will immediately become an obstruction, preventing liberation. If they encounter someone who clearly understands the Pure Land and frequently comes to exhort and encourage them, [they will succeed].
"It is a great blessing. If one relies upon this, one will certainly transcend the cycle of birth;
of this there is no doubt. He asked again, "May one still seek medical treatment and take medicine? He replied, "Seeking medical treatment and taking medicine do not initially hinder [the practice].
However, medicine can only treat illness; it cannot prolong life. When life is exhausted, what can medicine do? If one kills the lives of sentient beings for [medicine]..."
To take medicine for the sake of bodily comfort—this is not permissible. I have often observed that when people observe the fast because they are ill, they achieve slight recovery;
yet when physicians supplement their medicines with wine, food, and meat, their illnesses recur.
Thus one truly knows that the power of the Buddha can save, whereas wine and meat are of no benefit. Again, he asked: "What of seeking spirits to pray for blessings? He replied: "As for humans..."
The length of one's life is already determined at birth; why rely on ghosts and spirits to prolong it?

If, out of delusion, you believe in the heterodox and slaughter sentient beings to sacrifice to ghosts and spirits, you will only increase your karmic offenses and, conversely, diminish your lifespan.
When the great destiny is exhausted, what can petty ghosts do? To be needlessly terrified is of no avail for either. You must be most diligent and cautious; this text should be posted accordingly.
Direct it toward the present moment; see it from time to time so that you do not forget it when facing danger. He asked again:

"Can those who have never recited the Buddha’s name in their lives still use this method? He replied: "Whether they be monastics or laypeople, whether they have recited the Buddha’s name or not, all who use this method will attain rebirth in the Pure Land;
there is no doubt about this. I have often seen people in the world [neglect] their regular recitation of the Buddha’s name and...
They praise [the Pure Land] and fervently vow to be reborn in the Western Paradise; yet, when they actually face illness, they again fear death and say nothing at all of rebirth and liberation.
Only when their breath has faded and their life-force is exhausted, as their consciousness enters the dark realm, do they finally recite the ten recitations while ringing the bell.
This is just like closing the gate after the thief has fled—what can it possibly accomplish? The matter of the gateway of death is of great importance; one must...
This can only be achieved through one's own diligent effort. If there is even a single moment of error, one will suffer for kalpas; who can take one’s place?
Reflect on this, reflect on it! When you are free from worldly affairs, you should practice and uphold this Dharma with diligence; this is the great matter for the time of death.
Dharma Master Song Zhongming resided at Ba’en Temple in Shanyin. He had never previously observed the precepts or maintained any discipline.

Once, while suffering from an illness, he said to his fellow student Daoning, "My mind and consciousness are scattered and chaotic; what medicine can cure this? Daoning replied, "Simply recite the Buddha’s name in accordance with your breath;

this is the supreme medicine. Zhongming followed this method and practiced it. When the seventh day arrived and he was extremely exhausted, Daoning further instructed him to practice the visualization of the Buddha’s image.
After a long time, he suddenly said, "The two Bodhisattvas have arrived. A moment later, he added, "The Buddha is coming. He then closed his eyes and passed away.
The *Lungshu Jingtu Wen* (Treatise on the Pure Land of Longshu) states: "Regarding those of the lowest grade of rebirth:

at the moment of death, when the forms of the hells have already appeared, if they can wholeheartedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times (*namo amituo fo*), then the forms of the hells will transform into lotus flowers."
They will also be born in the Pure Land. This is because this Buddha’s compassion is profoundly deep and his majestic power is exceedingly great; thus he is able to act in this way.
What is called "ten recitations" refers to personally reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times during one's lifetime, not requesting others to recite it after death.
As for those who recite it themselves during their lifetime, when the end of life approaches, the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas will come in person to welcome them.
Therefore, one will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land. As for requesting others to recite [the Buddha's name] after one's death, there is no certainty that it will be effective. A sutra states:

"If others perform meritorious deeds on behalf of a person after their death, they receive but one-seventh of the fruit. However, those who perform them themselves while alive receive a reward a thousand or ten-thousandfold.
Why, then, do people not find it distressing to recite the Buddha’s name ten times every day while alive, rather than waiting until death to request others to do so?

It further says: For example, although iron and stone are heavy, they can cross a river by relying on the power of a boat; yet a single needle, though light, cannot cross the river without such reliance.
This means that even if a person has grave offenses, they may be reborn in the Pure Land by relying on the Buddha’s power;
whereas even if one’s offenses are slight, if one does not rely on the Buddha’s power, one will likewise fail to be reborn there. It is also like having committed evil throughout one's life.
One day they were summoned for amnesty and thus became peaceful citizens. Those who rely on the power of the Buddha to eliminate their evils and transgressions are likewise so.

Furthermore, it is like lice and nits: though they die and are reborn ten thousand times, they cannot travel even a single *li*; yet if they attach themselves to a human body, they can reach a thousand *li*.
Those who rely on the power of the Buddha to be born in the Pure Land shall likewise attain this; do not harbor any doubts.

Even those with sinful karma who cannot achieve rebirth through mere recitation of the Buddha’s name will nonetheless be reborn if they give rise to the thought of seeing the Buddha and attaining the Way, and resolve to deliver all their enemies and kin.
Some may say: "A person has committed evil throughout their life, slaughtering sentient beings and torturing others."

If even commoners who recite the Buddha’s name at the moment of death attain rebirth in the Pure Land, one must consider this: for the sentient beings who were killed or tormented by them, their hearts harbor grievances and injustices—when can these ever be resolved?
The answer is: After being born in the Pure Land and attaining the Way, one will deliver all those who were either enemies or kin.
Is this not far superior to the endless cycle of mutual vengeance where neither side finds release?
