From *Master Tianru’s Questions and Answers on the Pure Land*: Question: It is said that even if one has committed evil throughout a lifetime, by reciting the Buddha’s name at the moment of death, one may be reborn there while still carrying one's karmic burdens, and furthermore, there shall be no falling back. This power of Amitābha’s vows is truly inconceivable.
If this is so, may I simply attend to worldly affairs during my life and wait until the very end to then recite the Buddha’s name? Answer: [The text continues with the Master’s response.]
The answer was: "Alas, alas! What kind of foolish and deluded words are these? Arsenic and poisoned wine are the most virulent poisons;

yet these words of yours are more poisonous than arsenic and poisoned wine. They do not merely deceive and mislead yourself, but furthermore deceive and mislead all those throughout the world—whether monastics or laypeople, virtuous men or faithful women—all by means of these words. As for what was previously said:

As for perverse and evil ordinary beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha at the moment of death, they must have possessed roots of goodness and the causal conditions of merit from previous lives;
only then do they encounter a spiritual friend and only then are they able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Such fortunate individuals are not one or even half a person among ten thousand.
Do you truly believe that everyone has such good fortune at the moment of death? Have you not seen what the *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) states:

"There are ten kinds of people in the world who cannot practice mindfulness of the Buddha at the time of death. First, they may not encounter a virtuous friend, and thus there is no one to exhort them to mindfulness.
Second, they are so entangled by the suffering of their karma that they have no leisure for mindfulness. Third, they may suffer from a stroke..."
1. Loss of speech, such that one is unable to invoke the Buddha’s name. 2. Mental derangement and loss of consciousness, whereby focused contemplation cannot be achieved.
3. Encountering water or fire, leaving no leisure for sincere devotion. 4. Meeting with jackals or wolves, resulting in the absence of virtuous friends.
5. Having evil friends at the time of death, who destroy one's faith. 6. Overeating to excess, leading to a stupor and death. 7. Being in the midst of a military battle.
In battle, one may suddenly forget [the danger]. Tenth, one may suddenly fall from a high cliff, injuring or destroying one's life.
These ten kinds of events are all things commonly heard of and seen with the eyes; they concern both monastics and laypeople, men and women alike, for everyone encounters them.
Whether summoned by past karma or induced by present karma, they suddenly manifest before one, leaving no room for avoidance. You, moreover...
It is not that a sage possessing supernormal powers has the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and can thus know whether one will have karma at the time of death;

nor does he possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) or the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and can thus know whether one’s death will be auspicious or inauspicious due to the ten kinds of evil conditions mentioned above.
Suddenly encountering this kind [of situation], it is all over; you can no longer make a move. Even if you are surrounded by knowledgeable living Buddhas, they cannot save you.
You must then undergo retribution according to your karma, suffering pain and punishment within the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties.
By that time, even if you wish to hear the name of the Buddha, you will not hear it. Directly...
Even if you were not subject to such evil conditions and died merely of a common illness, you would still not escape the wind-blades that dismember the body and the separation of the four elements—
like a live turtle forced from its shell or a crab dropped into boiling water— overwhelmed by agony and struck with terror and panic.

It is impossible to practice the Buddha-recitation (nien-fo). Furthermore, even if you die while free from illness, or if your worldly affairs are not yet concluded and your worldly thoughts have not ceased—such that you are agitated in your breast by craving for life and fearing death—it is impossible to practice the Buddha-recitation.
Moreover, if you are a layperson, it is compounded by the fact that your private family affairs are unresolved and your funeral arrangements are unfinished;
with your wife weeping and your children crying, you are tormented by a hundred kinds of anxieties. It is impossible to practice the Buddha-recitation. Furthermore...
Even before you have died, when you are afflicted by even a slight illness, you will endure pain and suffering, wailing and groaning;
you will seek out medicine and physicians, offer prayers and perform repentance, and your distracted thoughts will fly about like birds, so that you will be unable to recite the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, even before you fell ill, it was simply that your years were advanced, signs of decay had appeared, you were exhausted and decrepit, and filled with sighs, lamentations, and anxieties;
you spent all your time arranging things left and right upon this aging body until you could no longer recite the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, even before you grew old, during the days of your youth and vigor, it was precisely then that you should have been best suited for reciting the Buddha’s name.

At such times, should one’s deranged mind not yet have subsided and remain entangled in worldly affairs—climbing here and clinging there, with distracted and chaotic thoughts, and a vast expanse of karmic consciousness—one will be unable to achieve success in reciting the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, even if you possess leisure and independence and are determined to practice, [you must remain vigilant].

If one cannot clearly penetrate the nature of worldly phenomena, cannot let them go, cannot maintain stability, and cannot remain seated in stillness, then when even a slight境 (object-condition) suddenly manifests before you, the master will follow it into delusion;
at that point, even the recitation of the Buddha’s name will be of no avail.

Look at him when he is old and sick; even during his days of youth and leisure, if there is the slightest matter hanging on his mind, he is already unable to recite the Buddha’s name. How much less so when he reaches the time of death?
And yet you say further, "Just carry out your worldly affairs"—you are truly a fool to speak such foolish words. I can guarantee that you have misapplied your body and mind. For now...
Worldly affairs are like dreams and illusions, like shadows and echoes. Which of them has any real efficacy? Which of them can take the place of [resolving] birth and death?

Even if you extensively construct monasteries, increase the permanent endowments, strive for fame and rank, and form alliances with officials and the wealthy—though you may imagine these to be many good deeds, you do not realize that you have violated the Tathāgata’s principle of not embodying the Way.
This concerns the precepts regarding the extensive construction of monasteries and the like. Have you not heard it said that conditioned achievements harbor many faults?
Before the heavenly realms are realized, the hells are already formed; before the nature of birth and death is clarified, all such acts become the root of suffering.

When the light of the eyes falls to the ground at the time of receiving retribution, one will finally realize that everything done throughout one's life was merely adding shackles to shackles, adding chains to chains, [and adding] cauldrons...
In the depths of the boiling cauldron, firewood and charcoal are added; atop the sword-trees, blades and spears are assisted. Beneath the *kāṣāya*, one loses their human body;
for ten thousand kalpas it will be difficult to recover. Even an iron-hearted man would shed tears upon hearing this.

When the Patriarch spoke thus with such bitter urgency to exhort people, did he ever permit you to merely pursue worldly affairs, waiting until the moment of death to recite the Buddha’s name? You should reflect that while living in this world, one can...
How long will it last? Like a spark struck from stone or a flash of lightning, it passes in the blink of an eye.
While you are still young and free from illness, rouse your body and mind and cast aside worldly affairs. Seize every moment of daylight to recite the Buddha’s name;
seize every hour of effort to cultivate pure karma. Then, when the time of death arrives—whether it be a "good death" or a "bad death"—you will have your own provisions ready.
I have made my preparations in advance. My future course is now secure and steady. Were it not so, repentance would be difficult to pursue later.
Reflect upon this, reflect upon it!
Master Udumbara said: "Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha and wish to be born in the Pure Land must constantly reflect that all things in this world are impermanent;

what is formed must inevitably decay, and what is born must inevitably die. If one does not personally hear the Buddha-dharma, then from body to body, one will transmigrate through the three realms and the four modes of birth within the six paths, with no prospect of liberation. Now, having met with the necessary conditions, I have been able to hear it."

The True Dharma enables one to cultivate pure karma and take the Buddha alone as one’s object of mindfulness. Upon casting off this retribution body, one shall be born in the Pure Land, enter the womb of a lotus flower, and experience all manner of bliss.
One will forever be liberated from birth and death and never regress from Bodhi. This is the lifelong achievement of a great man.
When illness first arises, it is precisely the time to press forward and keep the mind and body expansive and untroubled; do not give rise to doubt.

One must simply sit facing west in a formal posture and single-mindedly visualize Amitābha Buddha, together with the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and countless transformation Buddhas, all appearing before one.
With a focused mind, recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha," ensuring that each sound follows the next without interruption.
Regarding all worldly affairs and activities, one must not give them thought, nor should one harbor any craving for them.
If thoughts of attachment arise, you must immediately recite the Buddha’s name. Within that urgency, the obstacles of karmic hindrances will be extinguished;
by this single thought, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. If your life has not yet ended, you will naturally attain peace.
Be careful not to give rise to deluded thoughts of lingering attachment to the world. You should live when it is time to live, and die when it is time to die. Simply prepare for your departure.
Why need one harbor doubts? If one understands this principle, it is like casting off tattered garments to don superior robes.
Once one abandons the ordinary body, one immediately ascends to the stage of Buddhahood—is this not magnificent?
The *Dayou zhiguí jí* states: The verse from the "Benevolent Head" (*Xianshou pin*) chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Again, he emits a light named 'Beholding the Buddha.
This light awakens those who are about to die, causing them to see the Tathāgata according to their recollection; at the end of life, they attain birth in that Pure Land.

Thus, for those facing the end of life, one should encourage them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and furthermore, display sacred images for them to behold and revere, so that they may develop deep [faith] toward the Buddha.
They take refuge and look up [to him]. For this reason, he is able to accomplish this radiance. The first four lines state that the Bodhisattva emits immeasurable light;
among these, one kind is called "seeing the Buddha. By emitting this radiance, he enables those whose lives are ending to see the Buddha and be reborn there.
The latter four lines state that because this Bodhisattva exhorts those facing death to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they are further led to gaze upon and revere him.

Because of this Buddha image, one obtains such radiance. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "At the final moment of death, one can surpass the power of a lifetime of practice, because of its intensity.

Master Yìhé’s *Wújìndēng* records that in the northwest corner of the Jetavana Monastery in the Western Regions, at the place where the sun sets, an "Impermanence Court" was established, where a standing image was fashioned facing [the setting sun].
In the west, hold five-colored banners. Place the sick person behind the image, holding the base of a banner with their hand, while maintaining the visualization of being reborn following the Buddha.
Those attending the patient should burn incense, scatter flowers, and ring the chime, assisting in the recitation of the Buddha’s name to support the patient.
If there is any impurity, it must be removed immediately. One must resolutely attain rebirth. If the mind wanders through the Dharma-realm, one comes and goes [in accordance with reality].
Regarding "unimpeded": one is not constrained by these dharmas. Master Lianchi said:
An ancient had a saying, "Illness is the excellent medicine for sentient beings; therefore, when one is ill, one should give rise to great joy.
In all circumstances that are unsatisfactory, do not give rise to affliction. He further spoke of birth and death...
If there is life, then amidst this illness one should give rise to great liberation; accept death and birth as they come, and do not harbor fear.
Furthermore, the past is like an illusion, the present is like an illusion, and the future is like an illusion. Let go of everything with total sincerity and maintain only right mindfulness.
Endure all hardships within the illness by all means; do not harbor a restless mind seeking a swift recovery. This is precisely what constitutes [true practice].
This is an excellent remedy for swift recovery.

Furthermore, it is said: having settled all household affairs and relinquished all worldly attachments, with a mind that is utterly empty, one should simply recite the six-syllable name of the Buddha, never forgetting it for even a moment.
Thus, karmic obstacles will naturally be extinguished. Once karmic obstacles have been extinguished, [liberation] will naturally follow.
"You slept peacefully last night; your body and mind are healthy and strong. Those who practice the Buddha-mindfulness should make a vow to leave this evil world and be born in that Land of Bliss.
He also said to Zhu Xizong: "Your honorable illness has reached a very critical stage at this point; you should [speak] whatever you wish to say."
I have written this all at once and entrusted it to my son and my wife, so that their hearts may be free from any lingering attachments.

With single-minded right mindfulness, if you have gained sufficient faith in the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation during your daily life, you may then inwardly reflect with your mind and eyes upon the four characters of the Buddha’s name—distinct, clear, and uninterrupted. This may begin from today or tomorrow; even if...
Do not depart. It is even possible to live to the age of one hundred and twenty; this is a matter of vital importance. A lifelong friendship between friends rests precisely upon this point;
all other matters are trivial and cannot be afforded the time for consideration. By no means must you be greedy for life or fearful of death, thereby failing in this great undertaking.

Furthermore, he said to Wang Dazhu: "Regarding your noble illness, you should completely let go of all external matters, as well as this very body with its four limbs and hundred bones, until it is empty and devoid of a single thing.
If it is truly impossible to bring it to rest, then set it aside for the time being and wait to deal with it later.
If delusive thoughts blaze up and cannot be controlled, you should chant the Buddha’s name several times to suppress them. As for worldly glory..."
Prosperity and wealth last no longer than a brief moment; calamities, hardships, and afflictions likewise last no longer than a brief moment before they vanish in an instant.
Furthermore, all things belong to prior conditions (pūrvapratyaya); they are not something that human effort can alter.
Relinquish everything completely and recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion. My most earnest exhortation!

Furthermore, it is said: Someone asked, "If there is one who has spent their entire life diligently encouraging others to recite the Buddha’s name, yet at the moment of death experiences a single thought of regret, they will consequently fail to attain rebirth.
Conversely, if there is another who has spent their entire life accumulating evil, yet at the moment of death resolves to recite the Buddha’s name, they will consequently attain rebirth. Then...
Why is it that the virtuous suffer loss, while the wicked, conversely, obtain gain? Alas!
Among ten million people, there is but one who maintains right mindfulness at the moment of death despite having accumulated evil throughout their life.

If it were not for the roots of goodness planted in previous lives, how could one possibly give rise to right mindfulness when overwhelmed by the agony of death and rendered unconscious and delirious? Thus it is with the virtuous person.
To experience regret at the time of death is the fate of but one among ten million people; yet such instances do indeed occur.

These must be those who practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name throughout their lives with negligence and indifference, rather than with what is called diligent effort. For one who is "precise" (jing), the mind is free from confusion;

for one who is "diligent" (qin), the mind is without interruption. How, then, could such a person give rise to regret? Therefore, those who have committed evil should urgently engage in self-examination and reform.
Do not harbor deluded thoughts that such a stroke of luck will come at the moment of death. Those who sincerely seek the Pure Land should simply increase their own diligent efforts;
do not worry about falling back or regretting at the time of death.

Furthermore, the *Amitābha Sūtra Commentary* (*Anle ji*) states: "Those who experience disorientation at the time of death do so because, throughout their lives, they have followed after deluded thoughts and failed to cultivate right mindfulness;
thus, their minds are largely distracted. As previously mentioned, when the warmth of life is about to depart, all that one has done during this lifetime manifests simultaneously.
The spirit and mind become terrified, and one’s movements become frantic and unsteady. Those destined for the hells see a mountain of knives."
The Sword-Tree Hell is viewed as a grove; those destined to fall among animals perceive the wombs of mares and donkeys as their dwellings.

Even if one performs good deeds and is reborn in the human or celestial realms, one cannot avoid feelings of aversion and attachment toward parents. This state persists even for those at the initial stage of the Lesser Vehicle (Śrāvaka), who are still unable to correctly discern the process of entering and exiting [rebirth].
All such states are termed "inversion" (*viparyāsa*). Driven by these inversions, beings wander through the three realms and seven destinies.

One receives birth according to one's karma. Now that you have attained single-mindedness without distraction, your inner mind will be concentrated in right mindfulness and you will externally be met by the Buddha’s welcome.

Upon casting off this retribution body, you will proceed directly to that land. As the Buddha said, "According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure," and further stated, "All lands are sustained solely by perception.
Since you have perfected pure perception, it is certain that you will attain rebirth; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, the Wise One said: "The mind abiding in meditative concentration at the moment of death is itself the Pure Land.

Regarding the statement that "stirring a thought is the time of rebirth in the Pure Land," what is meant by "abiding in concentration" is ensuring that the mind is not inverted; what is meant by "stirring a thought" is the subsequent aspiration to be born in that land.
A Minor Preface to the "Verse on the World of Vast and Noble Lotus," concerning the single gate of the manifestation of the sacred realm:
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings, like the rising sun appearing as reflections in a hundred rivers.

However, even if the sun is in the sky, if the water in the rivers is turbid, it cannot be seen. Therefore, one must practice mindfulness through the gate of visualization (*guanmen*) before [the Buddha can appear].
It can clarify turbid water and open the eye of the mind, allowing for a broad vision of the impermanence of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment). As a sutra states:

"When a person is about to die, their body and mind suffer great pain; one should cause the patient to contemplate the *lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana* of the Buddha, maintaining this contemplation continuously so that they may give rise to the *bodhicitta*.

Furthermore, one should extensively explain for them how difficult it is to dwell within the three realms (*tridhātu*) and the sufferings of the three miserable paths (*apāya*), concluding that only the *bodhi* of the Buddha is [the refuge]."
This is the true refuge. Alas! This is the Tathāgata’s compassionate pity for sentient beings, his arduous effort to rescue them at the moment their lives are ending.
The Buddha said that the mind at the time of death possesses immense power; therefore, the thought at the end of life can eliminate even heavy karma.
Yet, I have observed that among those who have practiced the recitation of the Buddha's name throughout their lives, there may still be those who experience suffering when their end approaches.

When the body is oppressed, the tongue-root may become short and stiff, such that there are those who cannot recite the Buddha’s name. How much more so when, during ordinary times, one has not cultivated visualization to maturity;

yet at the moment when the eight sufferings press upon one another and the four mountains close in from all sides, one wishes for the voice of the spiritual friend to guide them so that the recitation of the Buddha’s name continues unceasingly and the mind of visualization remains undistracted—this must surely stem from the roots of goodness planted in the causal conditions of past lives.
Only those who are far-removed from worldly distractions can attain this; how could it be expected of ordinary, mundane beings? It must be as stated in the *Contemplation Sūtra*:

"Except for the time one sleeps, one should constantly keep this matter in mind. Furthermore, it says that only when one constantly hears the wondrous Dharma both upon emerging from and entering meditative concentration is one truly established in stability.
Ming Dynasty Yuan Hongdao had a son named Deng. At the age of thirteen, he was suffering from abdominal distension and was about to die. He said to Zhongdao, "I am dying.
Uncle, how can you save me? Zhongdao replied, "You need only recite the Buddha's name, and you will immediately attain rebirth in the Buddha-land."
"In this world of five turbidities, there is nothing to be attached to. He then joined his palms and recited the name of Amitābha Buddha; his kinsmen all joined him in unison.
After a short while, he smiled and said, "I see a lotus flower, its color a faint red. A moment later he said, "The flower is gradually growing larger;
its color is so brilliant that nothing can compare to it. A moment later he said, "The Buddha has arrived; his marks and signs, and his radiance, fill [the space]."

In his chamber, after a short while, his breath became labored. He said to Zhongdao, "You need only recite the name of the Buddha. Deng recited the name of the Buddha several times, then, with palms joined, he passed away.
The *Jingtu Shengxian Lu* (Record of Holy and Sages of the Pure Land) states: Qian Tang’s Ge Yian of the Ming dynasty took Master Yunqi Hong as his teacher;
his dharma name was Guangtai. He served his parents with filial piety and delighted in practicing hidden virtues (*yin-de*).

In his later years, he served the Buddha with great devotion and formed two seasonal societies with the monk Suanxu to hold *nianfo* assemblies and recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. After some time, he said, "My great life-limit is drawing near."
"I must now plan for my return to the West. He then shut himself in a room to practice meditation and recitation, never ceasing from morning until night.
Two days before his appointed date of departure, his family came to visit him and were deeply moved by grief. Dao’an said to them, "Birth is inevitably followed by extinction; why should you grieve?"
"I am now concentrating my spirit in the Pure Land to behold Amitābha face-to-face. You must not allow worldly attachments to disturb my right mindfulness.
Please summon Xu to join us in chanting the Buddha’s name. At the appointed time, he passed away.
It is further said that Zhu Yuanzheng of Haiyan, Ming dynasty, recited one scroll of the *Lotus Sūtra* daily. When his end approached, it was just at the crowing of the cock;
he gave instructions to his family in advance, saying, "When I depart, do not allow women to come. Wait two or three hours before they arrive, and even when they do, do not weep.
When dawn broke and his kinsmen arrived, they all began to wail. Yuanzheng opened his eyes again and shook his head, ordering the women—
He departed. He departed until he was completely gone, and then he passed away.
It is also said that Mingwen heard that Qichu’s initial aspiration was to transcend birth and death; he went to Yunqi to receive the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation.
Suddenly, he fell ill. Qichu said, "I shall go directly to the Western Pure Land; this illness will not harm me. When his illness became severe, [he remained steadfast].
His mind became clouded and confused; unable to support himself, he was filled with great terror. He urgently ordered his family members to invite a monk to chant the Buddha’s name.
After one day had passed, his confusion remained as before. Suddenly, with a start, he said, "The root and trunk of birth and death cannot be uprooted by another.
He rose immediately, washed and bathed, and donned his robes. Facing the Buddha, he burned incense and practiced the arduous penance of burning his arm, repenting through the entire night.
He did not feel the slightest weariness. When he returned to his seat, his spirit was at peace and his mind settled; the Pure Land appeared before him.
He then shaved his head, donned the *kāṣāya*, and passed away apart from the assembly. Upon hearing of this, Master Hanshan Qing sighed and said, "How brave is Wensheng!
He may truly be called a man of fierce resolve."
It is further stated: The nun Mingbiqiu, whose secular surname was Gong and who was a native of Chongming in Suzhou, renounced meat and began to uphold the sutras and mantras at the age of twelve.
She was most diligent in her morning and evening prostrations before the Buddha and vowed never to take a husband.

At twenty-eight, she shaved her head and received the precepts, subsequently residing at Taosu Shi’s Xiaoyi Hermitage in Hangzhou, where she maintained the Brahma-conduct with singular purity and devotion.

His character was simple and humble. He disciplined his body and toiled for himself without regard for his own weariness. Suddenly, he fell ill; he rejected medical treatment and waited for death with single-minded devotion.
His breath grew faint and his strength failed. Then, suddenly rising, he sat upright in the full-lotus posture. The master of the hermitage set up an image of Amitābha Buddha for him.
[Jing] opened his eyes and gazed intently at it, then joined his palms in refuge. Afterward, he washed his hands, put on clean robes, and took up his prayer beads.
He sat upright facing the Buddha as if entering meditative absorption. His attendant, fearing he might fall over, placed two pillows at his sides.

He waved his hand and said, "There is no need for this. The assembly gathered around him reciting the Buddha's name. Again he waved his hand and said, "I have my own Master; do not trouble yourselves.
He remained in the full lotus position without moving for two full days and nights, softly chanting the Buddha’s name until his breath gradually grew faint and ceased.
Yet she passed away.
It is further recorded that Ming Lu, whose name was Zhifu, was the wife of Cheng Jiqing of Huizhou. In her later years, she moved to Huzhou.

Cheng Jiqing served the Buddha with great devotion and diligently cultivated meritorious works; Lu exhausted her resources to assist him, maintaining a lifelong fast and reciting the Buddha’s name daily.

His name was Er-san-wan. He practiced self-restraint and bestowed kindness upon those below him; he never once reviled anyone. In the fifth year of the Chongzhen era, he contracted a life-threatening illness.
He invited the Dharma Master Gudé to receive the five precepts and inquire about the essential teachings of the Pure Land. Thereupon, he resolved his mind solely upon returning to the West.
Ji Qing recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for him, reaching the fifty-three gates of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, which he explained to him one by one. The Lu family...
He fully understood and comprehended it all. Ji Qing urged him again, saying, "A hundred kalpas and a thousand lifetimes depend upon this single moment.
Strive with all your might to go straight ahead; do not hesitate. He then chanted the Buddha’s name aloud, continuing day and night for half a month.
His mother and daughter came to inquire after him, but he dismissed them both, saying, "Do not disturb my mind. On the eighth day of the eleventh month, suddenly—
He beheld a lotus flower appearing before him, and a transformation Buddha extending a hand toward him. His body and mind leaped with joy;
he hurriedly sought fragrant water for an ablution, faced westward with palms joined, and repeatedly invoked the Buddha’s name. He passed away lying on his right side.

It was noon at the time, yet by evening, when they felt the crown of his head, it was so hot it could burn the hand. He was thirty-nine years old. Master Ouyi composed a biography for him, concluding with this eulogy: "How lamentable!"
The three realms have craving as their root. If this root is not uprooted, how can one hope for rebirth in the West, the Land of Lotus Flowers, where one is forever free from worldly passions?
When these conditions are severed, that reality is realized. How brave is your wisdom and merit, O heroine among women! For one day and one night, your practice of pure mindfulness was diligent;
thus the lotus pedestal came to receive you, and your faculty of sight became clear. Yet the affection between mother and child is like withered wood—[how can it be severed]?

O Śītānta, Auspicious Sugata, you who have forever departed from the wheel of suffering—I now rejoice with you. May I, together with all beings, suddenly cast off the net of craving and realize entry into the primordial gate.
It is further said that the Dharma Master Hengyi of our dynasty once remarked that a monk at a certain hermitage was dissolute and failed to observe the precepts.

A fellow practitioner of the precepts attempted to admonish him, but he would not listen. Subsequently, his illness became severe, and he summoned his friend, saying, "Because I did not listen to your words, I have come to this state.
Now, what shall we do? His friend replied, "In the West, Amitābha Buddha possesses fundamental vows. [If one] creates karma..."
"All sentient beings who recite the Buddha's name even ten times will be received and guided by him. Can you believe this, my son? The monk said, "I believe it, but my strength fails me;
what can be done? The friend said, "It is no matter. Set up an image to the west of the bed and have him fix his gaze upon it without moving.
Burn incense in the burner and chant the Buddha’s name for him while holding his hand and instructing him to listen attentively. After three days and nights, the patient suddenly—
She rose, sat down, and thanked her friend, saying, "Having been received by the Buddha’s guidance, I have attained rebirth in the middle grade. Raising her hand, she took her leave.
She further said: "In our dynasty, Lady Yang, the wife of Zhang Zhi, turned her heart toward the Great Dharma from her youth.
After marrying Zhang, she soon paid homage to the monk Dezhen and received the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, severing all attachment and desire. She was twenty-seven years old."

His illness was severe, and he made a vow to seek rebirth in the Western Paradise. He enshrined an image of the Buddha who Leads the Way (Avalokiteśvara) within his room and chanted the Buddha’s name aloud.
On the fifth day, the fragrance of sandalwood was perceived within the room. By the seventh day, he closed his eyes;

after a short while, he saw the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who said to him, "The seeds for your lotus flower are already half-grown; the remaining half depends on your own skillful means. He then asked, "From where shall I apply them?"
[The Master] replied: "I cast off my hands and go. He then pressed his palms together, chanted the Buddha’s name, sat cross-legged, and passed away.
Furthermore, the Preface to the *Record of Holy and Worthies of the Pure Land* states: When Su Shi was bedridden with illness, he dictated a verse to the Elder of Mount Jing-shan.
His liberation was serene and truly rare; yet when the subject of the Western Paradise arose, he said: "The Western [Paradise]..."
It is not that it is impossible. However, one cannot apply forceful effort here. Now, those who cultivate the practice of Pure Land must possess three minds:

namely, the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), the mind of utmost sincerity, and the mind of dedication and aspiration. Even regarding the ten recitations at the moment of death, there has never been a case where success was attained without applying effort.
To say that "one cannot apply effort" implies that the three minds have not been fulfilled, and thus one remains separated from the assurance of rebirth.
Zhou Kefu’s *Morning Bell for the Pure Land* states: "From the *Awakening of Faith* downward, the provisions for the Pure Land are complete.
Following this path, one sails with the current; the Land of Bliss is as if before one's eyes. Why harbor doubts about the end, and further trouble oneself with elaborate instructions?"
One does not realize that one must accomplish the Great Matter. The most critical point lies in the final stroke at this moment.

What was previously done with negligence cannot be procrastinated here; what was previously shrouded in delusion cannot be left in confusion here; what was previously superficial and vain cannot be borrowed from here;
what was previously a forked path cannot be traversed with hesitation here. One must simply employ the luminous clarity of one’s own mind.
When one awakens, the lotus pedestal immediately appears; when one is deluded, there is a division between the six realms and the three miserable paths.
Purity and defilement diverge in an instant—how perilous, how perilous! Ultimately, the essential key does not lie beyond the four characters:

"One Mind, Right Mindfulness. At this moment, it is like drawing a bow to its full extent; it is exceptionally difficult to release. One must apply focused attention and remain firm and steady, letting go with the preceding hand.
Only when the hand is withdrawn does the arrow finally hit the mark. It is like crossing the ocean by relying on a south-pointing chariot (*shibashiki*) to avoid erring in direction;
as you approach the other shore, you must urgently and carefully furrow the sails and grip the rudder.

If you falter for even a moment, you will once again be blown away by a mad gale, drifting aimlessly in the vast ocean with no place of arrival. A Song dynasty Confucian said that one's daily practice is precisely for this purpose.
This is where it is applicable; this is precisely the meaning. Nevertheless, one who travels a hundred li must stay overnight and grind their grain for provisions;
one who travels a thousand li must gather provisions for three months. How much more so for the Land of Ultimate Bliss, spanning ten trillion *kṣetras*?

If one does not prepare in advance throughout one’s life, yet wishes to seize the goal in a fleeting moment, I do not know if one could, amidst the panic of a single breath, assemble the vision of Zhuge Liang.
Fish. Does Anshi’s skill at Go suffice to withstand a great adversary? A saying goes: "Plan with foresight.

One fears that the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (the Amitabha Sutra) is not merely a worldly "rush-to-completion" composition. As for the words regarding the rebirth of a wicked person through ten recitations, do not let your gaze slacken;
while the principles of the scripture are indeed trustworthy, they were spoken by the Tathagata as a last resort.
The bitter words of Chuishou (Zhuhong) were not intended merely as a protective talisman for those of the Western Regions.

Furthermore, among human sentiments, none prefer excellence more than they loathe inferiority; yet, regarding this very matter, people are content to consider themselves the lowest of the low, which is truly pitiable.
The section titled "Or-Questions by Tianru" serves to awaken the stubborn and ignorant with a clarity that is peerless; therefore, it is placed at the end to serve as a final admonition.
Thereafter, for those who have not yet reached the end of their practice, one should provide prior instruction so that they may assist in the practice;
once they understand the method of *nianfo*, if there is even the slightest instance in their thoughts or actions that contradicts the Buddha, they will [desist].
To seek rebirth [in the Pure Land] while acting otherwise is like driving a carriage northward in an attempt to reach Yue; thus, should not the auxiliary practices be urgently expounded?

Among these auxiliary practices, the foremost is the abstention from killing. In the past, I published a work titled *Lu of Reviving Life* (*Huisheng lu*), in which the maxims and actual accounts concerning the precept against killing and the release of living beings were collected in great detail.
This should immediately serve as one section of this present book and may be excerpted [therefrom].

These have been mutually verified and will not be compiled separately hereafter. For now, I shall merely supplement what was incomplete and include all practices that ought to be cultivated as auxiliary conditions, none of which may be omitted. Thus, the Section on Auxiliary Practices is compiled.

The *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu) states: "To fully observe the precepts of fasting and abstinence, to pay homage to the Buddha and recite his name, to read and recite Mahāyāna sūtras, and to understand the primary meaning [of reality]—dedicating these merits with the vow to be reborn in the Western Paradise, one will certainly attain the highest grade of the highest birth.

What is meant by 'fasting' (*zhāi*)? It means not eating meat, not drinking alcohol, not engaging in sexual desire, and not consuming the five pungent vegetables. This is what is meant by 'precepts' (*jiè*)."
What are these? Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the three karmas of the body. False speech, frivolous talk, slander, and harsh words constitute the four karmas of the mouth.
Covetousness, malice, and wrong views constitute the three karmas of the mind. Taken together, these are the ten precepts.
To observe them without transgression constitutes the ten wholesome actions; to violate them and fail to observe them constitutes the ten unwholesome actions.
By fully observing the ten precepts, one is reborn in the heavens. By observing the first four precepts and adding the abstention from intoxicants, these constitute the five precepts.
One who can maintain these five precepts will never lose their human form. However, this does not apply to those who practice the Pure Land method.
If one fully observes the ten precepts and further cultivates the merits described above, they will certainly attain birth in the highest grade of the highest rank.
If one merely observes the five precepts while practicing for rebirth in the Pure Land, one will still not fail to attain birth in the Middle Grade Upper or the Upper Grade Lower.
If one is further unable to observe the five precepts, how can one possibly neglect the precept against killing?
Killing is the foremost of the five precepts, the foremost of the ten precepts, and likewise the foremost among the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu.
This is the foremost point. Not killing is a great good; killing is a great evil. Therefore it is said:

"For all who wish to kill living beings, simply look at yourself. Your own life cannot be killed, and the life of another being is no different from your own. Thus, by not killing, one receives the retribution of longevity;
by killing, one receives the retribution of a short life. This is because one desires for one's own life to be long, and other beings likewise desire their own."
To desire a long life by taking the lives of other beings—how could such a principle exist? Therefore, one must certainly exercise restraint regarding the killing of living beings.
Generally, if one kills for the sake of food, how can the desire for the palate ever be satisfied?
Once the chopsticks are laid aside, the flavor has vanished, yet the karma of killing remains entirely intact. If one kills to entertain guests, then...
On ordinary days, one does not kill; even others would have nothing to say about this, let alone that one must personally bear the consequences of such a crime.
As the Sūtra says: "Coming, one comes alone; departing, one departs alone. One wanders through saṃsāra alone, and one receives the retribution alone.
Contemplating this, how could one kill for the sake of others? If one kills to sacrifice to one's ancestors, why not simply use plain food instead?
Regarding the purity of food: Confucius said, "Even when eating coarse grain with vegetable soup and melon, one must maintain a state of solemn purification during the offering.

If this is so, what could be improper? If one thus recites the sutras while burning incense, relying on the power of the Buddha to offer merit for the deceased's deliverance, they will certainly transcend the realm of birth and death.
Therefore, none of these [lower grades] involve killing. If one can simply observe this single precept of non-killing to cultivate the Pure Land, one will certainly not be reborn in the lower grade.

It is further said: One may perform various acts of supreme veneration toward the Triple Gem, such as providing meals for the Sangha, making offerings to the Buddha, burning incense, presenting flowers, hanging banners, erecting stupas, reciting the Buddha’s name, and performing repentance rituals.
By dedicating the merit from these deeds, one may aspire to be reborn in the Western Paradise.
Alternatively, one may engage in various worldly beneficial expedients and virtuous deeds, such as filially supporting one's parents as a son, or acting as an elder brother...

He showed affection toward his brothers; as a younger brother, he was respectful and submissive to his elder brother. Within the four walls of the household, there was nothing that did not reach the height of excellence.
Among his clan and kinsmen, there was no lack of harmony. Toward his fellow villagers, neighbors, and relatives by marriage, he interacted with propriety and treated them with kindness.

Furthermore, in serving his sovereign, he offered his sincere heart for the sake of the state; in holding office, he was benevolent and sought the benefit of the people; and in acting as a leader, he...
He was skilled at bringing peace and security to the masses. As a subordinate, he was diligent in serving his superiors. At times he instructed the ignorant and deluded;

at times he assisted the orphaned and the weak; at times he relieved those in urgent distress; at times he bestowed charity upon the poor. He repaired bridges and lined wells; he dispensed medicine and distributed food.

He reduced his own provisions and sustenance to benefit others, and when encountering wealth, he gave more to others while restraining himself in self-examination and frugality. Or he would instruct people...
It is well to perform good deeds, or to praise goodness and restrain evil, doing whatever one can according to one's capacity.
One may dedicate all such worldly virtuous acts toward the aspiration to be reborn in the Western Pure Land.

Alternatively, for the sake of all worldly benefit—regardless of whether it is great or small, many or few—even if it is merely giving a single coin to another, or giving a single cup of water, down to the smallest extent...
Even for a good deed as small as a hair-tip, one must certainly give rise to the thought: "I dedicate these wholesome conditions toward rebirth in the Western Land.
One should constantly ensure that this single thought is uninterrupted, remaining in that state moment after moment; by doing so, one will surely attain birth in the highest grade.
It is further said: The Buddha taught that those who wish to be born in the Pure Land should cultivate the three types of merit.

First, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, maintaining a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten wholesome actions. Second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, and fully observing the various precepts.

Not violating the rules of dignified conduct; third, generating the bodhicitta, having deep faith in cause and effect, reading and reciting the Mahāyāna, and exhorting practitioners to advance in these practices—these are the primary causes for pure karma of the Buddhas of the three periods. The Three Refuges refer to taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, the *Jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land) records an account told by Ge Shouli: During the Daguang era, an official purchased boots in the marketplace of the capital.
He saw a pair of exceptionally large boots, which were those his father had worn for a funeral.

When he asked how they had been obtained, the seller replied, "An official brought them here to have them repaired. Upon asking when the owner would come to collect them, [the official] subsequently went to wait for him.
He followed him and indeed saw his father dismount, leave some money behind, and take his boots. The son bowed and did not look back; the father mounted his horse and departed.
The son pursued him for two or three *li*, but was about to lose him. He then called out, "I and my father have been father and son since birth;
why do you not say a single word to instruct me? His father replied, "Study the 'Ge Fan'. The son asked, "Who is Ge? [The father] said, "The world..."
A person from the vicinity subsequently inquired after his whereabouts. At that time, [the man] was serving as the Governor of Zhenjiang.
He went to see him and explained the circumstances. Furthermore, he asked why Ge was so highly esteemed by those in the netherworld.
He replied, "In the beginning, I performed one beneficial deed for others each day; next, I performed two; then three; and eventually up to ten."

"For forty years now, I have not neglected this for even a single day. When asked how this benefits others, Ge pointed to a footstool in the room and said, "If such an object is placed improperly, it will pinch a person's foot; I set it right for them—this too is a way of benefiting others.
Furthermore, if someone is thirsty, I can give them a cup of water—this too is a way of benefiting others. It is simply a matter of following [circumstances]."
To benefit others through one's actions—whether from high ministers and officials down to beggars—can be practiced by all;
it depends solely on doing so for a long time without ceasing. His son bowed and withdrew. Later, Ge passed away at an advanced age while sitting in meditation.
Observing this, one must strive in deeds that benefit others; how could one ever perform deeds that harm them? This is what is meant by "love."
"To benefit others is what is called benevolence (ren); Ge has attained this. Ge cultivated the pure practices (śukla-karma) concurrently and dedicated [the merit] thereto.
Later, a monk traveled spiritually to the Pure Land and saw Ge there."

Furthermore, the *Jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land) contains a chapter titled "Discourse on Giving and Retribution. Confucianism speaks of giving and retribution; Buddhism speaks of the karmic fruit of giving (*dāna*).
In reality, they are one and the same. The Buddha said: "If you wish to obtain grain and food, you must diligently plow and sow.

If you wish to obtain wisdom, you must diligently study and inquire. If you wish to obtain longevity, you must diligently refrain from killing. If you wish to obtain wealth and honor, you must diligently practice giving."
Generosity. There are four kinds of giving: first, the gift of material wealth; second, the gift of the Dharma; third, the gift of fearlessness; and fourth, the gift of the mind.
As for the gift of material wealth, it is to bestow riches upon others. As for the gift of the Dharma, it is to instruct others through the teachings of goodness.
As for the gift of fearlessness, it means that when humans and sentient beings are in a state of fear, one comforts them so that they are no longer afraid, or teaches them...
One is liberated from fear and rendered fearless. As for the "giver of mind," though one’s power may not suffice to save others, one constantly maintains the intention to save them.
The Buddha taught that filial piety and the nurturing of parents are also forms of giving; thus, whatever is bestowed externally constitutes *dāna*.
Therefore, as a subordinate, one serves one's superior with loyalty and diligence; as a leader, one brings peace to the multitude through benevolence and compassion; and as a teacher—
One should be diligent in instruction and sincere in refining one's companions through study. Between every word and every phrase, one must ensure they are beneficial;

at every movement and every pause, one must strive to avoid causing harm. Through various skillful means to benefit others, one must not allow them to suffer any injury—all of this is *dāna* (generosity).
When one acts in this manner and maintains such an intention, how could one possibly [fail] in future lives?
One shall not obtain the retribution of wealth and nobility. An ancient proverb says:
"Everyone knows there is a coming year, so every household plants grain for the coming year; everyone knows there is a future life, so why not cultivate the merit of that future life?
The blessings one receives in this present life are those cultivated in previous lives, just as the grain consumed this year was planted in the past.
Regarding what is sown in a year: one cannot sow grain in the morning and eat it in the evening; likewise, one cannot cultivate merit and receive its fruit immediately.

Thus, grain requires half a year to ripen, and merit necessarily spans across lifetimes. Confucius said: "In the matter of wealth, one dislikes its being wasted on the ground, but it need not be hoarded for oneself.
In the matter of labor, one dislikes its not being exerted by one's own person, but it need not be done for one's own sake. Laozi...
This means that when one gives to others, one has more oneself; when one gives to others, one has more for oneself. These are what is meant by "giving" (dāna).
Zengzi said, "What comes forth from you will return to you," and Laozi said, "The Way of Heaven loves to return favors. Both of these refer to karmic retribution.
Thus, both the Confucian and Daoist teachings speak of giving and its reward, though they do not mention rebirth in another life. This is what is called "love."

Those who treat others as human beings are always loved by others; those who respect others are always respected by others; and those who bring calamity upon others will surely be met with reciprocal calamity.
These are all instances of the retribution for actions in this present life. Knowing this, many have cultivated the roots of goodness by practicing the purification of the Buddha-land.
Furthermore, the *Jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land) contains an essay titled "On the Prohibition of Eating Meat. The Buddha addressed Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:
"There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat. I shall now briefly explain them for you.

That is to say, all sentient beings have, from the very beginning, been related to one another through a succession of causes and conditions and have constantly been one's own kin. Because they are regarded as kin, one should not eat their flesh. It is impure."
Because it grows from one's own vital energy (*vāyu*), one should not eat meat. Because all sentient beings are terrified upon smelling its odor, one should not eat meat.
Because it causes the practitioner’s mind of loving-kindness to fail in its non-killing resolve, one should not eat meat. It is merely that which the ignorant and foolish crave.
One should not eat meat because it is foul-smelling, impure, and lacks a good reputation. One should not eat meat because it causes various incantations and rituals to fail.
One should not eat meat because those who kill living beings perceive their forms and give rise to consciousness, becoming deeply attached to its flavor.
One should not eat meat because such meat-eaters are abandoned by the devas. One should not eat meat because it causes the breath to smell. It is not...
One should eat meat because it causes many bad dreams; one should not eat meat because tigers and wolves will smell its scent in secluded forests;

one should not eat meat because it causes people to lose moderation in their eating and drinking; one should not eat meat because it prevents practitioners from developing a sense of revulsion toward worldly existence;
one should not eat meat because I have always said that whatever food and drink is consumed should be regarded as feeding one's own child.
One should regard meat as medicine; therefore, one should not eat meat. There is no basis for the claim that eating meat is permitted.
Mahāmati, all those who kill do so for the sake of profit, slaughtering and selling living beings.
Those foolish sentient beings who eat meat use money as a net to catch various meats. Those who kill—whether by means of wealth or by means of hooks—[act in this manner].
With nets, they capture those beings that move through the air, water, or on land, slaughtering them in various ways and seeking profit through their sale.
Mahāmati, there is no fish or meat that exists without being produced through instruction, seeking, or conceptualization. For this reason, one should not eat meat.
The Buddha further spoke in verse, which says in brief: "To kill living beings for profit, or to obtain meat by means of wealth with nets—both of these are evil karmas."
Upon death, one falls into the Hell of Screaming. If there is no thought of instruction or seeking [the meat], then the three kinds of pure meat do not exist.
That [meat] does not arise without a cause; therefore, it should not be eaten. Alcohol, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic are all obstacles to the Noble Path. One who eats meat lacks compassion.
This forever turns one’s back on true liberation and violates the outward signs of the noble ones; therefore, one should not eat the flesh of sentient beings.
Flesh is fundamentally not a substance meant for consumption, yet because it has been familiarized through hearing with the ears and seeing with the eyes, one does not recognize its wrongfulness.

If one can abstain from meat, that would certainly be excellent. If one cannot abstain, then at least consume the three kinds of pure meat while reducing the amount eaten. As for those who combine various flavors:
Eliminate one [of the two]. For example, if both meals consist of meat, then for one meal at least, consume vegetarian food. Human life and its allotted sustenance have a fixed measure;
by acting in this way, one can naturally prolong one's lifespan. There are many benefits to eating vegetarian food in the morning:

first, it reduces karmic conditions; second, it brings about purity; third, it does not obstruct wholesome karma; and fourth, when one eats meat in the evening, one will not become weary of the vegetarian meal and crave the meat.
In this way, one may naturally extend one's lifespan. If you find it difficult to abstain from meat, you should instead use the funds spent on meat to provide vegetarian food;
thus, the practice will be easy to undertake and can be sustained for a long time. If you indulge the desires of your mouth and belly, there will be no end to them. As the saying goes:
If one wishes for the world to be free from the calamity of war, it must be that sentient beings do not eat meat. Are these words not to be taken seriously?

For those who cannot help but consume the "three kinds of pure meat," on the day following the consumption, they should recite the names of the Four Sages of the Western Paradise along with the mantras for the sake of the sentient beings whose flesh was eaten, thereby dedicating the merit to assist them in their rebirth in the Pure Land. In this way, one may perhaps resolve grievances and extinguish transgressions. According to Yama...

When King Rāvaṇa spoke these words to Zheng Lin, he said: "If one sincerely recites the names of the Four Holy Ones to offer posthumous merit for the deceased, they will surely attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

Regarding the three kinds of pure meat: those not seen being killed, those not heard being killed, and those not suspected of being killed specifically for oneself, as well as meat from animals that died naturally."
"Leftover from birds. These constitute the five kinds of pure meat.
Furthermore, the *Jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land) contains a chapter titled "The Discourse on Prolonging Life by the Supreme Person. I have heard the Supreme Person say:

"In human life, clothing, food, wealth, and official rank are all subject to fixed quotas determined by the Office of the Netherworld. If one practices frugality and refrains from greed, then one may prolong one's lifespan."
Excessive luxury and over-indulgence end when one's resources are exhausted. It is like a person who possesses a thousand coins: if they spend one hundred per day, they will last for ten days;
if they spend fifty per day, they will last for twenty days. Yet if they indulge their greed and extravagance, their ruin will be seen immediately.
If one were to exhaust a thousand such units in a single day, would it not be something to be feared?
The *I Ching* states that the numbers of heaven and earth total fifty-five, by which changes are perfected and the spirits are set in motion.

Thus, even the greatness of heaven and earth, the subtlety of transformation, and the profundity of ghosts and spirits do not escape these numerical laws; how much more so for human beings? Some may say that humans possess integrity...
Why is it that some who are frugal have short lives, while others who are greedy and extravagant live long? Those who are modest and frugal yet have short lives have few allotted years of existence;
if they were to become even more greedy and extravagant, their lives would be shortened all the more. Those who are greedy and extravagant yet live long have many allotted years of existence;
if they were to become even more modest and frugal, their lives would be lengthened all the more. Furthermore, Heaven and Earth are impartial toward humanity. Why is this so?
This refers to the number of times one will be reborn; how many are there? These are all the result of what was done in previous lives. Therefore it is said:

"One must know that the causes from previous lives are what one receives in this life. If in the present life one performs much that is auspicious and good, then blessings and longevity will increase.
Hence it is said: "The spirits listen to this; grant you great fortune. If in the present life one commits much evil, then blessings and longevity will decrease. Therefore...

It is said that those who practice much unrighteousness will surely bring about their own ruin. Furthermore, for one who cultivates the Pure Land, it is certainly not a matter of having great merit or long life;
however, actions that diminish merit and shorten life constitute a lack of virtue—how could one fail to refrain from them? As for matters that increase merit and prolong life...
This is indeed a matter of profound virtue; how could one not strive toward it?
Furthermore, in the *Jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land), there is an excerpt titled "A Tale of Greed Ruining One’s Future":
There was a certain official who sought a dream at the Temple of the Two Prime Ministers in the capital to inquire about his future prospects. That night, he dreamed that someone was holding...
A single scroll of a register was opened, and the tablet read: "This is the future career of the official who came with you.
Upon inspection, it showed ranks ascending from minor officials up to the Prime Minister; however, there were some names marked with a hook. The officials asked, "Why are these marked with hooks?
The one holding the register replied, "These officials were fond of wealth; they took one item through unrighteous means in this world."
There was one item concerning a "hooked interval. [The Master said: "If you repent quickly, you may still become a Surveillance Commissioner (Jiansi).
When the man heard this, he did not dare to take wealth improperly again. Later, he indeed attained the rank of Surveillance Commissioner. Furthermore, there was a Madam Xian in the world.
A certain District Magistrate’s family suddenly received a celestial book, but because they could not recognize the characters, they went to see Madam Xian to ask about it. Madam Xian...
She prepared an incense altar, and after bowing, she began to read. Having finished reading, she smiled. The Magistrate said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects and inquire after you;
for what reason do you smile? The Immortal Nun replied, "The Celestial Scripture states that you, Magistrate, have received ten taels of gold, which will reduce your official emolument by five years.
Observing this, one sees that ill-gotten wealth is truly to be feared. If you were to direct this mind toward the Pure Land, its wholesome roots would surely ripen."

It is many. Furthermore, the *Jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land) contains an essay titled "Discourse on the Practice of Compassion," in which Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva states that all myriad virtues arise from compassion.
Laozi says that among the Three Treasures, compassion is primary. The Confucians say that among the Five Constant Virtues, it is placed first.
O Benevolent One, their meanings are all the same. When people harbor much anger and resentment, it is because they do not contemplate this principle.

Before they have even harmed others or created karma through speech, they first damage their own vital energy and wound their inner harmony. Only when one reaches the state of compassionate benevolence does one realize that anger is unwholesome;
while in the midst of anger, one is unaware of its suffering, just as one walking amidst thorns is unaware of the pain until it is too late.
It is like entering a great mansion for peaceful dwelling. When one first corrects the anger of one’s innate nature, it is as if walking through thorns;
yet once compassion and benevolence have been cultivated, it is like entering a great mansion for peaceful dwelling. This cannot be fully expressed in words;

one must simply practice while in a state of anger, and after a long time, there will naturally be cause for joy. Regarding the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism, they are indeed already... [text ends]
One must refrain from anger. This is likewise the case in Confucianism. When Huan Tui sought to harm Confucius, did Confucius ever show anger?

When Zang Cang slandered Mencius, did Mencius ever show anger? Han Xin did not seek revenge for the humiliation beneath his armpits, and An Guo did not harbor resentment over the words regarding being drowned in ashes;
these are all worthy of being taken as models. In all matters—whether dealing with the poor and lowly, managing servants and concubines, or responding to insults—[one should follow this example].
Those who oppose one’s own will easily provoke anger; therefore, one must be especially cautious and reverent. After all, they too are human beings; they merely serve me due to their meager merit.
How could one indulge their own temperament and thereby create evil karma? To speak in conclusion, the compassionate and harmonious person gains great advantage for themselves.
As the *Tripiṭaka* says: "That one is seen with joy by people in this life is because of [merit] in a previous life."
Because one sees others rejoice, this is brought about by loving-kindness and harmony. How could those who cultivate the Pure Land not take this as their primary concern?
Even if all sentient beings commit great evils, do not give rise to anger that would defile your own pure and cool mind.
Contemplate that they act thus only because of ignorance; were they possessed of wisdom, they certainly would not do so. One should...
One gives rise to compassion for their ignorant minds. Thus, Master Zeng said: "If you discover the truth of their situation, then feel pity and sympathy rather than joy.
Cultivating the Pure Land in this manner brings the roots of goodness to full maturity to an extraordinary degree.
Furthermore, the *Jingtu wen* (Inquiry into the Pure Land) contains an essay titled "Discourse on Minor Causes and Effects":

"There is the person who builds a bridge and the person who destroys a bridge; these are minor causes for heaven and hell. There is the person who rides in a palanquin and the person who carries the palanquin;
these are minor effects of heaven and hell. One may extend this reasoning to all similar categories, and it will become evident. Constantly maintain such a state of mind.
If one cultivates the Pure Land and attains birth in the highest grade, how can there be any further doubt?
Master Gushan’s *Commentary on the Western Aid for Amitābha* states: "Observe that in the world today, people's minds toward doing good are light, while their minds toward committing evil are heavy.

How, then, can they attain birth in the Pure Land? Please verify this through present-day events. When facing an image [of the Buddha], it is not as effective as engaging [with the practice directly]."
The great guest’s reverence and caution were such that his study of the sutras and dharmas was not as diligent as his pursuit of wealth and profit.

When disparaging others, his breath was coarse and his speech slippery; when praising them, his breath was sluggish and his words stilted. If he disliked someone, he would conceal their virtues and broadcast their faults;
if he favored someone, he would hide their shortcomings and magnify their strengths. At times, having accumulated evil, he would vent his anger through private slanders against others, or...
One performs minor acts of goodness yet regrets that others do not recognize them; yet regarding evil deeds, one may secretly spend a thousand pieces of gold while remaining tight-lipped.
When bestowing a single meal upon a virtuous person, one immediately boasts of the merit. With such a mindset, one will surely sink into the evil realms.
How difficult it is, then, to seek rebirth in a Pure Land through such small acts of goodness!

Peng Chimu’s *Record of the Holy and Sages of the Pure Land* states: During the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, there was a man named Feng Jie, courtesy name Jichuan, a native of Suining in Sichuan.
While serving as a military commander in Lunnan, he led both monastics and laypeople in establishing a "Recitation Assembly," taking the Western Paradise as his ultimate refuge.

At that time, following the chaos of the Jianyan wars, many famous temples and their Tripitaka collections had been destroyed. Consequently, he donated his official stipend to commission a new set of the Great Canon.

Forty-eight locations were established, and the four great divisions of the Minor Canon (*Kṣudraka-piṭaka*) were likewise distributed among various monasteries in equal numbers. He inscribed a vow stating:
"In this single undertaking of my gift of scriptures, two kinds of giving are encompassed. To provide the funds for the production of the scriptures is called the 'gift of wealth' (*āmiṣa-dāna*);
to transmit the Dharma through these scriptures is called the 'gift of Dharma' (*dharma-dāna*). Through the gift of wealth, one shall obtain merit and virtue in both the heavens and the human realm."
The reward for this is that the gift of Dharma shall bring about the retribution of worldly wisdom, eloquence, and brilliance that surpasses all others.
One should know that both these rewards are causes for saṃsāra and the root of suffering. I now make this vow:

may I dedicate these two rewards so that, at the time of my death, I may be adorned with the merit to be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, taking birth within a lotus flower as its womb, and there behold the Buddha.
Having heard the Dharma, they realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), ascend the stage of non-retrogression, and enter the rank of Bodhisattvas.

Returning to the realms of the ten directions within the world of the five turbidities, they manifest their bodies everywhere to perform the work of Buddhas. By virtue of the causes of these two present gifts—of material wealth and of the Dharma—...

Just as Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, endowed with great compassion, traverses the five realms of existence, manifesting forms according to the various classes of beings to preach and recite the wondrous Dharma;
thereby awakening those who have not yet realized it, causing them to forever leave the path of suffering and attain wisdom,
so that all sentient beings may universally achieve Buddhahood— this is my vow for bestowing this scripture.
It is further stated: Ming Yuan Hongdao, courtesy name Zhonglang, was a native of Gong’an in Hubei. During the Wanli era, he served as a Langzhong in the Ministry of Personnel (Jixun Si).
He retired from office on account of illness and passed away in a Buddhist monastery. His elder brother, Hongdao, and his younger brother, Zhongdao, were both fond of the Chan school.
One night, Zhongdao finished his recitations and entered meditative absorption. Two youths led him westward, where he saw Hongdao and said, "We have already reached the Pure Land.

Generally speaking, those who are diligent in both the Mahayana vehicle (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*) attain the highest grade of rebirth. Next best are those diligent in the precepts, whose rebirth is most stable.
If one possesses the vehicle but lacks the precepts, they are mostly dragged away by the power of karma and flow into the ranks of the eight classes of ghosts and spirits."
I have personally witnessed many such cases. My brother’s *prajñā* (wisdom) disposition was quite profound, yet his discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) were very slight.

Now, if one realizes the principle but cannot give rise to discipline and concentration, that is "wild wisdom" (*unmatta-prajñā*); it leads back to the five turbidities. While you are still strong and healthy, realize the truth and practice authentically.
Furthermore, maintain pure vows and diligently practice skillful means; have compassion for all beings, and before long you shall attain awakening. To enter another path is terrifying and fearsome.
If you are unable to uphold the precepts, there exists the "Six Fasting Days Method" (Ṣaḍupavāsa-dharma) by Nāgārjuna which remains extant today.

Follow and practice it; the precept against killing is especially urgent. I entrust these words to my fellow students: never let the carving knife be opened at dawn, nor let the mouth greedily crave savory flavors.
It is precisely those who can be born in this land. Although one may preach the Dharma like clouds or rain, what benefit does it bring to the matter at hand?
During the Kalpa of the Empty King, you and I were brothers in every lifetime, even throughout the six realms of existence; this was always so.
Fortunately, I have attained a state of goodness, yet I feared that you might fall away. Therefore, through skillful means and spiritual power, I have brought you here.

The Mirror of Buddha-Recitation. An appended brief exposition on the Buddha-recitation and the liberation of living beings by Zhilang states: "Now, for one who wishes to perfect benevolent virtue, nothing is superior to the liberation of living beings;
for one who wishes to escape the wheel of suffering, nothing is like Buddha-recitation. To deliver the masses of deluded beings, one opens the vast compassion of the Buddhas and Patriarchs."
He bore the title of "Awakened One" and guided others in the pure conduct of the Lotus Land.

Thus, our Great Master Yongming was an emanation of an ancient Buddha who took upon his entire being the two dharma-gates, leading tens of millions of devas and humans to take refuge in the Pure Land.
Now that the Buddha-dharma is in decline and the capacities of beings are shallow, to cultivate other dharma-gates and achieve the great matter is as far apart as heaven and earth; it is only...
By upholding the great name of the Buddha, one suddenly comprehends the nature of birth and death. Like a single prescription for curing a disease, it is direct, straightforward, and concise;
a single day of practice surpasses the merit of eternal kalpas. Even if one’s karmic offenses are deep and heavy, one may still attain rebirth while still bearing such karma.

For achieving completion in a single lifetime and crossing horizontally through the five realms of existence, nothing is superior to the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation. Although I am not quick-witted, [I have come to this realization].
Having heard of this Pure Land, one should exert all effort to praise it, universally wishing that all people may ascend together to Sukhāvatī.

Furthermore, observing that in the world there are various instances of premature death and illness where beings fail to complete their natural lifespans, one sees that these are all caused by the residual retribution of karmic acts of killing.
The Sūtra says: "The sin of killing leads to falling into the three miserable realms to undergo suffering. Even if one is reborn among humans, two retributions will be received:

first, much illness; second, a short lifespan. If a person wishes to attain lightness and ease of the four elements and a long, enduring life, they should make a vow to refrain from killing and practice the release of living beings (*fangsheng*).
As for the method of releasing living beings: set out a bamboo sprout and attend to it daily."
In the intervals between one's duties, recite the Buddha’s name a few times. Save one coin each day; at the end of a year, the accumulated total will be three hundred and sixty coins.
This requires neither great wealth nor much physical exertion; who, then, would be incapable of doing it?
It is simply a matter of practicing for a long duration, never growing weary throughout one's life. Truly, though a single drop is minute, it fills a great vessel. Furthermore, one must...
Generate a heart of great compassion. Contemplate those of different species who, due to heavy karmic obstructions from past causes and conditions, are by nature ignorant and foolish.
Their bodies are cast into nets; their lives hang by a thread. They are seared, slaughtered, and carved, enduring unbearable agony. Who can take pity on them?
Only you, O Benevolent One, may cherish them with a heart of sorrow. Within this coming year, whether at a specific designated time or without restriction as to the hour, [act upon this].
Month. Cultivating the causes for longevity, one performs the practice of releasing living beings. One exhausts all aquatic creatures and sets free all that flies and runs.

May all sentient beings of water and land roam freely beyond the mundane world. Having completed the release, one calculates the location of the release as well as the year, month, day, and the number of beings released by [Name].

With single-minded devotion, one prays that there shall forever be no calamities of illness, suffering, or misfortune, and that the lifespan may further increase like the age of cranes and the span of pines. Once again...

I recruit those of profound and sincere faith to uphold the great name of the Buddha, categorized into three grades. Those of the superior grade possess firm and steadfast power of faith; they shall recite the Buddha’s name ten thousand times.
Those of the middle grade have somewhat more worldly affairs; five thousand recitations shall be their standard. Those of the inferior grade are most deeply immersed in the secular world;

they must steal moments of leisure from their busyness to ensure three thousand recitations are never lacking. Having completed this throughout one's entire life, they vow never to change—yet this may not be achieved.

If those who attain rebirth in the Pure Land were not so, the Buddhas of the three periods would be speaking falsehoods. A verse says: "Releasing life and reciting the Buddha’s name are two difficult tasks;
It is only valued that one’s own mind-ground be firm. The ancestral lamp of Yong shines through the night; May you raise the true command to gather humans and devas."
