I am now seventy-one years old; I no longer devote myself to chanting or composition. Reading the scriptures strains my eyesight, and performing meritorious deeds I fear the toil involved.
How, then, can I cross over with the mind’s eye? With a single utterance of "Amitābha. Walking, Amitābha; sitting, Amitābha.
Even if one is as busy as a rushing arrow, one must not neglect Amitābha. The day grows dark and the road is long; my life has already been wasted.
Morning and evening, with a pure mind, I shall simply recite the name of Amitābha. The man of realization might laugh at me for having too much of Amitābha.
If one has attained [realization], what then? And if one has not attained it, how is it so? I universally exhort the multitudes within the Dharma-realm to together recite the name of Amitābha.
A Five-Syllable Regulated Verse by Cai Chengzhi, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
A guest longing to return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, I am but a decayed Confucian by the Xiang River. I do not worry about what tomorrow holds; I seek only the talisman for rebirth.

I dwell as chance directs in a small room, Sustaining myself with simple soup from whatever comes my way. With all hatred and love extinguished within my breast, I let others call me whatever they please—horse or ox.

"Recalling the Buddha" Pavilion by Xuexi of the Song Dynasty Three rafters in old age allow me to dwell in poverty; Nothing compares to the excellence of truly recollecting the Buddha. I have come to know that even the completion of all affairs still falls into [the realm of]...

A steamer basket—through a hundred years, this alone may be inscribed upon one's sash. Quietly entrusting oneself to a rush mat at night among the crags; casually offering a tea bowl in spring beneath the pines.
Shuttering the door, one does not forget, always recollecting the Buddha; may our vows endure forever, like a shadow following the body.

Early on I sought the histories of Sui and Han to cultivate my literary style, and I presumed that throughout my life I had been a man of broad learning. Yet now, every moment of time has been cast aside like flowing water;

when I reflect upon it, all my efforts have been but drifting clouds. In leisure, I alone recognize the stability of my hidden essence; who else knows my diligent remembrance of the Buddha in these superior places?
Where are Shen Yue, Xie Tiao, Cao Pi, and Liu Zhen today? There are but three feet of weeds over their desolate graves.
The former monk Utpala urged others to practice *nien-fo*;
his discarded remains lay piled high like mountains. Parting tears flow on to become the waves of the four seas. At the end of the world, all things must reach their fixed conclusion;
in human life, what joy is there in a mere snap of the fingers? Having been born as men and women a thousand times over, one has donned horns and shed fur through countless lifetimes.
Ten thousand matters arise; if one does not seek birth in the Pure Land in this very life, a single mistake in taking rebirth makes regret difficult to overcome later.

Master Mingchushi cherished the Pure Land, finding leisure even amidst the busiest moments—this too depends on the person. In human life, who can fulfill a hundred years of spring? Parting and welcoming [birth and death] ultimately have no fixed time.
All is understood. Sorrow and joy intertwine, renewed day by day. Cease thinking of fame and office; only recite the Buddha’s name. Worry only about your spiritual practice, not about poverty.
Suddenly, even an iron tree will bloom, and you will wonderfully turn the Tathāgata’s True Dharma Wheel.
The great affliction is clearly the existence of this body; one must know that illness spares no one. It is merely bound up with deluded thoughts, all of which are false;

even if one attains the status of a True Immortal, it may not be truly real. When the masses of heat gather, the wind fans the fire; in a single lifetime, one is cast away, leaving only bones and sinews.
Only through mindfulness of the Buddha can one transcend birth and death; those who merely cling to Jambudvīpa will turn to dust.
A Verse on the Pure Land from the Gate of Prajñāpāramitā:
Your lofty talent and grand strategy possess an extraordinary spirit; At such a critical moment, who would not be flustered?

Striking at the rain and beating at the wind with idle calculations— These are but empty writings that startle heaven and shake the earth. If the river of craving has not yet been dried up, One must still labor against its shallow waves.
Thesis: The Six-Character Amitābha has no commentary; taking refuge in it is itself the Great Compassionate Vessel.

In our dynasty, Lianyin contemplates the Pure Land as his hair gradually turns white with frost-like traces. Reflecting inwardly, he realizes he is not himself; discussing this with himself, he wonders what has been accomplished in a single lifetime.
Karma! How many more mornings and evenings remain in this hundred-year span? You must resolve to seek the secure abode; do not again submit your heart to the gate of death.
The Land of Bliss is not far—there is a path to return. Go gladly to the Lotus Throne to behold the Compassionate Honored One.

King Gong has nothing more to deliberate upon; he has dreamed his way into the great resting place of the Lotus Land. There, the assembly of noble beings discourse on the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), while each of the Śakras rains down flowers and incense.
The songs of birds and the music of trees resound without ceasing, and the pearl pavilions and golden terraces are all complete.
Radiant Light Shines Forth: The source of the immortals is but a few feet away—never obstructed. Do not let the fisherman lose his way and sigh in regret.
A Heptasyllabic Quatrain by Zhou Baturuo.
Failing to form auspicious bonds or wholesome affinities, you suffer from greed for fame and profit, tormented day and night.
How could you know that the gold, silver, and treasures of this world are merely lent to you for a leisurely viewing over several decades?

Cakra was ensnared by the fetters of desire and lost his life; daily afflictions followed him constantly. Though one may encounter a pardon within the prison of the state, there is no time of pardon for those bound by worldly affairs.
Song Dynasty, Su Zizhan’s Vow Verse:
Life and death are like the bending and stretching of an arm; Our attachment to this world brings but bitter sorrow.
If I am not a guest of Penglai, I rely upon the Western Paradise as my host.
Song of Beishan Praising the Pure Land:
The evening drum and morning cock ceaselessly urge us on. In a mere moment, one’s appearance grows frail and decrepit. Do not say that white hair is a trivial matter;
It is all the arrival of the message of impermanence.
Song Yuan-yi’s "Eulogy on the Western Land":
The Dharma Master of the West transforms those lost in delusion; through the Buddha’s sustaining power, the Way is easily accomplished. Cast off your hands and walk forth—there is no other path;
you must clearly discern that very first step.
In the West lies a path few ascend; the single phrase "Amitābha" is the Supreme Vehicle. One cannot lead another by the hand;
only when one is self-accepting will there be accord.
Return quickly to your native land in the West; human life is impermanent, lasting but a breath. Cherish this limited time;
lament its passing now, for it will be difficult to emerge from it again.
In the West, practice with urgency and haste; birth and death are impermanent and cannot be predicted.
The sunlight outside the window passes in the blink of an eye—how much time do humans truly have?
Song Yiyuan’s *Verses on the Pure Land*:
The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is universally acclaimed as supreme. I exhort all people to enter this gate. Those with mouths need not engage in idle discourse;
Simply uphold the Buddha’s name to pass through morning and evening.
The great vows of the West shall be widely disseminated. Apply yourself diligently to even a single phrase of Amitābha. Let it be clear and distinct without interruption;
with every sound, awaken the true master.
Yuan Zhongfeng’s *Verses on the Pure Land*:
"From kalpa to kalpa, as numerous as motes of dust, The count of these motes of dust has not ceased.

Having served as a high minister and a court official, your worldly fame and merit were beyond measure.
Yet if you do not contemplate the Amitābha of your own nature, I know not how you will withstand impermanence.
He has already attained Buddhahood this very morning; the Master who transforms the Land of Bliss considered even this too late. How much more so for those who wish to go there now?
Take it for granted that their cycle of rebirth will have no end.
Yuan Zhongfeng’s *Six Periods of Contemplation on the Pure Land*:

The golden father knocks at the door; the wayward child wanders—when will he return? When the conversation reaches the point where saṃsāra is endless, Looking at one another, we cannot help but have our tears soak our robes.
To plant the nine grades of lotuses of the Western Land throughout the entire three-thousandfold world system of this defiled realm—upon careful reflection, there is no other method;
it requires nothing more than a single resolute thought.
Master Wushu’s Warning to the World:

When the rain has passed over the thatched eaves, the sun shines red. In an instant, the weather shifts from dark to bright; how much more so for the matter of life and death, which occurs in the space of a breath?
At twilight, one cannot guarantee reaching the morning bell.

On New Year’s Day, observing my longing for the Pure Land, I weep in my dreams before the Venerable Golden Immortal. I pray that you grant me the aid of your secret influence to spur me forward. Innumerable lotuses exist within the golden pond;
may I surely grow one flower so as to avoid mere salivation.
I have heard the accounts of the Western Land with perfect clarity; this journey must rely upon auspicious causes and conditions.
Grind your mind until a single thought is as bright as a mirror, and you need not fear that Amitābha will not appear before you.
I have long gazed upon my body and mind as I watch the setting sun; where the sun sinks away, the fragrance of lotus blossoms lingers. Waterfowl and wind-tossed trees seem to understand my intent;
yet I remain sorrowful, for the dream of the human world has not yet been forgotten.
How can one escape the cycle of birth and death? If this mind remains unawakened, all effort is in vain. Now, I shall no longer dream of saṃsāra;
I will simply traverse this single journey through the human world.
The former master Utpala exhorted those who practice nianfo (Buddha-recitation):
"Birth is inevitably followed by the four signs of decay; how could one ever escape the five signs of decline in the heavens?
It would be better to dwell in the lower grade of the nine lotus realms than to return to this floating world and undergo birth from a womb."
To achieve longevity, one need not rely on the secrets of the immortals; for urgent relief, one must turn to the prescriptions from the Isles of the Blest.
By relying upon the Lord Amitāyus, it turns out that this surpasses all other considerations.
The single phrase of Amitābha is the gate of transformation; how could it be restricted to cities or villages?
Even if those with wrong views should hear it, it will surely fall upon their ears and enter their sense faculties.
Yuan Guang composed these verses on the recitation of the Buddha’s name:
“The Buddha is within your heart; you must keep your eyes open. Do not cast Him behind your head and fail to look upon Him. To miss this moment would be a true failure.
If you wish to be like this today, I fear it will be too late.”
The bright and clear lotus does not wrap itself in the womb of the six dusts; within the cage of sun and moon, it fashions itself. I am prepared to cast aside this heap of impoverished bones;
in this spring dream, I must personally push it away.
Mingduanyu seeks what he knows in the north, south, east, and west; fearing his head, he recognizes its reflection and is utterly deluded.
Even if one were to awaken to the affairs of before birth, one still requires Amitābha as a guiding teacher.

The Buddhas of the ten directions praise the West; it is not for no reason that they manifest their broad and long tongues. It is only for fear that deluded practitioners of Chan might indulge in mere quiescence, mistakenly taking annihilation for true permanence.
Fix the mind on a single phrase of Amitābha; whether in daily life one is at leisure or busy, regardless of how much or little one does.
Even if one does not attain wondrous enlightenment by the end of this life, it will still enable one to depart from Saṃsāra with one's karmic burdens.
The Western Land is clearly the land of the mind-only; to speak of the mind apart from the land is truly perverse. Every thought and every moment returns entirely to the ocean of the Buddhas;
why need one seek the Zen of the Patriarchs anew?
The Western Land is precisely the realm of Mind-only. Before reaching that Western Land, one is truly in peril. Past karmic obstacles already surge like billowing waves;
how can one endure new afflictions following in their wake?
The Western Quarter is precisely the land of Mind-only. Hold fast to pure precepts and do not let them slacken. All human realms are but states of confinement;
there is no need to seek a peaceful dwelling in guest houses.
The Western Land is precisely the land of Mind-only. If you do not recognize the West, how can you recognize the Mind?
Why do you mistakenly seek the sudden and perfect understanding, yet take fallen leaves for gold?
The Western Land is precisely the realm of Mind-only; it can only be brought forth through the union of compassion and wisdom. Do not say that Great Compassion should merely pity the turbid world;
to transform others, one must first achieve success within oneself.
The Essential Summary of the *Ciqiu Guiyuanjing*:

The Dharma drum beats repeatedly; a million beings from the realms of humans and devas surround Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Sandalwood incense smoke curls upward; where the flowers scatter, [the truth] is known.
To what extent?

The Land of Ultimate Bliss has been transmitted through both ancient and modern times. A journey of one hundred thousand *li* is not far; in the Western Pure Land, Amitābha preaches the Dharma to lead beings back to the source.

The causes and conditions are not slight, and the fruition is no ordinary matter. Through his sixty-eight vast and profound vows, he launches the compassionate vessel to ferry across and guide all the ignorant masses.

Freed from the boundless ocean of suffering, adorned with infinite merit and wondrous splendor, like a great golden lotus as vast as a chariot wheel, blue, yellow, red, and white, fluttering in the pure breeze—subtle, wondrous, and natural.
(I) repeatedly extend my compassionate exhortation; sighing at the swiftness of impermanence, returning home is the way. The lotus pedestal.
The nine grades above set forth their names; they realize non-arising and forever sever afflictions and resentment.
Hurry! Be alert from this very source of consciousness. May each and every one of you reverently recite the Buddha’s name, holding it with single-mindedness without interruption.
With fervent and intense resolve, sever the ties between enemies and kin. Every speck of dust is as vast as this world.
The realms: one directly attains this state of bustling and pressing forward, boarding the Prajñā vessel together; joyfully and contentedly facing the wondrous realm of the West;
laughing heartily as one pays homage to the Golden Immortal upon the ground of lapis lazuli.

Praising those who uphold this sutra, their fruition is most perfect; rejoicing in those who hold its name, their efficacy is foremost. Suddenly, the dusty mind is washed clean; suddenly, the dusty mind is washed clean.

One must personally recite the name of Amitābha;
he has repeatedly and earnestly exhorted us with his compassionate vows. Deep and vast is the sea of suffering; binding and heavy are the debts of karma.
Amidst clamor and bustle, one wanders through saṃsāra a thousand times over. Hasten to board the vessel that returns to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.

From time to time, pay homage to the ancient Buddhas who look down with compassion. Far and wide, along the ancient path to the West, dwell forever in the Land of No-Birth to realize the true teaching.

Who among those in their robes recognizes the priceless pearl? How could it have been cast adrift at the ends of the earth? With the talent for governance and the power of thought, one cuts through the clouds and mists.
A hundred years of spring grass and dew; wealth and honor are flowers by the roadside.
I sigh for Jambudvīpa—a mere theater of play. I laugh at deluded people who give rise to false imaginings, busily rushing day and night for the sake of a speck of a snail’s horn or the head of a fly.
Day after day within the Hall of Drunken Flowers; night after night, longing for the vermilion-dressed maids. One simply says that a hundred years will pass without ailment;
who could have known that in an instant the body would perish? To me, the affairs of the world are like the morning dew or the spring mist—suddenly, impermanence strikes! Aha!
A single human body is submerged in the surging waves of the river of craving.
Sages and worthies of all ages have praised the Western Land; its wondrous adornments are all contained within the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Amitābha, the Ancient Buddha, is the Great Physician King of Immeasurable Life. The Compassionate Ferry that receives and guides—yes, the Compassionate Ferry that receives and guides—delivers all sentient beings together.

I take refuge in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. I lament that saṃsāra’s suffering has no end. Fortunately, our Buddha extends a compassionate vessel to receive us. He speaks in detail of the adornments of the Pure Land, delivering the deluded masses from the fiery pit.
Within the five turbidities, how piteous and desolate it is! Alas for the three miserable realms; their sorrow and chill are beyond description. May I—
Each and every one returns to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, sitting upright upon lotus pedestals. Alas!
For this reason, I grieve for the multitude and proclaim it with my utmost voice. Aha! How could I ever manage to transform Jambudvīpa into the Flower Treasury World?
In a frantic rush; this floating life is like a flash of lightning. How agonizing! One wanders through the cycle of rebirth a thousand times. Waves surge on and on; the sea of suffering is boundless.
With every single thought, who is willing to recite the name of Amitābha? Most pitiable are those who, for no reason, are dragged by the bonds of desire and lust.

When impermanence arrives, one fears only that the kite’s string will snap. The four elements separate and myriad karmas entangle us. Our grievances and offenses lead to ten thousand sufferings in the hells.
A thousand [years] pass. Hanging on by a thread. The Eyes of the Compassionate Honored One of Ultimate Bliss gaze out until they are worn through.
Like shuttle and loom, years and months are cast away. Alas, a hundred years have all been disturbed by flies and snails. That youthful vigor—by this day, both temples are thin and wispy.
Seeking fame and office, one peers into the ant-holes of others; worldly affairs are entirely like the dream of the deer or the banana tree. Sing!
Delicate and refined; dancing with slender waists. The furs and horses of the Five Tombs have long since faded into silence. There is no limit to impermanence; how can one escape it?
All grandeur and splendor accompany the weeds and brambles through the ages.

Lamenting fame and profit, they exhaust their human essence. Rejoicing in the other shore, today it has suddenly arrived. Listen to these words; every phrase is true, and all meanings are fundamentally profound and wondrous.
Suddenly awakening, my heart’s chambers are cleared and enlightened. From now on, I shall awaken from this "Yellow Millet Dream. I shall erase the splendors of sound and form with a single stroke.
One must practice early; do not let Old Yan issue his summons to invite you away.
The weight of their kindness is like a mountain; even five tripods of sacrificial meat and three types of livestock would not suffice to repay it.

For this reason, they strike through the five-colored imperial edicts with a single stroke of the brush.

(Chā) Plain rice is better than delicacies; a patched robe is like embroidery. Earth and heaven are my dwelling; why need I construct a great mansion?
Therefore, I have struck through my house and fields all at once. My learning flows like a vast ocean;
its literary brilliance shoots toward the Dipper and Ox constellations. I move through the midst of a hundred arts; for a single measure of wine, I compose a thousand poems. (Chā!
Brocade fills my breast—there is no need for boastful words. Yet, in the presence of life and death, not even half a character can save me.
For this reason, I have struck through all worldly fame and literature with a single stroke.
In summer’s appreciation and spring’s excursions, pleasures abound within the halls of song and dance; yet amidst misty rain and flowers, chess and wine betray one's kin and friends.

though dwelling among humans, they possess five kinds of deformed appearances; they are beset by anxiety, suspicion, alarm, and fear, and suffer many calamities and illnesses.
These are the roots of sin from past lives and the karmic causes of this life. To cast off this base shell, one must cultivate realization. Contemplate the rapidity of impermanence. No...
Always swift, one should be diligent and energetic; with a focused and pure mind, do not be negligent. Moment by moment, let the mind remain undisturbed.
The Lotus Land is as close as the rising sun.
In the cool, secluded bamboo courtyard, by a quiet window, leisurely re-examine the scriptural texts. Turn westward toward Sukhāvatī; this is the teaching of Kāśyapa.

I admonish you with bitter words: he has merely been deluded by mistaking the reflection for the head. Having turned his back on his father and left home, he has yet to receive news of returning to his native land;
therefore, I instruct him to take up the Name and go back. Do not be negligent; it depends solely upon the purity of one's own single thought. It is the ground of lapis lazuli.
With every speck of dust purified, I am moved by the Western Honored One. At all times, I shall diligently invite him; let me not fail the grace of the Supreme Person.
This ephemeral life is but a single illusory body. Do not be deluded regarding its causes. True and true, play and play—originally there is no fixed state. One must return to the Correct.

Accord with worldly conditions and respond according to circumstances; do not allow yourself to mistakenly enter the battle-array that bewilders the soul. Once this human body is lost, it is difficult to regain. A traveler’s sojourn...

As the slanting sun sets and the waters flow away, my sorrow deepens; returning to the source cannot yet be entrusted to the lamp of the Dharma. This is the mirror for those lost on the way.

A lamp in a dark room; returning home is near. It is just like a potent medicine that dispels the nature of delusion. As this lamp is transmitted throughout the great earth, it shall surely be inexhaustible.
I only pray that the gateway of the True Dharma may circulate widely, so that every person may enter the realm of the Lotus.

How truly lamentable! The people of this world suffer for food and clothing; they burn with the fever of profit and fame. Clutching at a single broken thread, they pine for their "A-iao" (their beloved).
How could they know that one day the dream will awaken and the shadow will vanish? How bitter it is! On the road to the Yellow Springs, one stands alone in desolation;
looking up, there is nothing but weariness. Such refined elegance and heroic spirit—when it comes to this point, it all falls away, leaving nothing but a scene of sorrowful mourning.
How painful it is that life in Jambudvīpa is so short! One rushes about in vain toil for fame and profit. Alas for Nanke (The South-Cot), where dreams are brief and the dawn comes too soon.
Youthful faces age all too easily; do not boast of your youth. Do not linger in the splendor of the halls amidst the laughter of the crowd.

Though you may wield power over the wealthy and noble, you commit every manner of boundless karmic transgression. How could you know that impermanence lurks in the shadows, making no distinction between morning and evening? In a mere instant—
The engraved talisman has arrived. You should know that the sea of suffering is vast and boundless; you must cultivate the Way early, lest you wait until you are buried in the wild grasses.

For over sixty years, this single verse of "Manchuang Yanman Tingfang" (Flower Garland Adorned Courtyard) has been but a fleeting spring dream. Upon awakening, the millet was already cooked. What value is there in these floating glories and illusory shadows?
What a fine scene! With cold eyes, one lightly pierces through it. Suddenly turning over, one snaps the silken tether.
Let children and grandchildren perform their plays; there is no need to watch to the end. A handful of thatch upon the green mountains—a livelihood for the remainder of one's life.
Make other arrangements; simply pass the time according to conditions. Wash the bowl, burn incense, and first send the mind back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Enjoying carefree wandering—precious.
The trees are cool and refreshing; how truly pitiable! Turning my head to look back, the ocean of karma stretches vast and boundless.
From the present dynasty, Huangfu Shifang composed the *Verses on the Twelve Hours*.

At dawn, during the hour of Yin (3–5 AM), the regular Buddhist recitation takes place at the break of day. With but a single moment’s effort and ten invocations, one can transcend the cycle of birth and death.
Death leads to sinking into the depths of saṃsāra. This Dharma is rare; its subtlety is difficult to discourse upon. Rebirth [in the Pure Land] takes faith alone as its cause.

If you can receive this with open mind and without doubt, you are one who has received a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) for many lifetimes. The sun rises in the morning; the dew on the grass dries easily, and man grows old with ease.
Try carefully reflecting upon your kinsmen and friends: how many before your eyes are now buried in fragrant grass? If you wish to practice the Way, you must do so while there is still time.
Early morning. A single moment of time is a priceless treasure. If you are unwilling to recite the name of Amitābha during your leisure, you will surely suffer in vain at the moment of death.

High noon. When humans move from one dwelling to another, they invariably choose their neighbors; do not seek karmic rewards from gods or humans, for when your life ends, it is difficult to avoid sinking back into the cycle of rebirth.
Born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, becoming a Cakravartin King—though such pleasures may be fleeting, they are not the ultimate truth. I exhort you: [to seek the Way].
You should recollect the Buddha and seek the Western Land; you shall forever become one who dwells in carefree liberation.

At the hour of *yuzhong* (the fifth watch), when the smoke of cooking rises everywhere at the time of eating, eat your fill of rice to satisfy your hunger. Cultivate yourself to bring an end to birth and death.

A child remembers its mother, and a mother remembers her child; ultimately, the effort rests entirely within oneself. Sacrificing body and mind, behold the King of Vows. One hundred thousand [verses].

one turns instead toward the long journey and undergoes bitter toil. No talk of Chan, no brandishing of the fly-whisk; with every thought, Amitābha is made the constant master.
Although the body has not yet left Saṃsāra, the spirit already dwells within the Lotus Land. Before the sun sets—six snakes.
Sharing a single room is truly fearsome; how many times have you appeared and vanished in Jambudvīpa? Through many lifetimes, one still fails to distinguish between the clear and the turbid.

Turn your head sharply! Wash away the dust from your mind! Human life is impermanent—do not avoid this truth. Let the word "death" be constantly suspended above your brows. Only then will you perceive the flavor of the Western Land.
At the hour of Shēn (3–5 p.m.), sigh: "This human body is like a turning wheel. If this body does not [turn toward the West]...
If you do not attain liberation in this life, toward what other birth shall you turn to deliver this body? Do not let it slip away; do not remain complacent. How many beings bear horns or scales!

Though the compassion of a thousand Buddhas is vast, they cannot save them; through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they sink into delusion and decay. The sun sets in the hour of You (the West).
Reflecting back upon other lights, they do not endure for long. How laughable are the fools who gaze only at what is before them! Do you know the great matter of birth and death?

Foul wealth and idle tea and wine deceive ordinary people into wandering all day long; they have no leisure to recite the name of Amitābha, and when the days and months come to an end, their hands are empty and bound.
At dusk, in the hour of the Dog (戌), a single lamp illuminates the night chamber as one goes up to bed.
Parting from socks and shoes, the soul and dreams drift in a darkness as black as lacquer. Alas for the human body, so easily lost! To escape the cycle of rebirth, one must recite the Buddha’s name;
boundless karmic obstructions will vanish in an instant. The Buddha’s light is as bright as a thousand suns.
At the hour of Ren (9–11 p.m.), wealth, nobility, and fame do not endure forever; the dream of the yellow millet on the pillow has not yet awakened, and deluded passions still persist.
I grieve for a thousand years. I have been negligent and complacent, falling into indolence. If even one breath does not return, I shall repent for kalpas beyond measure.

I have brought shame upon the King of Vows from the Western Land, who from afar extends his golden arm with grace like the sea. At the hour of the rat, midnight, the pure and the defiled manifest their forms, dividing self and other.

It is not the bitter torments of this Sahā world that cause one to lose heart and weary of birth and death; rather, it is because one has already developed weary detachment. Once weary and detached, one must know how to find rest.
Upon the golden ground, bliss is beyond compare. For whose sake do afflictions arise before one’s eyes? They are all merely messengers urging one to prepare for the journey to the West.
At the hour of the Cock (1–3 a.m.), if you wish to be reborn there, who can restrain you? It is precisely within the field of afflictions that one should cultivate the practice of Buddha-recitation.

One must teach the mind to respond to the mouth, remaining free from right and wrong, and devoid of affirmation and negation. In all matters, follow conditions as they arise; what have I to do with them?

neither going west nor departing elsewhere, I vow that my aspirations shall be fulfilled at last.
By the Buddha's grace, I have fortunately encountered his vast renown; I must return to the West with all haste in this one life.
If I do not exert my full strength in this lifetime, I shall enter the womb again and fall back into ignorance.
Casting aside fame, profit, sorrow, and joy—nothing is more vital to oneself than this single point. Sever the cords of attachment with the sword of wisdom;
contemplate the Seven Essays of Yunqi ten thousand times over.
Diligently cultivate pure deeds and recite mantras; the myriad practices have always originated from a single source. According to circumstances and timing, employ skillful means;
with every thought, dedicate the merit to assist others in returning to the origin.
Boarding the vessel of great vows to cross the mundane world, the thoughts of self-benefit and benefiting others are one and the same. First borrow a branch to rest until the lotus realm is secure;
once your feathers are full, you may fly back as you please.
Having seen through the conditions of worldly dust, weariness and renunciation arise; with right mindfulness firmly maintained, one settles into a single practice.
Advancing directly with valor and without turning back, even if one resides at the lower grade, one must still strive.
As soon as the Buddha’s name is invoked, the hordes of Māras invade; how can they be subdued? Only by reaching single-mindedness. When mouth and ear communicate, the mind responds with the hand;
one must trace and seek each distinct syllable of the Muni.

At this temporary juncture (the second month of the Guiyou year), one must maintain the original resolve of the Uninterrupted [Samādhi]. This especially depends on the single thought-moment of the present being fused with reality.

It is truly lamentable that although Master Su Dongpo’s testimony remains as evidence—having constantly carried an image of Amitābha Buddha with him and claiming to be reborn in the Western Pure Land—he was unable to exert himself and abandon his former attachments.

Lord Gong (Suzhou Lord Gong) seemed to have been intent upon the Pure Land. However, according to the *Nianlu* (Record of Annals), when Lord Gong reached Changzhou and his illness became critical as he was about to draw his last breath, he heard Guanxian leave Lin and call out loudly into his ear, "Duanming, you must not forget!

Lord Gong said, "The Western [Pure Land] is certainly not non-existent, but one cannot apply effort here. Qian Shixiong said, "It is precisely because of your usual practice, Master, that at this moment you must apply effort. He replied, "To apply effort is itself an error. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
(This shows that Lord Su ultimately failed to apply effort at the time of death and could not attain rebirth; it is truly lamentable.)
Most feared is acting with haste at the last moment; when rushing about, it is difficult to complete the recitation of mantras. It relies entirely upon the power of the four great names;
hold them with single-minded devotion, and the responsive voice will arise.

Most feared is the confusion of consciousness at the final moment; the tongue becomes stiff and breath is difficult to sustain. Were it not for single-minded devotion cultivated in daily life, how could one rely on the provisions to journey to the West?
Most feared is the last-moment mind that fears death; as one hurries to and fro, myriad conditions encroach. Firmly maintain right mindfulness, always returning to the One;
gallop westward with vigor, applying deep effort.

The principle of the self-nature of mind alone is difficult to clarify; the analogies of water, fire, mirrors, and reflections are precise. When mindfulness reaches the single mind, the mind and the Buddha merge;

at that moment, the Buddha will naturally come to welcome you. (Zen practitioners often say, "The Pure Land is but the mind alone; how could there be any further Pure Land? Amitābha is one's own self-nature; there is no need to seek another Amitābha. These words seem plausible yet are erroneous.

This has been repeatedly clarified by the ancient masters, whose intent is profoundly deep and subtle. It is difficult for ordinary beginners to comprehend at once. Only Layman Longshu has provided a discourse with both principle and evidence that is relatively clear. I have respectfully read it.)

My late grandfather recorded the analogies of water, fire, and the mirror from the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*. He stated that the mirror’s possession of the natures of both water and fire is a metaphor for the power of the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by sentient beings.

The necessity of relying on the light of the sun and moon to illuminate it is a metaphor for the power of Amitābha’s compassionate light to gather and sustain beings. The fact that the pearl and the moxa can respectively draw forth water and fire is a metaphor for the power of faith and the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Thus, one comes to know that the self-nature is solely mind; it is not a matter of relying on empty contemplation.

If one can indeed focus the mind and practice pure cultivation until reaching the state of "single-mindedness without distraction," then this mind and this nature will restore their original state and merge into one with the Buddha. At the time of death, one will naturally be able to see the Buddha. This is just like drawing forth the light of the sun and moon—it is not the pearl or the moxa itself that possesses the light.
Focus intently. If one were forced into water or fire within a mirror, although the mirror possesses the natures of water and fire, how could it spontaneously produce water or fire?
If even a slight trace of attachment remains undiscarded, one fears being pulled by it at the critical moment.

To escape this *Sahā* world, one must exhaust the mind; the discourse of Master Cigong (Yang Cigong of the Song dynasty) permits this further clarification: "If attachment is not profound, one will not be born in *Sahā*; if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī. Now, regarding Sukhāvatī...

To say that birth must necessarily arise from a single thought is indeed a profound truth. Yet, if one wishes to depart from this Sahā world, even the presence of a single attachment that has not been eliminated may prevent one from breaking free from the net of worldly existence. This applies not only to those with heavy attachments; it should be said: "If attachment is not eliminated, one will not depart from the Sahā world."
[This version] seems even more refined.
*Layered Progression and Pressing Verses* (September, Guiyou Year):
With so much karma, I constantly fear losing this human body; Even if one obtains a human body, it is but a pit of fire. To emerge from this pit of fire, there is no other way...
Method: When the wind and sails meet the current, one is born in the Land of Bliss.

That Land of Bliss is not far away; it lies in the holding of the Name. One must understand that the holding of the Name values single-mindedness. How can one attain single-mindedness without interruption?
By threading together every drop of dripping water, one’s application of effort becomes profound.
Self-Exhortation (First Month of the Bingzi Year): The world of endurance (*Sahā*;
translated as "endurable") is unbearable; I pray you leave it quickly. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is truly delightful; I pray you hasten toward the West.
Do not practice meditation; do not read the sutras. Use this single method to cure the illness: hold the Great Name. Holding the Name will surely [save you].
Rebirth [in the Pure Land]. The Buddha said: "How could I deceive you? When the mind is pure, the land is also pure; why then doubt the guidance [of the Buddhas]?

If faith is deep and vows are earnest, yet all affairs cause agitation and the mind flies about in distraction—if one does not attain birth in this life, regret will be difficult to remedy for eternal kalpas.
Heaven! Why do You not grant me a realm for quiet cultivation? I alone am beset by worldly toil without end. Thus he turned his thoughts.

The Jade Maidens of Heaven do not encounter afflictions nor feel weary of them; they merely lament that their natures are stagnant and difficult to liberate, and they resent their own heavy obstructions and deep delusions.
Awaken yourself by yourself; let the mind rely upon the sound, and with every sound, hold fast and guard it without losing it.
With every word, reflect back with sincerity and do not deceive yourself. Like a cat catching a mouse or a hen brooding her eggs, focus on this and release that.
It is always present here. The pillar-inscription states:
"Affection does not cease; one does not depart from Sahā. When anger, joy, fear, and anxiety do not attain their proper balance, they all..."
Because craving has not yet been forgotten, brandish the sword of wisdom once and do not linger in the realm of objects.
When mindfulness is unified and non-arising, one reaches the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Whether facing emptiness or leisure, afflictions or slander, gain or loss, unify the mind in all things.
When such mindfulness becomes fully matured, the Buddha and the mantra beads will illuminate both simultaneously, responding spontaneously to the capacity of the practitioner.

To practice mindfulness of the Buddha, one must necessarily cease discursive thoughts; to eliminate discursive thoughts, one must necessarily practice mindfulness of the Buddha. This is called "attacking with mindfulness through mindfulness.
To cultivate purity, one must first purify the mind; to attain a pure mind, one must necessarily cultivate purity. This is called "purity being evoked by purity."
Always maintain such faith; always cultivate such practice (the words of Master Xingce).
Nothing obstructs oneself more than craving; nothing conceals oneself more than doubt (the words of Master Boting).
